The series of five numbers on the left-hand side indicates the location of the key term within the primary texts. In the case of the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (SV),...
In the HB and the VN,
the first three figures indicate the page number.

And the final two figures indicate the line number (for example, 10). In the case of the *Pramāṇavārttika* (PV) and the *Nyāyabindu* (NB), the second figure indicates the chapter number and the final three [figures indicate the verse number].
The figures indicate the *kārikā* or *sūtra* number (for example, PV02232 = PV,
the *Pramāṇasiddhi*-chapter, verse 232; NB03015 = NB, the *Parārthānumāna*-chapter, sūtra 15).
In the case of the *SP*, the last two figures indicate the *kārikā* number (for example,
3). In this database,
Sentences are artificially divided into word-units,
although they involve a phonetic fusion or union in the basic texts. Furthermore,
Compound words are divided into their shortest constituent elements (a hyphen is used to indicate that hyphenated elements originally form a compound word).
with the following exceptions: 3.1. The prefix a-;
*Dur-* and *nih-* remain undivided,
regardless of their attachment to [a following vowel].
words or compound words. 3.2. Suffixes forming adverbs, for example, -vat.
...are divided; however, [those] suffixes forming possessive adjectives...
For example, the suffixes *-vat* and *-mat* remain undivided, as do [the following] terms:
Compounds ending in suffixes such as *-dha*, *-vidha*, or *-prakāra* following a numeral likewise remain undivided.
3.3. Compound words with the suffixes -ta/-tva or -bhava/-bhūta fundamentally [denote]...
Remain undivided. For example:
*kāryakāraṇabhāva* / *-bhūta* / *-tā*.
3.4. Compounds with *evam-*:
that,
thus,
other, beyond.
The word-initials *yatha-*, *su-*, and *sva-* fundamentally remain undivided. For example:
of such a nature, arising from that, produced in such a way, and dependent on others.
According to reality,
according to its own nature, the state of being well-knowing, and intrinsic nature.
3.5. Certain compound words that are regarded as technical terminology also remain undivided. For example: *agnihotra*, *ayogavyavaccheda*.
presumption, word-meaning,
ultimate reality,
and non-presuppositional negation.
contradictory deviant reason,
immediately preceding condition,
transformation of the continuum.
1. Universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
2. Essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*).
3. [The term] *samāsa*. 4. Those words whose initial member is subject to the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*) (e.g., *-d-*).
The forms of the items (e.g., *-d hetu-*) are cited in their original shape for the purpose of utilizing this database to construct a KWIC index.

Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
Homage to Samantabhadra, whose form is profound and sublime, who has shaken off the net of conceptual construction, and whose radiance pervades everywhere.
For the most part, people are attached to the vulgar and lack the strength of wisdom;
they do not merely fail to benefit from well-spoken words, but are even filled with malice due to the stains of envy.
Therefore, let us not even think for a long time that this is not a benefit to others;
rather, let our longing be fixed upon this, as it is a passion increased by the practice of well-spoken words.
Since the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful relies upon inference, and because there are conflicting views regarding it, [the author] says the following in order to establish it:
"The reason (*hetu*) is that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds."
Because of the restriction of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), those others are fallacious reasons (*hetv-ābhāsa*). //1//
The "subject" (pakṣa) is the locus of the property (dharmin),
because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part;
[the opponent claims] there is no reason for such metaphorical usage.
If this is argued, it is not so; for the purpose is the negation of all properties of all subjects.
Since it is a part of that [negation], it is for the sake of understanding those subjects and properties that are fit for such figurative designation (*upacāra*). Thus...
And thus, there is the avoidance of [the fallacies of] being visible by the eye (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, even though the locus of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is established by the word "property" (*dharma*), the establishment of the *sādhyadharmin* (the subject of the thesis) occurs through proximity, by virtue of the capacity of the term "property-bearer" (*dharmin*).

If this is argued, it is not so; for there is also proximity to the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*). Since its existence is established in the subject of the example through the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), the mention of the "subject" (*dharmin*) entails the inclusion of the "subject of the probandum" (*sādhyadharmin*).
Even though [the presence of the reason] in similar instances is already established, a further statement might be suspected to have the purpose of restriction (niyama)—
just as, even though the exclusion from dissimilar instances is established, there is the statement of its non-existence in the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva).
The statement of the thesis (pakṣa) is for the purpose of establishing the meaning through implication and for the sake of avoiding the burden of [repeated] comprehension;
since the property (dharma) belongs to the thesis— its...

If it is argued that a qualifier is "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) because it does not apply elsewhere when dependent upon [a specific] qualification, we say no; for the qualifier functions by way of excluding non-connection (ayogavyavaccheda), as in the case of "Caitra is an archer."
It is not by way of excluding connection with another,
as we shall explain in the case of "Pārtha is the archer.
That part is its property (*tad-dharma*).
This is due to the intention of the speaker;
it is not a part of that [whole],
because the word "pakṣa" does not denote the aggregate.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists either in the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) wherever [the pervaded is], or in the presence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) only where [the pervader is]. By this, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), as well as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), are stated to be ascertained by their respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
These three reasons are characterized by effect, essential nature, and non-perception;
for example: "There is fire here, because of smoke."
This is a tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*. In a particular location, there is no jar because of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception.
If [an object] were non-existent, it would necessarily be non-perceptible, and not otherwise;
therefore, it is said that [the reason applies] to that which has attained the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).
Therein, two [types of reasons] establish a positive entity (*vastu*), while one is a reason for negation (*pratiṣedha-hetu*).
For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one thing does not deviate from another; and that—

If it is argued that because [the probans] has that as its essence, there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans when they have that same essence, we reply: No; for we shall explain that this is due to the conceptual construction of a distinction between properties (*dharma*).
And so it has been said: "This entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference proceeds by means of a distinction between property and locus that is mounted upon the intellect."

The distinction between property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*) is produced by the form of the intellect (*buddhy-ākāra*) and does not exist in the object itself; for conceptual distinctions (*vikalpa-bheda*), being independent, do not have the object as their basis. If there were a cognition of the object based on an object imagined by those [distinctions], there would be no attainment of the actual object at all. This is because [the object] is the effect...
Furthermore, there is the essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*),
based on the fact that [the effect] has that as its nature or arises from it.
These two types of inferential cognition are direct [cognitions] when they do not arise otherwise and do not manifest anything other than that [object].
Furthermore, because they arise from that [object], those two [inference and verbal testimony] are non-deviant with respect to it, just like perception.
For even in the case of perception, its validity consists precisely in its non-deviance from the object; for in the absence of that [object], there would be a deception regarding it.
And what other [cause] could there be for the non-deviation [of one thing from another] than its arising from that?
For there is no rule of coexistence for things whose natures are not dependent [on one another],
unless it be because of that arising.
The effect is the indicator; in every respect, the relationship between the indicated and the indicator arises from the relationship between the produced and the producer. No;
for [the relationship] exists even in the absence of that [causal production], since it occurs through origination from that.
Because there is no such restriction. Therefore:
"In relation to a cause, whatever effects are invariably concomitant with certain essential properties [of that cause], [those effects may be inferred from those properties].
Regarding these...
It is the cause because of the necessity of being its effect; that is, by those very properties (dharmas) without which it does not come to be.
If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of partial production and production, we say: no.

Because it is accepted that there is the apprehension of specific qualities produced by that [cause], and because the general properties (sāmānya) are themselves qualified by the specific limiting conditions (upādhi) of the marks (liṅga); therefore, when one intends to express the general property without such qualification, [the definition] is not desired, as it would lead to over-extension (vyabhicāra).
Even an entity exists in its own nature when that nature conforms to the mere existence [of the entity]. //2//
The term "cause" (hetu) carries over [from the previous context].
For the identity (tādātmya) of an object depends solely upon that [object] itself,
and not upon anything else.
Because there is no necessity for that which has not yet come into being to exist later when those [causes] are present, and because causes deviate from their effects,
there is a non-operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Non-apprehension has non-engagement as its result when [the object] is absent;
it has the negation of the cognition, the term, and the conventional usage regarding an existent as its result.
"Because these [non-existents] are preceded by apprehension"—
this is the common form of the reasons for the negation and affirmation of existence and non-existence. For instance,
existence is indeed apprehension itself, characterized by the fitness of the object, or that which is based upon it.
The occurrence of cognition; from that follows the occurrence of the linguistic usage of the term "existent" for what is real. And for non-existent things, their non-existence is non-apprehension.
Some [cognition] has non-existence as its result, depending on a distinction in its cause. //3//
The reason is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Its distinction is the qualification that [the object] has attained the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta-sattva*).

In this case, since non-existence is established through the mark (liṅga) of non-apprehension, the absence of apprehension would itself have to be established by another non-apprehension; thus, due to infinite regress, there would be no cognition [of it]. Alternatively, if the absence of apprehension could occur without another non-apprehension, then likewise—
Existence might even be non-existence;
it would be a purposeless non-apprehension.
Or, [it might be established] by the apprehension of something else.
"Non-apprehension is established" means that non-apprehension is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, why is non-existence not established by the existence of something else?

Furthermore, when such non-apprehension itself constitutes the non-existence of non-existent things, then, even though the object is established, one who— due to delusion— does not understand the cognitions, words, and conventional usages regarding the non-existent that pertain to that object, [is instructed] by the demonstration of the object.
At that time, [the inference] is set in motion:
"This is a cow, because it consists of a collection of features such as a dewlap and so forth.
In this way, even the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) is refuted.
Even when an object is being apprehended, one observes that there are those who do not apprehend the subject [of that apprehension].

Thus, these two types of non-apprehension are equal in their result— the negation of the conventional usage of "existence"— by virtue of the presence or absence of the cause for their respective opposites.
In one case, due to doubt, and in the other,
due to error; therein, the former is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it serves to negate the conventional usage of existence.
It has been stated [that the first type of perception] is not useful for the observation of exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth,
because it results in doubt. The second type,
however, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this context, because its result is certainty.

And that non-apprehension of the object, which consists in the absence of perceptible things, is fourfold due to the difference in its application: the establishment of two contradictory effects, and the non-establishment of two causal factors. (4)
Whatever negation there may be, it is all due to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). For it is established in two ways:
either by the affirmation of something else or by the negation [of that very thing].
In the case of a prescription, would that which is contradictory be prescribed, or that which is non-contradictory?
For if a non-contradictory thing is prescribed, there is no contradiction regarding its coexistence.
There is no negation.
Even in the case of a contradictory [thing], because there is no non-perception [of it], the contradiction is not established.
For instance, when that which has unlimited causes exists, even if another thing is present...
The cognition of contradiction arises from non-existence,
and that [non-existence] results from non-apprehension;
[contradiction consists in] the mutual exclusion of apprehension.
Alternatively, there is a contradiction between having the characteristic of being stationary and [the opposite], just like permanence and impermanence.
In that case as well, it is simply said that by the perception of one, there is the non-perception of the other.
Otherwise, since non-existence is not established through the perception of something unprohibited,
non-perception is indeed established when the absence of one thing is proven by the negation of another,
because negation is of the nature of non-perception.
In that case as well, when there is a negation of another object— whether it be of cause and effect or of experience—
since experience therein is unimpeded, its...
How can it be established that "in the absence [of the effect], there must not be another [cause]"?
Furthermore, even in the case of the non-perception of an effect, causes do not necessarily possess that [effect]; so how can there be an absence of that [cause]?
Therefore, it is only the non-perception of the cause that leads to the cognition of non-existence;
however, the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is itself non-existence.
In that case, only the subject (viṣayin) is established.
Even here, when one states the absence of the pervaded (vyāpya) through the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpaka), then it is indeed an absence (abhāva).
This non-apprehension of the object of negation is fourfold according to the distinction of its application:
by the establishment of the contradictory, as for example, "there is no cold touch."
In this context, the establishment of the contradictory of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhasiddhi*) by means of fire should be understood as follows:
"There is no sensation of frost here, because of fire.
An example by means of the establishment of a contradictory effect (*viruddhakāryasiddhi*) is: "There is no cold..."
00604 Here, there is contact because of smoke.
By way of the non-establishment of the reason (*hetv-asiddhi*), as in: "There is no smoke here because there is no fire.
By way of the non-establishment of the essential nature (*svabhāva-asiddhi*), as in: "There is no smoke here because it is not perceived."
By this, the non-establishment of the nature of the pervader has been explained, as in: "There is no *śiṃśapā* here because of the absence of trees.
And in all such cases of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) that establishes non-existence, it applies only to those things whose nature is perceptible.
The establishment and non-establishment of those [things] and their opposites should be understood [in this way], because for others there is no proof of non-existence through contradiction.
If, even by the perception of a contradictory effect, non-existence—
Why is it that the establishment [of an effect] is not accomplished through the perception of its cause?
When the perception of a cause that is contrary to that [intended cause] is employed, it is inconclusive provided there is no mutual contradiction between the two causes. (5)

For example: "There is no sensation of cold here because of the wood. Furthermore, when two causes are in opposition, they serve as indicators [of the absence], as in: "He does not have specific symptoms such as horripilation, because of the presence of fire."

Because it is a specific [effect], by this same principle it should be understood that the cognition of the absence of an effect contrary to it is also stated through its effect; for example: "This place does not contain a person possessed of specific qualities such as horripilation, because there is smoke."

And since this establishment of the opposite [of the probandum] through the very non-establishment of the reason was already indicated previously, this non-apprehension is eightfold due to the different modes of formulation. Among those, regarding what was stated as the apprehension of an incompatible effect:
It is accepted that even in the case of a contradictory effect, there is a dependence on place, time, and so forth;
otherwise, it would be inconclusive, like ashes used as a means to prove the absence of cold.
But then, how is that inference of the production of an effect from a complete cause included within the three types of reasons?
[That] production of an effect which is inferred by means of a complete cause— how does it fit?
Because it does not depend on any other entity, that is described as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva). //7//
Just as this [effect] does not depend on anything else when [the causes] are present, so too the nature of an entity is necessarily bound to that alone;
for in that case, the production of the effect from the complete collection of causes occurs solely [from them].
The occurrence [of the effect] is inferred from the inference of the causal complex's capacity to produce the effect.
And since this capacity is invariably concomitant with the mere presence of the causal complex, it is inferred as being of the very nature [of that complex].
But what is the reason that the effect itself is not inferred from the causal complex?
Because a causal obstruction can occur, there is inconclusiveness regarding the effect in relation to the continuous transformation of the potencies of the causal complex. //8//
For causal substances do not produce their own effect merely by being complete;
this is because the production of an effect depends upon the transformation of the potencies (*śakti*) born from that completeness.
Furthermore, during this interval, the possibility of an obstruction (*pratibandha*) exists; therefore, there is no inference of the effect.
However, because capacity does not depend upon another substance, inference is not contradicted;
[this applies] to each subsequent [instance].
This causal complex is capable of producing an effect through the transformation of its potency (*śakti*),

because there is no other condition to be depended upon for that transformation of potency. Since the production of potency has as its cause only that which belongs to its own preceding class, the capacity of the causal complex does not depend on anything else.

Thus it is said. But how, then, is there the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth by means of another thing, such as taste (*rasa*), which stands in neither a causal nor a non-causal relationship to it?
That too is the cognition of color-form and so forth—which, though not [directly] present—by virtue of its dependence upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
By means of inference from the property of the cause, like the transformation of smoke and fuel. //9//
In that case, it is precisely the cause in such a state that is inferred.
For the taste-cause produces taste when it possesses its active capacity and is accompanied by the material cause and the auxiliary conditions.
It is like fire and smoke, which arise from a specific transformation of fuel, taking up a particular cause and cooperative conditions. For it is thus:
Through the operation of its capacity,
by being directed toward the production of an effect from its own cause,
that very taste does not exist without another cause.
It is the cause for the activity of the causes of the appropriation of form;
it is also the cause for the activity of the appropriation of taste,
acting as a cooperative condition for the activity of the causes of the appropriation of form.
Therefore, since a taste has arisen from a cause of such a nature, by inferring that [cause] as it truly is, one infers the visible form.
In that case as well,
there is the movement of each past [moment],
but not of future ones, because of their deviation.
Therefore, this [inference] arises from the mark that is an effect. //10//
Therefore, there is no other cause that can serve as a means of cognition,
because for that which lacks an essential connection (*svabhāva-pratibandha*), there is an absence of the necessary rule of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*).
By this, the inference of rain and so forth from the emigration of ants, the transformation of fish, and the like has been explained;
even there, it is the transformation of the elements alone that is the cause of the rain.

[It is said: "The cause of disturbances such as those caused by ants and so forth. However, when an effect is inferred from an incomplete cause, that is *śeṣavat* [inference], because of its lack of capacity, like the inference of passion from the body. //11//
For only complete causes allow one to infer even the capacity [for an effect] in that which is incomplete, because what is incomplete is invariably incapable;
just as passion and so forth are inferred from the body, the sense faculties, and the intellect.

For attachment and the other afflictions are preceded by the dogmatic adherence to "self" and "what belongs to self," because all faults arise from being preceded by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*),
even though [the body and so forth] serve as their causes.
It is not that [the reason] has efficacy when standing alone;
even if its presence in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is not observed, doubt arises from the inference of the "remainder" (*śeṣavat*). Likewise...

The cognition of a cause based merely on not seeing [the effect] in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) due to the observation of the general nature of the effect is a semblance of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa), just like [inferring] passion from speech. //12//
For movement, speech, and so forth are not the effects of passion (*rāga*) and the like alone, because they have the general desire to speak (*vaktukāmatā*) as their cause.
If it is argued that this [desire to speak] is itself passion, we say no; since this is accepted [by us], nothing is contradicted.

It may be so. They say that passion (*rāga*) is an attachment of the mind directed toward objects consisting of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), which is projected by the views of permanence, pleasure, self, and what belongs to self;
but compassion and the other [immeasurables] are not like this, for they are otherwise.
We shall explain that [the meaning] is possible even from this.
In this regard, just as one who is passionate speaks, so too does one who is dispassionate; thus, there is no comprehension from mere speech alone.
Nor can it be established by means of a distinction,
because the underlying intention is difficult to discern and because all [reasons] are subject to deviation due to the confusion of conventional usage.
If it is argued that there is no supplementation [of words] because there is no purpose, we say no, because [the teaching] is for the sake of others.

If it is argued that it is not appropriate because [the Buddha] is free from passion (*vītarāga*), we say no, because he acts out of compassion (*karuṇā*). If it is argued that this very [compassion] is itself passion, [we reply: no.
This is accepted.

There is no fault because it arises from non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*). Even in the absence of the grasping of a self (*ātma-graha*), [compassion] is produced by the power of cultivation through the mere perception of specific forms of suffering.
Compassion certainly arises;
for instance, loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] have sentient beings, phenomena, and so forth as their objects.
These [mental states] are accepted as functioning through the repeated practice of their own kind, and they do not depend upon passion (*rāga*).
Passion and the like are not so, because they are absent when there is an absence of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*),
even in the case of one who is compassionate.
If it is argued that the undertaking is fruitless because there is no error [in one's perception], we say no;
for the welfare of others alone is intended as the fruit.
Because the fruit is characterized by desire,
it is faultless due to the complete absence of any superimposition of what is unreal.

If it were established that [the speaker] possesses faults by means other than that [inference], there would be nothing undesirable. However, if one were to infer those [faults] in another person simply because they are observed in the speaker himself, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Because of deviation; for what certainty is there that there is non-deviation here in the case of an inference from nothing else?
For speech would lead one to infer the desire to speak of a quality possessed by the instrument [of speech],
because speech is not observed in one who lacks the capacity to produce passion; otherwise, it has been stated that such an inference would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If passion is not employed [as a cause], how could its power be employed?
For if the power were employed, then that [passion] itself would be employed; yet it has been stated that this is not the case.
Therefore, it is only an effect that is invariably concomitant with its cause that allows for the inference of that cause.
Because of this necessary connection, it is not otherwise, even when there is no observation [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
For only the observation of one who sees all things could lead to the understanding of non-existence everywhere through the exclusion of observation.
Because even those things seen in such a manner are sometimes seen otherwise due to differences in place, time, and processing—
as is the case with *āmalaka* fruits.
By the sprinkling of milk, fruits become sweet;
yet they are not seen to be so very often.
Therefore, it would be appropriate for one such as me to say, "I am a speaker who possesses passion."
Because of the connection with the specific condition for the arising of passion— namely, the improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) consisting in the view of a self—
even then, the citation of the statement is pointless.
Therefore, non-perception in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not a valid reason (*ahetu*).
Nor is there non-deviation from the counter-example (vipakṣa) by mere non-perception;
for deviation is possible, just as in the case of rice being cooked in a pot. //13//
For even when one observes that [food] is mostly cooked, cooking is not established merely by its being inside the pot, because of the observation of deviation. However,
it would be so if it were of such a nature.
Those things which have the same causes for their ripening are "ripe.
Otherwise, this inference would be of the *śeṣavat* type and thus fallacious.

But what is this "remaining-like" (śeṣavat)? That [reason] for which the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is demonstrated by mere non-perception is called "remaining-like" because it is a cause of doubt. //14//

Since its exclusion from that [heterologous instance] is not certain, one might suspect its occurrence in the heterologue (*vipakṣa*), because the mere non-perception that serves as the proof for exclusion is a cause for doubt. Not every non-perception [establishes absence].
Therefore, by one who desires the exclusion of the other through the exclusion of one,
some essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) between the two must also be admitted; otherwise, it would not be indicative.
The reason would be [valid] because its certainty has been described by him in terms of all three forms,
through the exclusion of the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viparītārtha*), and the deviant (*vyabhicārin*) opposites. //15//

For when there is no obstruction, there is no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, by demonstrating that very [absence of obstruction], he states the ascertainment;
therein, by the ascertainment of positive concomitance, [the contrary] is excluded.
That constitutes the rejection of those [fallacies] belonging to that side:
namely, the inconclusive [reason] based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), its corresponding position, and the *śeṣavat* inference and so forth.

The phrase "of two" constitutes a negation of what is established for one alone. By the term "well-known," there is the exclusion of those cases where both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) are doubtful, namely the *śeṣavat* and the *asādhāraṇa* reasons.
Furthermore, otherwise, if there were no obstruction [to the relationship], one might [erroneously] establish a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) based on mere non-perception;

and as for that statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) regarding a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) that is deviant, it is as he said: "This is the rule—that both [the similar and dissimilar instances] must be stated—[otherwise] there would be the fallacies of the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."
Regarding "by way of the counter-argument":
the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is by way of the counter-argument against the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
for if that [reason] were not seen to have a result, it would be so.
If by that [reason] its non-observation in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is made known, then it is understood even when it is not explicitly stated. //16//
For he has no prior error of perception that could be removed by speech. If it is argued that memory is produced regarding what was not perceived, [we reply:
indeed, a perception that is not being experienced [cannot be recalled].
In that case, it is logical to establish the recollection [of the object] as being "without a constituent part" (anaṅga); however,
non-perception is simply the absence of perception, and it is sublated by perception.
But since that [non-existence] is already established in the absence of that [object], a statement for the sake of establishing it is pointless; for indeed,
[it is not possible] for one who does not perceive [the object].
If it is argued that the statement exists for the purpose of making it known that "it does not exist" to that extent, [we reply:

It is not the case that something simply does not exist merely because of the statement "it does not exist. For example, if that [non-existence] were being made known by some logical principle (*nyāya*), then it would be understood that "it does not exist. //17//
If one does not understand that "it does not exist" simply because one does not perceive it, then one will likewise not understand it from a verbal statement either;
for that [statement] also merely indicates non-perception.
And the non-perception of one thing [does not entail the non-existence of another].

It does not establish the absence of another [thing], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor does it become so simply by the statement "it does not exist" through that [absence], because that too would lead to an over-extension.
Therefore, how can it be established by a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)?
01212 The refutation of the inconclusive [reason]:
Therefore, by one who desires its exclusion, a logical justification must be stated for that [exclusion], on account of which it comes to be that "this is excluded from that. 01213
[Objection: But surely, in the absence of that [object], its exclusion is established because it is not perceived. [Response:
If cessation were to occur simply through non-perception, why would the *śeṣavat* inference be fallacious?
For example: "These fruits are ripe, or they have such a taste, because of the lack of distinction in their color, like those [fruits] on the same branch."
Or, [it may be argued] that it is like something already used because it possesses causal efficacy (*prabhavatva*).

Even in this case, since the entirety of what is intended to be proven is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*) is not observed in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*); so how could there be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*)?
Some say that the suspicion of sublation by perception constitutes a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is not so; for [the probans] is absent from the subject (*pakṣa*) under consideration.
If it is argued that "it might possibly be so," such a suspicion leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
because there would be no certainty of non-existence even in other cases.
The occurrence [of the reason] is the subverting proof (*bādhaka*). If there were no subversion by its non-occurrence, there would be a lack of confidence in all cases;
however, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established.
Thus, [the proof] likewise depends upon the ascertainment of non-existence;
for even if non-existence is established in some cases through non-perception, that which is not invariably concomitant with it [cannot establish non-existence] everywhere in its absence.

Because non-existence is not established and because of doubt, there is no negative concomitance; thus, the "remainder" (śeṣavat) inference is fallacious. Furthermore, even a reason that possesses negative concomitance might [be fallacious].
"This living body is not devoid of a self, because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of it lacking breath and so forth.
Since breath and such are not observed in things like jars which are seen to be devoid of a self, the cognition of the self would arise through the exclusion of those [selfless things].

Since non-existence is not established by the non-perception of the imperceptible, the selflessness of jars and other such things is not established; therefore, there is no exclusion of breath and so forth.
This is established through [our] own admission.
If this is so, how is the self established now? And for the opponent as well, how is the absence of self established without any means of valid cognition?

Furthermore, by accepting the distinction between that which possesses a self and that which lacks a self, and then asserting that [the absence] serves as a probans therein, one would be admitting that the existence of a self is based on scripture (*āgamika*).
It is not a matter of being inferable; therefore, even in the absence of perception,
the cessation of the self is not established.
Even if that [breath] were to cease, since there would be no obstruction to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth even when it has ceased in some instances,
its cessation is not established in all cases; therefore, it is not a probans.
Furthermore, that application of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) which occurs in cases such as "present in the similar class" (*sapakṣa*) or "absent," and so forth—
likewise to be illustrated according to the circumstances—
is also not to be stated as an application of non-establishment. //18//
It is precisely non-perception [that establishes it], because doubt arises from perception; since that [doubt] is absent when there is perception,
it follows from non-perception.
And thus, the doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would remain unavoidable.
If it is argued that it is indeed not avoided because of the statement "as appropriate" (*yathāyoga*), we say no.

However, because of such statements as "only that which expresses certainty regarding both [sides]," one might think that even when there is non-perception (*anupalambha*), there is no cessation of doubt; therefore, he states its refutation. Furthermore:
The exclusion of a particular [property] would be the cause [of its negation] because of non-perception.

Since audibility is also not perceived in either the eternal or the non-eternal, it would follow that there is an exclusion [from both], and thus it would be the cause for the exclusion of those [two].
For there is no exclusion other than the exclusion of that [object].

However, non-exclusion [of something] arises precisely from the lack of certainty regarding its exclusion from something else. For how could that which is ascertained as "not being present in a certain place" not lead one to understand the absence of that thing?
If it is argued that there is sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): even so,
there would be another means of valid cognition that sublates [the claim] of the exclusion of both,
because among things whose nature consists in mutual exclusion, the affirmation of one occurs through the exclusion of the other.
There is no negation [of existence], because affirmation and negation are contradictory.
Now, non-existence does not follow from mere non-perception. //19//
Non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this way, because contradiction is impossible.

Likewise, even in other cases, the sublation by another means of knowledge must be considered possible. If there were no possibility of contradiction for that which possesses the defining characteristics [of a valid cognition], then those very characteristics would be undermined.
If it is argued that there would be a lack of confidence in all cases,
because even regarding the object of inference, one observes contradictions between perception and inference, leading to the consequence of a general lack of confidence— [we reply]: No.
Because [the reason] is impossible in what has been stated,
and because that which is possible does not possess the characteristics [of that object],
there is no mention of the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
If it is argued that [the object] is accepted because it is not mentioned within the scope of inference,
we shall explain its scope.
Furthermore:
The observed lack of logical connection would also be non-contradictory to the unobserved tactile sensation. //20//
For if non-existence were established by non-perception,
as it has been said:
"If [there is] non-observation..."
A negation is made based solely on what has been observed;
yet even that is not tenable. How is it untenable?
Because non-existence is established through non-perception.
[Objection: But surely, since touch meets the conditions for perceptibility, its negation is indeed logical. [Reply: It is not logical.
Because there is no negation of the mere object that is the nature of what is perceived;
having apprehended earth and so forth in a general sense, he states this negation.

Furthermore, since a difference in touch is observed even when that [nature] is present in things such as cotton, stone, and sprouts, it must be possible for this [touch] to exist in some particular case; therefore,
it is improper to conclude [its non-existence] based on mere non-perception everywhere.
"Regarding the term 'negation':
thus, a certain teacher who asserts non-existence on the basis of non-perception has been criticized. Furthermore:"
Due to differences in location and other factors, potencies are seen to differ among substances.
Therefore, it is not logical to determine the presence of a potency in one place based on its observation elsewhere. (21)
If, by some means, there were non-deviation from that [reason] even for something that lacks an essential connection, merely because it is not observed in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa)—
then since certain substances are observed in certain places in certain ways, [what would prevent this?]
Furthermore, they are seen otherwise in other places;
just as certain medicinal herbs possess distinct tastes, potencies, and post-digestive effects depending on the specific field in which they grow.
Not otherwise; likewise, due to the differences in time and conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*),
and because they are not perceived as such by those in that location, all [things] are [established] in their true nature (*tattva*).
Those things that have become such are established [as they are],
because other qualities depend upon other causes;
however, in the absence of a specific cause, there would be inference.
Just as even a sentence whose author is unobserved is preceded by human refinement,
because there is no difference between such sentences [and those with known authors].
Since it is observed that persons employ all types of instruments,
it is not the case that persons lack specific reasons [for their actions], such that [the Veda] could be [considered] merely on account of some slight similarity to speech and the like.
Identity in all aspects would have to be inferred [from similarity],
because a distinction is observed among all qualities,
due to the perception of distinctions arising from differences in their cultivation (*saṃskāra*).
Likewise, because it is possible for another [cause] to exist,
and because there is no subverting reason (*bādhaka-hetu*) for an inference of impossibility, detachment (*vairāgya*) is not perceived;
and since the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is not established by means of the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).
Because there is an absence of any effect that is invariably concomitant with passion and the like;
and even if such effects were possible, their specific characteristics would be impossible to perceive.
And because such [statements] do not have the purpose of negation;
for sentences are not like that, because they possess a specific perceptible character (dṛśya-viśeṣatvāt).
Even if they were imperceptible, it would contradict the admission of their being of a different genus (vijātīyatva) since their specific characteristics would remain unobserved. Therefore—
Because specific qualities can be produced elsewhere as well;
and because there is no absence of the perceptible nature of words that are themselves perceptible.
Because the cause of error is absent,
and because error is not established due to the absence of any subverting factor.
Because the perception of a distinction among persons acts as a sublation [of such a claim],

it is not the same [as the case of words]. Furthermore, since a specific sentence, being of the nature of something else (parabhāva), does not possess that [person's] distinction, there would either be human agency for all things whose nature is non-distinct, or none at all.
Furthermore:
That very same non-perception which does not establish the non-existence of the self, clay, consciousness, and so forth—does that itself establish the absence of the [logical] reason? //22//
Furthermore, for one who takes non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this [self], the doctrine of the self (*ātmavāda*) would be without foundation;
for since the self is not perceived, its effects are not established.
However, in the case of the sense faculties and so forth...
Because the effect of consciousness is occasional, its establishment through dependence is stated as follows:
"It has some cause," but not that "it is of such-and-such a nature."
The effect of pleasure and so forth, established in this manner, does not support any [conclusive] point,
because one accepts that it possesses a cause by whatever means;
and thus, there is non-perception [of such a cause].
If it were indeed so for the self,
why would one who rejects that [self] by means of that [reasoning] be countered [by the objection] that "non-apprehension is not a proof"?

How could that which lacks a probans establish a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? For indeed, someone might— desiring to find consciousness in clay even though it is not perceived— assert its exclusion from speech and so forth on the grounds of non-perception.
Furthermore, another [argument] is that curd and so forth are distinct from milk and so forth because the state of being a composite (saṃghātatva) is not observed in them;
for what necessity is there here that things which are composites must necessarily exist for the sake of another?
There is indeed the perception of curds and so forth in milk and so forth, which constitutes an inference [of their potentiality], because they do not arise from that which lacks capacity.
Now, what is this "capacity"? It is that very entity itself.
Or is it something else entirely?
If it were the same thing, it would be perceived in that very same way, because there would be no distinction [between the two states].
If it is something else, how can that [original thing] exist when something else is present?
But [if one says] "it would be a mere metaphorical designation" (upacāra-mātra),
this is a mutual contradiction among these [positions].
Therefore, the nature [of the cause] is either a relation consisting of that alone, or it is the entity itself.
One should exclude [the former from] the latter,
just as a tree [excludes] a *śiṃśapā* tree; for it is only a certain particularity possessing branches and so forth that is [so designated].
Because it is well-established, that is its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
And how could an entity (bhāva) exist while abandoning its own intrinsic nature?
Because the very nature (svabhāva) is itself an entity, there is no deviation [from the probans] due to its essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha);
or else, the cause [is the probans] because of the non-deviation of the effect. //23//
The cause, by ceasing, causes the effect to cease;
otherwise, that would not even be its effect.

Once the relation of cause and effect is established, it restricts the essential nature [of things]; thus, in both cases, the exclusion [of one thing] occurs solely through the essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha).
Otherwise, how could the exclusion of one thing result in the exclusion of another?
A mortal who is traveling should not think, "I do not possess a horse. How much less so when he has already reached his destination? //24//
If [the universal] exists due to proximity, how can there be proximity for another?
Why should a mortal necessarily possess a cow simply because he possesses a horse? (25)
Therefore, it is solely due to an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) that a reason (*hetu*) makes known the probandum (*sādhya*).
And that [connection] is characterized either by identity with it (*tadbhāvalakṣaṇa*) or by origination from it (*tadutpattilakṣaṇa*);
this alone is the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*).
This is demonstrated by two examples.
Therefore, in the case of a negative example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), a locus (āśraya) is not necessarily required here;
for that [absence] is understood even from the statement: "In the absence of that, this is not. //26//
For this reason: "Indeed,
for one who does not perceive that [invariable relation], the presence of the effect and the presence of the cause are demonstrated by means of an example."

For in an example, the presence of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) in that [subject] is demonstrated by its being of the same nature (tat-svabhāvatā), through its necessary connection with that alone; namely,
that which produces a produced nature (kṛtaka-svabhāva).
The proof that it produces something possessing an impermanent nature is demonstrated by means of an example;
otherwise, because of the presence of a single property, there would be no restrictive rule (niyama) that it must also possess the other [property],
and thus there would be a suspicion of the probans deviating from the probandum.
And by that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the necessary concomitance of the property to be proven with that [cause] alone is demonstrated:
that which is produced from its own causes arises as such— that is, as perishable and having the property of abiding for only a moment.

Because its existence is denied elsewhere; or rather, the state of being a cause [is established] because it exists only when that [other thing] exists—this is demonstrated by means of an example. For if, in the case of another object, such [causality] were not established, then in the absence of impermanence, there would be no state of being produced (kṛtakatva) when that [impermanence] exists, nor would there be the state of being a cause.
And in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist;
for such is its nature or its cause.
How could it exist without its own nature or cause?
Thus, even without a substratum, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established in a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
However, for those for whom the existence of that [effect] and the existence of the cause are already established, [the negative concomitance is established] through that very establishment.
For the wise, indeed, only the logical reason (hetu) is to be stated. //27//
Since the purpose for which the example is stated has already been established, what is the use of stating it then?
Furthermore, even if that [purpose] were to be demonstrated, why rely upon a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)? Thinking thus, he rejected the basis [of the example].
Therefore, when the relationship has been known, through the statement of either one of the two, a recollection of the second also arises by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti). //28//
As for what was said— that by means of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), one [statement] demonstrates both— there too,

considering that the presence of the probandum and the presence of the reason are demonstrated by way of an example, he states the establishment of the second [term] through presumptive implication by means of a single expression.
For instance, when it is stated that "whatever is produced is impermanent," if there is no difference in meaning, it is evident that this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
because it is observed through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be invariably concomitant with that alone, its existence is necessarily restricted to that. Thus it is known.
The state of being that [result] follows by implication: in the absence of impermanence, "being produced" does not occur.
For when there is an absence of its own nature (svabhāva), an entity (bhāva) cannot exist, because they are non-different;
otherwise, the very expression "it occurs when that exists" would be impossible.
Likewise, when it is stated that "it does not exist in its absence," for one who understands its existence precisely from that [statement],
this [reason] belongs to it.

The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is that by virtue of which [the effect] does not exist in its absence; for otherwise, it would be impossible. Thus, through the realization of that specific intrinsic nature, there occurs the recollection of the positive concomitance (anvaya).
Likewise,
when it is stated that "where there is smoke, there is fire," smoke is the effect of fire,
by virtue of which fire necessarily exists where there is smoke.
Otherwise, because there would be no necessity for another entity to be invariably concomitant with it, the entity would possess independence;
therefore, in the absence of that [necessity], [the entity would be independent].
Furthermore, because its own nature is not deficient, it is not non-existent;
however, with respect to an effect, a cause must necessarily exist.
For this alone is the causality of a cause: that when another thing exists...
The presence of the effect is also its presence by way of intrinsic nature;
and that [intrinsic nature] exists in smoke.

Therefore, by the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) "smoke is the effect [of fire]," once that state of being an effect has been established through affirmation, the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) arises by implication: "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist.
Likewise, "where there is no fire, smoke is not present."
When it is stated that "fire necessarily exists when there is smoke," the understanding of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) follows by implication;
for otherwise, one would ask, "In the absence of that [fire], what would not exist?
Now, [one might object]: "But [regarding] the eternal and the non-eternal..."
Even in the absence of the production of an object, auditory cognition does not occur in its absence.
It is certainly not the case that it does not occur;
for from those two [factors] alone, doubt arises. Otherwise...
How could there be doubt through the conceptualization of its existence when it has been ascertained by means of non-existence?

It is merely said that "it does not exist" because of the absence of an ascertainment of its existence. However, when the causal relationship between fire and smoke is not demonstrated by means of an example, then—
It would not be the case that "where there is smoke, there is fire," because of the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
How, then, is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) established by implication—that smoke does not exist in the absence of fire? It is so [established].
Because non-existence is not established through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the recollection of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is therefore demonstrated by means of this very example;
for when one [of the two] exists, the aforementioned essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*) is shown.
For the sake of establishing another [property],
since it is impossible in its absence; therefore,
there is an absence of the nature of the reason when something is negated.
For it is those two [the reason and the pervader] which,
when they themselves are excluded, cause that which is tied to them to be excluded; thus,
even by one desiring to establish the negation of some object, [one relies on] the pervading reason.
Or rather, the cessation of the intrinsic nature [of one thing] should be stated as the reason [for the cessation of another].
For if there is no necessary connection, how could the cessation of one thing establish the cessation of another?
And there is the non-perception of that which is capable of being perceived. //29//

The reason for negation (pratiṣedha-hetu) is said to be the cause for the conventional usage regarding the object of negation; this is because non-apprehension itself, being of such a nature, constitutes the form of negation.
The non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the pervader are both reasons [for negation].

Thus, this threefold non-perception mentioned above is further divided into many types through the application of the various modes of non-cognition and cognition regarding those [objects] that are contradictory and so forth. (30)

For there are indeed only three types of probans for negation: the non-perception of a probans that is capable of being perceived when its existence is thus determined, the non-perception of a pervader, and the non-perception of one's own self. That [is the case].

By virtue of its application, it is said to be of many kinds through the application of the distinction between the non-perception and perception of various [objects] that are contradictory [to the probandum] and so forth.
This occurs through the non-perception of that [probandum], through the perception of what is contradictory to it, and through the perception of its contradictory effect.

Through such various applications as mentioned previously, the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is established by either the relation of cause and effect or by essential nature (*svabhāva*) as the regulator; it is not [established] through non-observation, nor is it [established] through observation alone. (31)

Otherwise, what necessity would there be for others to establish a rule of inevitable occurrence for another [factor], as in the case of a color [appearing] on a cloth due to a cause that is a distinct entity? //32//
These are the intermediate verses. Furthermore:
For if a phenomenon (dharma) were caused by something other [than its own nature], it would be something entirely different.
Indeed, when that [other cause] has been produced, that which is unproduced or has a different cause cannot have that as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
This is indeed the distinction, or rather the cause of distinction, between entities: the imposition of contradictory properties and the difference in their causes.
If these two were not differentiators, then—
If there were no distinction of anything from anything else, the entire universe would be a single substance.
Consequently, there would be simultaneous arising and perishing for everything, and everything would be functional in every respect. Otherwise, it could not even be called "one."
Or it is a different name,
because it is designated as such after having accepted a difference in meaning.
But surely, even if it were the cause of a distinct entity, since impermanence is not yet established at the time of the existence [of the thing], its lack of that nature remains the same;
for there is indeed no other [impermanence].
That which is called impermanence would have to be produced later;
for that very entity, whose nature is to abide for only a moment, is itself impermanence.

Even though there is a distinction in terminology, we shall explain the cause [of this] by way of the property-bearer (dharmin) and its property (dharmatā). Furthermore, although one perceives that very nature of his— the fact that it abides for a single moment— precisely because it arises in such a manner from its own cause, the person of dull intellect [clings to] existence...
One who is deceived by the apprehension [of an object] at all times does not reach a certain determination because of the suspicion that it might still exist,
or because of being deceived by the production of another similar [moment];
for certainty belongs only to those who perceive the final moment.

Subsequently, because it is no longer perceived, there is the determination that it has ceased to exist; at that time, its impermanence is established. This is provided that the capacity to produce an effect is the very nature of the cause.
Just as one who has not previously perceived its effect may nevertheless apprehend that [effect] upon seeing its cause, even though they have not yet realized its existence;
otherwise, it would be a different thing altogether.
In that case, impermanence would belong only to that [specific thing],
whether it has another cause or no cause at all;
and such would be the nature of the entity.
It would not possess that [quality], because that [quality] would be of no use to it; or, if it were of use, then that [quality] itself would be its [nature].
Impermanence is its very own nature; what need is there for anything else?
For even if it were to connect with another entity, nothing would arise that is not of that same nature, since that which is immovable by its own essence cannot change.
And that [cause], arising from a different entity, would have to be either a property distinct from impermanence or another property that is either a cause or an effect;
for there can be no relation between what is neither a cause nor an effect.
In that case, because the inference of existence is impossible; since it occurs subsequently, it cannot be a cause. How, then, could there be certainty regarding the result? //33//
For how could that which arises later from another entity when the thing has already been established be its cause?
Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that the effect exists at the time of the cause; therefore—
The reason based on existence (*bhāva-hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, the claim that a property caused by something other than the object itself must necessarily exist when the object exists is not a valid inference.
If, then, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are not the basis for understanding [the relationship], how is it understood that smoke does not deviate from fire? Because:
Smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the properties of its effect.
When those [conditions] are perceived, that which was previously unperceived and characterized by them is perceived;
yet, even when one of those [conditions] is absent, it is not perceived.
That is its effect,
and that exists in smoke.
If that [cause] were absent, however, its existence would transcend the state of having a cause. //34//
Because it is not observed even once in that manner, the effect is established; for if it were not an effect,
it would not exist even once due to the absence of a cause.
Furthermore, if an effect were to exist without its own cause,
it would simply be causeless; for that which exists without something else cannot be said to belong to it.
[Objection: Smoke becomes the cause [of fire], yet smoke can exist even in the absence of fire; therefore, it is not caused by that [fire].
If you argue that it is not causeless because it has another cause, [we reply as follows].
No; for that [reason] is equal even in that case: [the smoke] occurs in the fire even in the absence of that [fuel]. Or how [could it be otherwise] from that?
Or it might arise from something else that does not have the nature of producing it;
for that which is itself not of that nature does not produce it, and thus it would lack causality.

Indeed, it does not become that very same thing, because such a state of being arises from something dissimilar. How could that which arises from what is dissimilar be similar? For only by arising from what is similar could it be similar.
Even if [the cause] were of a different nature, since there would be no restriction on its capacity for producing such an effect,
the difference in causes would not be a differentiator; thus, the manifold variety of the universe would be without a cause,
or else everything would be produced from everything.
Therefore, the difference and non-difference of the effect follow from the difference and non-difference of the cause.
Thus, smoke is not [inherently] seen as the object.
[An effect] arises from a cause that is of a different class [from its own form], because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of it being causeless. And thus:
"An uncaused thing must either exist eternally or not exist at all, since it does not depend on anything else;
for the occasional occurrence of entities is possible only through dependence. (Verse 35)
For if that smoke were causeless, it would never fail to exist because of its independence;
or else, since there would be no deficiency in the conditions for its existence, it would never exist at all, just as it does not exist at the time when it is not desired.
Because there is no distinction between the time of existence and the time of non-existence.
For entities are occasional only by virtue of dependence [on other factors].
Since the capacity for that entity's existence and the incapacity for its non-existence are present during both the times of existence and non-existence, their capacity is equal.
Because it is impossible to establish a restriction for the other two [space and time] regarding their possession of that capacity,
and since that capacity is nothing other than the state of being a cause,
therefore, by excluding one space and one time, [the cause exists] in another—

An entity existing at a particular place and time is said to be dependent upon them; for indeed, such a mode of existence itself constitutes dependence, since it is impossible for that which does not depend on the assistance rendered by those [factors] to be restricted to them. Because its place and time are thus determined, smoke is seen here once.
Furthermore, when there is a deficiency [of the conditions], its nature—which is produced by them—is not observed;
otherwise, it would not exist even once. How could that which is restricted to those [conditions] occur elsewhere?
Or, if it were not present, there would be no smoke;
for smoke is a specific nature produced by that [fire]. Likewise, the cause as well possesses a nature that produces such an effect.
If that [effect] were to exist even from something else, then that [cause] would not be its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and thus it would not produce it even once;
nor would that smoke [arise] from an entity whose intrinsic nature is to produce non-smoke.
And if that [smoke] has that [fire] as its intrinsic nature, then that very thing is fire; thus there is no deviation. If the head of Śakra has the nature of fire, then it is indeed fire.
Now, how could this smoke, which does not have fire as its intrinsic nature, exist there? //36//
For fire, which has smoke as its cause and intrinsic nature, possesses a specific causal capacity;
if smoke were to arise from a cause that is not smoke, it would be without a cause. //37//
These are the summary verses.
How, then, is it that an effect now arises from distinct auxiliary causes, as in the case of consciousness arising from the eye, visible form, and so forth?
Indeed, no single thing whatsoever possesses that nature as a producer;
rather, it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces and possesses that nature. That very [complex]—
That very [cause] is the basis for the existence of the nature of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and of the effect.
For this very reason, there is no simultaneous production even by the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Furthermore, whatever [is produced]...
It is observed that lotus roots and the like arise from heterogeneous sources such as cow dung;
even in that case, if one were to designate them in such a manner, there is nonetheless a distinction in their intrinsic nature due to their arising from their own seeds.
Because of the difference in the nature of their causes:
for example, the plantain tree clearly arises from seeds and bulbous roots.
The world distinguishes such [causes] based on the difference in their forms;
therefore, an effect whose form is clearly distinguished does not deviate from its cause.

That which is observed through positive and negative concomitance to be the follower of another is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of that [other]; therefore, it has that as its cause. Consequently, there is no possibility [of such a nature] arising from something different. (38)
This is the summary verse.
Therefore, since the causal relationship is established even by seeing and not seeing [the effect] just once, the cognition of that [relationship] arises from that; it does not arise otherwise.

Because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) depend upon the observation of all instances and the non-observation [of exceptions], even if permanence is observed in some cases where there is incorporeality, it is not seen otherwise in other cases;
and even in the absence of permanence, that which was previously unobserved is observed again. Let this be so for an effect.
For what reason is there an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)? Because [the effect] arises from that [cause].
Now, how is there an inseparable connection in the case of essential nature (*svabhāva*)?
There is an inseparable connection even in the case of essential nature, provided it conforms to the mere existence [of the property].
For when an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) follows from mere existence, the inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) of that entity is accepted;
in the absence of that [nature], the entity itself would be absent, because there is no distinction between them. //39//
That very entity which conforms to mere existence is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva). That itself is the entity as it exists in reality;
and how could that exist by abandoning its own self?
"In that case, whatever is produced is itself impermanent, since there is no difference [between them];
thus, the reason would be a part of the meaning of the thesis (*pratijñā*). This is not a fault, because:"
All things, by their very nature, are established in their own individual natures; for they all partake in exclusions from both their own-nature and other-natures. (40)
Therefore, from whatever [object] things are excluded,
conceptual distinctions of universals (jāti-bheda) based upon that [exclusion] are constructed, which penetrate those specific differences.

Therefore, whatever specific distinction is perceived by means of a particular property cannot be established by anything other than that; thus, the determination of difference is based on that [property].
For all entities indeed abide in their own nature;
they do not mix themselves with another.
Because that would entail the consequence of it being something other than them;
furthermore, that form which is non-different and constitutes their very essence is not [itself] those [atoms].
Because at that time those [other things] do not exist;
for that alone would exist because it is non-different,
whereas anything distinct from it would be different.

And because that [distinction] does not exist, and because it is contradictory for that very thing to possess differentiation; furthermore, that [consciousness] is established as residing within the self,
entirely unmixed.

Even if there are multiple relations, another entity [distinct from them] cannot be their universal (*sāmānya*), because it does not possess their nature; this is also the case for duality, conjunction, and effects.
Because this would lead to the undesirable consequence [of it applying] even to substances;
for things are not called "identical" merely because they possess another related entity; rather, they would be called "possessors of that."
Like "bhūtavat" and "kaṇṭheguṇena," [words] do not have as their object a single undifferentiated cognition.
Like a real entity; for it is the intellect itself,
by uniting with that [object], which appears as having a universal as its object.
If it is argued that [the cognition] is not of two things related as one,
like the case of [perceiving] a real entity (*bhūta*), and that this [cognition] is an error for one who perceives that—
how is it established that she perceives that?
If it is argued that this is because an error without a seed (nirbīja-bhrānti) is impossible, [we reply:

those very [causes] which produce that single effect are the "seed. Furthermore, [the concept of a "whole"] is absent in the elements (bhūta) and so forth, because they possess number, conjunction, effects, substances, and the like.
Therefore, it is not so;
because there is no entry [of the universal] into the cognition of the universal, the universal is not something else.
Or, even if it were, that [universal] too—

Because they are established within their own selves, there is no commingling with anything else. Therefore, these entities are distinct from both those considered of the same class and from others, by virtue of their nature being of a single form.

In whatever ways they are differentiated, by means of words arranged for the purpose of conveying those specific differences, entities possessing multiple properties are perceived as having distinctions corresponding to each [word], even though there is no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Even those words, although they do not imply all particularities, result in being restricted to that specific particular (svalakṣaṇa) because they enjoin a single particularity; thus,
from one [particular], [all others are excluded].
Moreover, does it have differentiation?
Therefore, for a single entity, there are as many exclusions (vyāvṛtti) as there are forms of other entities in relation to it.

Because the cause of that which is impossible as an effect is distinct from it; for as many as there are exclusions (vyāvṛttayaḥ), so many are the linguistic expressions (śrutayaḥ) intended for practical usage through the exclusion of what is neither its effect nor its cause.
For example, [the statement] "sound is produced immediately after effort and is audible" is for the purpose of excluding what is neither its effect nor its cause.
Therefore, even when there is no difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), whatever specific property or name [is applied], by that [property] a particular distinction [is established].
Since a distinction is perceived and it cannot be made known by anything else, all words do not have a single referent.
Therefore, the reason is not a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). How so?
Furthermore, it is understood that exclusion (vyavaccheda) is what is conveyed by words and logical marks (liṅga),
and not the positive form of the thing-in-itself; [this is so] because there would otherwise be the necessity for another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and another word.
And because [cognition] proceeds in such a manner:
for when a single objective nature is itself directly perceived, what other unperceived part could there be that would need to be examined by means of further instruments of knowledge? (43)
For the nature of an object is one;
it is directly perceived, because a proof is impossible when the subject (dharmin) is not established,
just as when impermanence is the property to be proven, sound [is the subject].
Since that [object] is established by direct perception itself,
there is the establishment of all its aspects;
for there is no non-existence of anything other than that which is not so established, or if such were to exist, [it would be perceived].
It is the state of not having that as its intrinsic nature (*atat-svabhāvatva*).
For it is not logical that something which does not share the same security and fate (*ekayogakṣema*) with another should have that as its intrinsic nature.
Because the conventional usage of distinction is based solely upon that [conceptual construction];
otherwise, the consequence of non-existence would follow, as has been stated.
Therefore, since the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is fully determined by perception, there would be no occasion for the operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding it.

If another quality were not associated with it by means of a cause of error—just as the form of silver [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance—[then the illusion would not occur]. (44)
If, even for an entity whose true nature has been perceived, another quality is not superimposed by a cause of error that obstructs such ascertainment—
as in the case of silver [superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl— then [the entity remains as it is].
This is the form [of the cognition]. For there are not two forms in the mother-of-pearl—a common one and a specific one—because that would entail such a perception [of both];
or, if they were not perceived, it would be impossible to have a conceptual construction of duality through their distinction.
And because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument],
therefore, while seeing the specific form of the mother-of-pearl,
one sees it as such; however, due to a deficiency in the causal conditions for certainty, one does not ascertain its general character.
He thinks, "I see it," and from that arises his superimposition of silver;
so it is.

Due to the arising of successive moments that are similar to one another, the diversity [of these moments] is not perceived; thus, through the superimposition of that [permanent] state upon them, there arises the delusion of stability.
For as many as are its extrinsic states (parabhāva), so many are their respective causes.
Since superimpositions (samāropa) regarding future entities [do exist], the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that exclude them would be fruitful;
however, for those [means of cognition] whose fruit is exclusion, there is no portion of an object not already cognized.
Its activity toward communication occurs because that [activity] is observed;
furthermore, it is impossible for that which is partless to be perceived through a single part.
Therefore, every quality of a perceived entity is indeed perceived;
it is only because of delusion that this is not ascertained, and thus the means of proof is set forth. //45//
This is the summary verse.
Therefore, when something is already perceived, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition for the sake of apprehending the unseen.
And when a single property (*dharma*) is ascertained through inference upon the apprehension of the factual basis (*vastu*), [the unseen is not thereby established].
In the case of exclusion (apoha), this fault of grasping all phenomena (sarva-dharma) does not follow. //46//
Not only does another means of valid cognition not operate with respect to what is already seen through perception;
even when inference makes an object known by way of affirmation (*vidhi*) rather than through exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), then [the object is established] as a single—

When there is certainty regarding one phenomenon (*dharma*), because of its non-distinctness from all phenomena, there is certainty regarding all phenomena; thus, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is not logical that when that [one phenomenon] is ascertained, its very nature (*tadātmā*) remains unascertained. However, when the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*) is effected by inference, then [it is not the case that] one—
