Because superimposition (samāropa) is excluded, the exclusion of others (anyavyavaccheda) is thereby accomplished; it is for this purpose that another [cognition] proceeds.
Now, is it not the case that what is unperceived is not necessarily preceded by error?
Certainty arises,
just as the cognition of fire occurs from smoke that appears suddenly; for in that case, the superimposition of "non-fire" is not possible.
Therefore, exclusion is not made in all cases. It has been stated in this regard:
"When the subject (dharmin) is apprehended, because there is no distinction [between its properties], there is the apprehension of everything."
Or, if there were a difference [between the two], there would be no cognition of that which is unconnected with it.
Therefore, even in that case, how could one who perceives it have certainty regarding its nature? It is because of error (*viparyāsa*).
And he, determining that place by means of a form distinct from it, [engages in] the cultivation of the existence of fire.

How can one who possesses a liberated cognition be said to be non-erroneous? Furthermore, being free from superimposition and doubt regarding its form, one would not follow a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the apprehension of that [object],
nor would one pay heed to its positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Therefore, the logical mark (liṅga) is proclaimed to have exclusion (apoha) as its object;
otherwise, if the locus (dharmin) were already established, what could remain unestablished beyond that? (47)
This is the summary verse:

Even when something is perceived in a particular instance, the conceptual cognition whose object is a universal has as its domain the exclusion (*apoha*) of that alone, provided that other parts [of the object] have not been superimposed upon it. (48)
When a certain cognition that lacks a logical mark (aliṅga) arises immediately after the perception of form and so forth,
how can it have exclusion (vyavaccheda) as its object if there is no superimposition (samāropa)? For that [exclusion] is absent in the object of superimposition.
For where there is a superimposition (samāropa) upon it— such as [the notions] that it is "stable" or "possessed of a self"— there is no certain determination regarding its particularity (bheda),
because of the relationship of sublated and sublator between the mind of certain determination and the mind of superimposition.
For even when an entity is perceived as distinct from everything else, it is not recognized as being exactly the same [as before],
because in some cases there may be an intervention [of difference],
as in the case of a mother-of-pearl shell's status as "mother-of-pearl."
However, where there is no cause for the cognizer’s error, it is precisely there that a mnemonic certainty arises despite the lack of distinction in the perception of that [object];
for there exists a relationship of sublation between superimposition and certainty.
It is understood that the activity of this ascertainment occurs when there is the exclusion of superimposition. //49//
And that very exclusion [of the object] from others is precisely *anyāpoha* (the exclusion of other).
Therefore, that [cognition] also has as its objective domain the exclusion of that alone;
it does not consist of a determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a real entity (*vastu*).
For it is observed that even when one thing is ascertained, another may not be apprehended;
and because it is impossible for that [other] to be ascertained as having the same nature as the first.

There are as many superimpositions of parts as there are, and there are exactly that many determinate cognitions for their removal; likewise, there are that many words. Therefore, they have distinct domains of operation.
Otherwise, if a single object were pervaded by one word or by one cognition, there would be no other object [for another word], and thus they would be synonyms. (51)
This is an intermediate verse:

Even for one who holds that the cognition of an object possessing various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) apprehends that object as differentiated—by whomsoever it may be thought that the limiting adjuncts themselves are mutually distinct and distinct from their substratum; [for such a person, the following applies].
The scriptural passages based upon that [universal] apply to its substrata,
or indeed to that [universal] itself;
therefore, this objection does not apply to it either.

When there is the apprehension of a self that is non-different from the capacities of its various constituent parts, which are aided by diverse limiting conditions (upādhi), [the cognition of difference does not arise]. //52//
What could possibly differentiate an assistance that is provided in its entirety?

Even if the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indeed distinct causes for various words and cognitions regarding an object, that object— possessing those adjuncts— is nonetheless apprehended as a single unity.

Since that [entity], whose nature consists of powers that serve as the substratum for the assistance of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is non-different within itself, if it were apprehended in its entirety, what limiting adjunct whatsoever could remain unascertained?

Because it is apprehended as being the benefactor of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For there can be no such thing as its quality of being a benefactor— which is grasped by its very nature— that remains unapprehended.
Therefore, that very apprehension which occurs through its own nature also occurs through its capacity to assist;
because these two are related within a single self, there is the apprehension of both in the cognition of one. //53//
Because the relationship of mutual assistance between the substrate and its attributes— which are identical with the self— is apprehended,
both are apprehended within a single cognition; thus, when that [substrate] is apprehended as qualified by even a single attribute, all attributes are apprehended.
Because the apprehension of that which possesses the limiting condition (upādhimat) is inseparable from the apprehension of that [condition];
otherwise, it would not be apprehended even in that manner.
For there is no such thing as one thing being a benefactor to another that is not itself apprehended; nor, when the benefactor is thus apprehended, can there be a non-apprehension of the beneficiary,
because that would entail the non-apprehension of the benefactor as well.
It is like the relationship between a thing and its owner;
therefore, the same logical consequence applies even to the theory that [the properties] are adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*) distinct from the entity itself.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the powers (*śakti*) are indeed distinct from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), by means of which [powers] the adjuncts...

[The opponent argues: "It assists [the entity]; therefore, this undesirable consequence does not follow. [The author replies: If there is a difference between the capacities that assist the property (dharma) and that [property] itself, what [benefit] do those [capacities] provide for it? If there is no assistance from them, then there would likewise be an infinite regress. //54//
If its various modes of assistance corresponding to each respective attribute are neither identical with its own nature nor do they experience assistance from it,
then what [assistance] does it have? These are called "assisting attributes" (upakāra).

Or rather, this single [entity], while assisting its powers through those powers that are identical with its own self, is indeed apprehended in its entirety even when it is apprehended through a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). For instance, when one limiting adjunct is apprehended, there is the apprehension of the power that assists that [adjunct].
When that [object] is apprehended,
the entity which assists it is apprehended as assisting all its powers inherent in its own nature;
it causes all those powers to be apprehended, and they in turn cause their own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to be apprehended— thus it remains in that state.
This leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Now, if those powers that assist [the primary] power are themselves distinct from the entity, then—
since this process of adjuncts and their powers would continue infinitely through further and further powers— the one [entity] could never at any time be grasped by them.
That which consists of the assistance rendered by those [limiting adjuncts] is not apprehended as possessing them;
for if words and cognitions were to depend upon the limiting adjuncts alone, [the object would not be perceived].
At that time, because it is not included therein,
there is no comprehension of everything by way of the comprehension of that;
even then, for that [person],...

Because there would be no engagement with it through words due to its not being indicated by them, the employment of words would be useless. For all practical activity consisting of affirmation and negation is based upon causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*);
and in that regard, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are incapable [of such efficacy], while that which is capable is not expressed at all.
Thus, what is the use of employing words?
Consequently, adjuncts (*upādhi*) would not be adjuncts.

For when something functions as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to some primary entity (*pradhāna*) in a particular instance, it is only in relation to that [primary entity] [that it is called an adjunct].
It is said thus:
since they are not implied by words, they are not constituent parts of anything; so how could they be limiting adjuncts (upādhi)?

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the object] is characterized by its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies. For as long as that [object] is being perceived through those limiting conditions (*upādhi*) by way of invariable concomitance, then even when it is perceived by a single [condition], it is perceived in its entirety; thus the situation remains the same.

This leads to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). For what distinction is there here between the words that might characterize this [universal], or the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) characterized by them?
At that time, it is determined to be the benefactor of all.
Thus, this [objection] is of no consequence. Therefore:
When one thing that provides assistance is apprehended, there are no other assistances apart from it.
When that [one] is seen, those which are unseen are apprehended; thus, upon the apprehension of that, there is the apprehension of the whole. (55)
This is the summary verse (saṃgrahaśloka).
If it is held that even when [an object] has been apprehended, something else is still desired for the sake of removing error, then it might be argued:
"When a partless entity is apprehended, what else could there be that is not then apprehended?"
It is indeed so; however, because it is not ascertained due to error, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates.
If this is the case, then it is established that [the first cognition] has exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its object, and therefore another [cognition] follows from it. (56)
Because its activity occurs within the domain of non-superimposition,
that means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which has set out for the purpose of removing error [is directed] toward the superimposition of something else.

It is established that [the word] has exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) as its result, and thus has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object; the same applies to other [words] as well, because they function with respect to an object where there is no superimposition (*asamāropa*). That is to say, it does not function with respect to that wherein such superimposition occurs.
Thus, "ascertainment" (niścaya), occurring in the absence of superimposition (samāropa), is established as having the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) as its object.
Furthermore, by means of ascertainments:
how can that form which is not ascertained be their object? (57)
Indeed, this very determination of an object is what constitutes the apprehension of its own nature by determinate cognitions;
for if that [nature] were as indeterminate as any other form, how could it be grasped by them?
Furthermore, how can something that is not being determined be said to be "grasped" even by perception?
Perception is not determinative for anyone;
thus, even when this [perception] apprehends that [object], it does so without determination.
What then?
It is by means of its appearance;
therefore, it is neither certain nor uncertain.
In the case of perception, apprehension and non-apprehension occur due to its own power;

it is not so with determinate cognitions (*niścaya*). Even for one who determines something in one respect, there is apprehension and non-apprehension due to the difference in activity arising from non-determination regarding other [aspects].
Therefore, the apprehension of that [object] is precisely its ascertainment;
otherwise, even if there were a single form, that [apprehension] would not occur.

But what is the reason that, even though an experience arises regarding the nature of an object which is distinct from everything else, a corresponding certain recollection does not occur? It is due to a deficiency in the auxiliary causes (sahakāri-kāraṇa), and consequently:
Even when a particularity devoid of parts has been grasped by perception, that perception which exists in the determination of a specific [aspect] is what is cognized. //58//
Even if an entity is experienced as being devoid of parts and having a nature distinct from everything else,
nevertheless, certainty regarding all its differences does not arise by that much alone;
[this is due to] other causes.
Because it is dependent [on other factors].
For experience generates determinate cognitions in accordance with the habituation of conceptualization;
thus, even though there is no difference in the perception of form, [one may perceive it as] a corpse, a beloved woman, or food.

Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise; in this regard, the acuity of the intellect, the cultivation of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth, are the auxiliary factors for the production of the ascertainment of difference from experience. And it is precisely due to differences such as the degree of proximity among these that there is a sequence of priority and posteriority. For example:
Even though there is no difference between being a progenitor and being a teacher, upon seeing one's father approaching, one thinks, "My father is coming," and not, "The teacher is coming.
That certainty also exists even in the absence of error.
It occurs with respect to the cause;

therefore, the determination of all aspects does not consist merely in [the cognition] "it is non-existent. Furthermore, in that case as well, there is both the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) and that which is excluded from others (*anyavyāvṛtta*).
And words as well as conceptual determinations conform to linguistic convention. //59//

In that case as well, if there were an exclusion of another, there would be no further exclusion; for that which is excluded is itself [the exclusion], since it follows that for that which is being turned away from that exclusion, it would result in being that very thing.
And thus, regarding the exclusion...
It is non-existence. Therefore, that which is the exclusion is itself the excluded. However, the difference in the cognition of words arises from a difference in convention;
there is no difference in the referent itself.
But surely, because there is no distinction in the object to be expressed, even a difference in convention is improper for the two [words],
since they denote the same thing;
and thus, the use of a case-ending that implies a distinction would be inappropriate for it.

Because it is based on difference, even when two things are expressed by a single word, the case-ending appears as if distinct; due to a slight particularity in what is to be expressed, it follows as if the referent were different. (60)
Indeed, the operation of words does not depend at all on the nature of their objects, for otherwise it would follow that they could not operate according to one's will;
rather, they may be employed [to denote] things as either distinct or non-distinct.
In the same way, when they are so employed, they manifest that object through a connection [to it].

Therefore, even though "cow" (*gauḥ*) and "cowness" (*gotva*) denote a single object, there is a distinction in meaning expressed by the difference in convention (*saṃketa-bheda*), for the purpose of conveying a certain specific quality.
A case-ending appears as if indicating a distinct meaning, even when there is no distinct meaning,
due to the habit of observing such usage;
however, that alone does not imply a difference in every instance.
In other cases as well, there is no restriction on that which proceeds by the power of human intention; for example,

although a single thing is expressed in the singular number in some instances, it may be expressed in the plural number when one intends to convey qualities such as its weight, even though there is no difference in the object itself.
However, due to the absence of a purpose, there would be no distinction in convention;
yet that [distinction] certainly exists. For instance:
The exclusion and non-exclusion of other distinctions between those two [universals] are the basis for the difference in linguistic convention, which follows the desire of the cognizer. (61)

When this cognizer, without regard for the existence of the exclusion of others, desires to know merely the exclusion of "horse" regarding a particular individual, he is then awakened by a word whose convention has been established in that manner for the purpose of making known what was previously unknown: "He possesses non-horseness."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, when one desires to know that [exclusion] without any further expectation for another exclusion,

then, while not abandoning the other exclusions, one employs the expression "this is not a horse" with respect to that very exclusion of a horse (*aśva-vyavaccheda*) so that it may be manifested in such a manner.

For this very reason, since the application of words has already been rejected as involving a distinct difference [between them], there can be neither grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) nor the relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva).
[The cognition] "the cowness of this [is] white" [does not arise],
because the cognition which has that [cowness] as its substrate does not appear as a unity due to the distinction of those [qualities] alone,
and because [the cognition] is free from expectancy.
In the second case, however, it occurs: thus, according to convention,
[the cognition] pertains to a single entity possessing distinctions, through all properties of exclusion that have been withdrawn.
Because it appears as if [it were an external object] through its manifestation,
and because it requires another exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).
This very distinction exists everywhere between two words denoting a substance and its state; there is no difference whatsoever in their referent.

Therefore, in every case, there is no distinction between two words— one expressing the property (*dharma*) and the other the property-bearer (*dharmin*)— with respect to the object denoted, insofar as both serve as the objective domain for a certain cognition.
When one [word] conveys that very same [object], it does so in this manner.
One [word] causes comprehension by excluding other distinctions,
while another does so by means of exclusion;
this is the distinction.

If one wishes to make that meaning known, whether by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a primary derivative (*kṛt*), or by some other [means], there is no difference [in the result] beyond that. And demonstrating only this much of a difference, one might demonstrate it by means of a secondary derivative.

Whether by using the term "the state of being a cooker" (*pācakatva*), or by using "cooking" (*pāka*), or by some other convention established by oneself to indicate such a thing, [it is understood] through that convention; but not merely by the act of denoting it in that way.
That [word] indeed has a different meaning,
because the convention for the word was established precisely to indicate something that is of such a nature.
But is it not the case that "the state of being a cook" (*pācakatva*) refers to a relation, and not to cooking itself?
Indeed, no entity called a "cook" distinct from the act of cooking is ever denoted.

Whatever [nature] is described, its referent has already been explained; that very same [referent] is also expressed by the term "cook. Therefore, enough with these unstable and false conceptual constructions.
And we shall demonstrate how there is no action that exists as a distinct entity, nor its inherence [in a substance]; therefore,
the description of the "possessor of that" (tadvat) position is merely with respect to the exclusion of others (anyāpoha).
For if [the universal and the possessor of the universal] were distinct, the fault already refuted would apply to the universal and its possessor. //64//
As for what they say— that even if the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because it denotes that which is qualified by it,

all the objections raised against the position [that the word denotes] the possessor of that quality (*tadvat*) apply equally here— that too has been refuted by this [argument]. For in that case, the word, having taken up a different object, operates upon another.
It is afflicted by defects such as lack of independence;
nor is "exclusion" (vyāvṛtti) a distinct entity from that which is excluded, because it has been stated that both [the exclusion and the excluded] are denoted by a single term. How so?
Now, because that which is excluded from one thing does not follow into another,
the exclusion of the other is the universal (*sāmānya*), since it appears as such in the cognition thereof.
Indeed, there is nothing [else].
There exists what is called the universal (sāmānya).
A cognition based on words arises through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (vāsanā),
joining together even those phenomena that are not actually conjoined.
By the force of its appearance, both the universal and co-referentiality are established,
even though they lack a real objective referent.
Because there is no distinction in the combination of objects,
all those objects, being differentiated from others by virtue of being its cause and effect, constitute its basis.
And since a word causes one to act by avoiding what is undesired, it is said to have "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) as its object.
In that regard, a single entity— though independent of external reality—

is made the object of words by virtue of the appearance in cognition, being excluded from many [others], through the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by the experience of that [appearance].
Through births and conceptual constructions whose objects consist of the apprehended states [of things],
this conventional discourse of property (dharma) and substratum (dharmin) is extended therein as being inexpressible in terms of identity or difference from one another.
For a property is not something other than the substratum, because it is not denoted as a distinct entity; nor is it that very same thing,
just as in the case of those [words] that denote the substratum itself, so too with those that denote its properties.
Furthermore, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of implying other exclusions (*vyavaccheda*),
and because the intended object is thus communicated,
there is no need to establish a separate linguistic convention (*saṃketa*).
This inexpressibility of the property and the substratum applies to the referent of a word;
however, with respect to the real thing as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that is inexpressible.
Because [the distinction] does not exist. Now, if there were non-difference or difference between the property (dharma) and the property-bearer (dharmin),
then the genitive and other case-endings seen [in usage], as well as the diversity of number observed there due to the plurality of properties, would not apply to the property-bearer.
It has been stated in this regard that words lack independence. Furthermore:
"For those for whom words are governed by the nature of things and do not depend primarily upon the speaker's intention," [words would be non-deviant].
Against them, the objection regarding the use of the genitive case, the difference in verbal expression, and so forth, is logically sound. //65//

If indeed these words, even though they might be intended to be produced by persons in some instances, cannot be produced because of their essential connection with the object— just like smoke and so forth—
then this [following] objection applies.
How could there be [the use of] the genitive case and so forth? Furthermore:
"In whatever way a word is assigned by speakers as a signifier, that word is a signifier in that manner, regardless of any external object. (66)

For it is not the case that the genitive occurs when there is distinction (*vyatireka*), nor that the nominative plural suffixes such as *jas* occur when there is plurality; rather, these [grammatical rules] function by themselves through the mere presence of the object, independent of any intention on the part of the person [using them].
However, since those [speakers] employ them in such a manner in those contexts, comprehension accordingly arises from them.

In the same way, in other cases as well, when they are employed by those [speakers] in some manner, they become causes for cognition in that very way. Regarding that, there is an investigation into the operation of words— which function depending on persons, which do not reveal real entities, and which serve as causes for the awakening of conceptual constructions according to habituation— with respect to the objects to be expressed.

To establish real entities based on that [conceptual distinction] is merely a manifestation of stupidity. Why is it that words, having been established in such a manner regarding properties (dharma), the substratum of properties (dharmin), and so forth, do not [correspond] to a distinction between separate real entities (vyatireka-vastu-bheda)?
Because such linguistic usage would be impossible;

for if there were a difference between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin), or if they were of the nature of distinct realities, then the relations of universal, its connection, grammatical coreferentiality, and the qualifier-qualified relationship would not be tenable.
Or, as we shall explain later, it is because words do not function according to the actual state of things (*yathā-vastu-vṛtti*).
Furthermore, for one who maintains that the differentiation in the application of words everywhere is based solely on real entities (*vastu-kṛta*), [the following applies]:

In cases such as "the wife" (*dārāḥ*) or "the city of six" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*), there is an established distinction between difference and non-difference; or else, what is the basis for [the usage] "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāvaḥ*) or "spaciousness" (*khatvam*)? (67)
When even a single woman is designated as "wife" (*dārāḥ*), and even a single substance of sand is designated as "sand" (*sikatāḥ*), what plurality is there in those cases by which such usage occurs?
If it is argued that this is due to a difference in capacity (*śakti-bheda*), [we reply: no.
In all cases, the singular number is now obsolete because of the absence of a single power [to denote unity]; thus, effort [to establish it] is futile.
If it is argued that the singular number applies elsewhere due to the non-difference of the object, [we reply: no.
Let it be so here as well.
Thus, this rule being formulated without a real basis (nirvastuka) reveals the independence of one's own will in the employment of words.
And as for the expression "the six cities" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*), how can there be a singular number when there are many? For the cities themselves are not some single entity.

Whence could there be a collection of those [parts], since heterogeneous things such as a palace and a person do not originate [as a single substance]? Whence, then, could their aggregate be a substance?
And because it is not conjoined:
there is no conjunction [of the palace],
since the palace, being itself of the nature of a conjunction, does not conjoin with anything else.
And for that very reason, there is an absence of number. If it is argued that "city" is existence (sattā) as qualified by its conjunction with persons;
What is the qualification for this unsurpassed [existence]?
Since existence (*sattā*) is one,
even when there is a plurality of cities, the plural form "cities" (*nagarāṇi*) is used.
It would not be so. If you argue that it is the mutual accompaniment of the two, then what kind of assistance can there be between that which is neither assisted nor assists?
What, then, is the state of being a companion?
And since there is a plurality of existences consisting of the conjunction with persons,
how can there be the singular expression "the city"? [If it is argued that] such things [are referred to] in some cases...
If it is argued that there exists an undivided potency (*śakti*) in the object and that this is the cause [of the cognition], we say no;
for potency is not distinct from the nature of the thing itself.
Alternatively, if there were a difference [between the entity and its capacity], dependence would be impossible for that which is not assisted.

Or, if there were assistance, since the capacity that assists the capacity would itself have to differ [from the entity], there would be an infinite regress, and thus no cognition [of the entity] would occur.
Or, if there were no distinction between them, the same consequence would apply to the first case as well; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
The statement "the nature of space is spacy-ness" (khatva) relies upon a distinction.
The genitive case would not be possible;
for in that case, there is no universal (sāmānya), nor are qualities such as omnipresence (vibhutva) and so forth spoken of in that manner.

Because it is impossible for a different entity to have that as its intrinsic nature, and because it would follow that those [other entities] themselves would lack intrinsic nature; for if that [intrinsic nature] were also to have a different entity as its intrinsic nature...
There would be an over-extension [of the definition], and thus there would be a failure of comprehension. In this way, the group of six categories and so forth [would be undermined].
Alternatively, they should be stated [as follows]: for in that case, neither a universal (*sāmānya*), nor number (*saṃkhyā*), nor conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is possible.
How, then, can there be "the nature of space" (*khasya svabhāva*) when no excellence (*atiśaya*) exists, and not merely "space" (*kha*) itself?

When there is a desire to know the specific form that serves as the basis for the application of the word "space" (*kha*)—a form that is not perceived as being common to other objects—the following is said.
[Objection: But surely, it is impossible to denote a form that is excluded from everything else.
Indeed, that very form is not presented to the cognition,
because it would follow that [the form] is beyond the senses; rather, by means of the word, one intends only to cause [the listener] to understand something of such a nature.
It projects a conceptual reflection whose nature is not fused with that [external object] for the listener;

as it has been said: "Regarding an object not [directly] perceived, there is merely a conceptual construction of the object. In this way, neither the proponent nor the listener has apprehended or communicated the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Or else, even upon hearing of heaven and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence that there is no difference in the mental appearance for those who experience it [there], just as for those currently experiencing it. Therefore,
even though this person does not perceive it [directly],...
One who determines [the object] within a conceptual reflection that possesses the very nature of an entity is satisfied with it as being just so;
for it is precisely because of its being just so that the meaning of the word is understood.
Therefore, it is said in this way that "the word expresses its own form" (svarūpa),
not because it generates a cognition in which the form itself appears.
How, then, can there be such a thing as a "universal" (sāmānya) among entities whose forms are now entirely excluded from one another?
For they do not coalesce.
And because there is no other [universal].
It has been stated what kind of universal belongs to things that are unmixed: it is the commonality of those distinct from it, consisting in their non-mixture with one another. Furthermore:
That cognition by which the form of another is concealed by its own form.
Based upon distinct entities that manifest as a single object, [the conceptual cognition arises]. //68//
By that [concealment], various objects whose meanings are concealed by convention appear, though they are themselves distinct, as if non-distinct through some form. (69)
By virtue of her intention, the universal (sāmānya) is proclaimed to exist;
however, it is non-existent in the ultimate sense, just as it was conceptualized by her.
Indeed, cognition, arising by depending upon objects that are distinct from one another,
being conceptual and conforming to the nature of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), conceals their differentiated forms and superimposes its own undifferentiated appearance upon them.
It manifests those [entities] by conjoining them;

and this is the nature of both the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction regarding those entities— which are distinguished from others because they are to be accomplished and their means are one— and of the entities themselves, such that it appears in this way.
This [cognition] appears as arising from that;
and it is a conventional reality (saṃvṛti), because by means of it one's own nature conceals the nature of others.
And those [entities], whose distinctions have been concealed by that [conceptualization],

although distinct in themselves, appear as if non-distinct through some form; therefore, for those who conform to this appearance in cognition, [the operations] concern only those entities that exist within the sphere of cognition.
Because they grasp a specific form, that which appears as if flashing externally is called a "universal" (sāmānya). How, then, is the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) the universal?
Indeed, it is that very [exclusion] itself.

The exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*); grasping that very [exclusion], it appears as if it were grasping a real entity due to an innate delusion of conceptual cognitions. For it [operates] only with respect to those things that are distinguished from what is other than them.
It is understood that [these cognitions] have differentiation as their object.
But surely external objects are distinct from one another, and conceptual construction does not operate with respect to them; so how can it occur in relation to them?
Indeed, it is the commentators who analyze in this way, not those engaged in conventional usage;
for the latter [perceive] their own objective support.
Thinking that only such [an object] is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*), people proceed by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object;
it is on the basis of this intention that it is said thus.
Because they perform that [function],
they represent them as distinct from those that do not perform it by means of the word,
on account of the difference in their appearance and so forth.
However, those who contemplate reality do not admit non-difference. If one were to conform to the intention of the cognizer, then even the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) would not be the universal,
for there is no such cognition [of it as a universal].
Indeed, there is not only this lack of comprehension;
[there is also the failure to grasp that it is] distinct from individuals, non-distinct [from them], unitary, eternal, all-pervading, and so forth.
Nor is there comprehension even by means of forms;
rather, a cognition arises that possesses no differentiated form. As for its basis, it is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha).
Because that [conceptualization] exists with respect to entities, because there is no contradiction, and because conventional usage— which is based on words— functions in that manner.

Because it is seen that there is no such thing as a real entity called a "universal" (sāmānya) existing apart from the way this cognition appears; for individual instances do not follow one another, nor does any other following entity appear [in the cognition].
For these individuals do not enter into one another;
otherwise, in the absence of distinction, it would follow that the universal itself does not exist.
Furthermore, nothing distinct from those two appears to the cognition in that manner; and how could that which does not appear cause another to grasp itself, or how could it designate it?
Furthermore, it has been stated that a universal does not exist merely because there is one thing connected with those [individuals], as this would lead to over-extension; rather,
a universal is that which is the cause for a single denotation and cognition, and not everything.

If this is argued, [we ask]: how can there be the application of a cognition to one thing based on another? [If you say] "because of its connection with that," then the same consequence would apply even to number, action, substance, and so forth, since they too lack the nature of a universal (*asāmānyātmakatvāt*).
If you say "no," then surely this very point is what is being investigated:
what is this nature of the universal (*sāmānya*)?
In that regard, if there is a connection, the occurrence of the cognition [arises] from that; thus, it is the universal.
To this it is replied:
Because there arises from various relations— such as effects, substances, and so forth— the occurrence of a cognition based on a cause, there follows the nature of a universal.
Otherwise, let it not be so even elsewhere, for there is no distinction; and thus [it would apply] to substances, qualities, and universals.
Regarding the point that there would be a confusion of forms:
if that is the case, then since it is of the nature of cognition, the manifestation of cognition itself is the real universal.
That is not so;
for how could that which is non-different from cognition become a distinct object? (71)
How can the form of cognition be the universal of objects?
For that [form] does not exist in them.
If it is argued that there is conventional usage through such an error based on the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its existence [in them], then [the response follows]: In that case:
Likewise, what would be the cause for the arising of cognition? And if it were to arise without a substratum, it would occur everywhere.
Alternatively, since [cognition] is non-different from [the object], how could there be the form of another cognition arising from a different individual instance? And therefore—
If it does not pervade other cognitions or other individuals, how could it be a universal?
Therefore, this apprehension of a single nature in objects is a false conceptual construction.
For objects are not identical with any nature whatsoever, whether distinct or non-distinct [from their properties];
thus, their apprehension is merely a false conceptual construction (*mithyā-vikalpa*).
The seed of this [construction] is mutual exclusion (*itaretara-bheda*), which is the referent of the designation (*saṃjñā*). (72)
The conventional designation is applied for the purpose of making known those entities whose effects are identical,
so that one might act by avoiding them after having recognized them as distinct from those things that do not produce such effects.
This mutual exclusion (*itaretara-bheda*) is the object of that false conceptual construction which appears as a single essence.

The seed; grasping that very [seed], this conceptual construction appears in such a way due to the nature of its own latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). But how can there be a non-differentiated effect from things that are differentiated, by which...
Because it is distinct from others, it is called "non-difference.
This is the nature of all beings.

Even though they are distinct, certain things are restricted by their own nature to accomplishing a single purpose—such as a single unifying reflection, an object, or a cognition—just like the sense organs and so forth. //73//

Just as the sense organ, the object, light, and attention— or the self, the sense organ, the mind, the object, and their contact— produce a single visual cognition even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*) fixed to that existence, so too do particulars such as the *śiṃśapā* tree, despite lacking mutual continuity.
By their very nature, individual [causes] produce either a single recognition of a uniform form or other effects,

according to the conditions, such as the functional activity (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by wood, like fire or a house; however, even though the distinction [of being distinct entities] is equal, water and the like do not produce the cognition of color and so forth, just as the ear and other senses do not.
Just as certain medicinal herbs are observed to alleviate fever and other ailments either together or individually, while others are not. (74)
Or, for example, just as individual instances of *guḍūcī* and so forth, whether together or individually, perform a single effect characterized by the pacification of fever and the like;
and in that case, they do not depend upon a universal (*sāmānya*).
Even though there is difference, [the cognition occurs] because those [entities] have that as their nature;
it does not occur even when there is no such distinction, as in the case of yogurt and wood-apples and so forth.
It might be argued: "There must be some universal (*sāmānya*) in those things that exist in such a way."
"Therefore, that single effect exists"—
this is incorrect,
because there is no distinction.
The universal does not possess another universal;
it performs its own function, and that [function] also [does not possess another].
Because it would follow that there is no distinction [between them],
even though there are differences in their fields and so forth;
for if the effect— the alleviation of fever and the like— were to arise from the universal alone.
Because that [universal] would lack differentiation,
there would be no distinctions such as slow or rapid subsidence even when there are differences in the field and so forth among individual instances,
nor would there be any gradation of qualities.
Alternatively, if the universal were distinct from the particular, it would lose its own nature because of the difference in its intrinsic being; furthermore,
this would contradict its permanence.
Because the universal provides no assistance [to the individual]. //75//
For if it were to assist [the effect], then because that which cannot have any further particularity added to it requires nothing else, it would either produce its entire effect all at once,
or else it would not possess the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) to produce it. [This applies to] individual manifestations (*vyakti*).
However, there is no contradiction in the fact that [causes], through the influence of time, place, and processing (*saṃskāra*), produce specific results characterized by particular qualities;
likewise, certain objects, even when there is a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [may produce the same effect].

Those things which perform a single function, such as recognition and so forth, are said to be "non-different" from those that do not perform them because they are excluded from the latter; or, a single [effect] is produced by many [causes] because it is excluded from those not produced by them. But what does this universal, characterized by exclusion (*apoha*), have to do with the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)?
Is it to be understood as identical [to the particular], or is it something else entirely?
What follows from this? If it is the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), how can it be the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Or else, how could there be causal efficiency from anything else?
Furthermore, since impermanence and so forth are perceived in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), those [universals] lack that nature.
And [it is] the nature of things that lack substantial reality.
This is not a fault; for in the case of an object appearing to cognition, there is a universal—

The linguistic conventions of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relationship between property and substratum (*dharma-dharmin*) arise by relying on the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited through the experience that grasps the intrinsic nature of things.

A conceptual cognition arises which, although not having that [external object] as its domain, appears as if it does; because its nature is produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of that [object], it has as its essential form the determined state of that [object];
and because it is produced from things that have non-different effects, it is as if it grasps a non-different object, [namely] the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
In that [cognition] which has a form identical to the ultimate reality, whatever objective form appears as if external,

as if singular, and as if performing a causal function— even though it does not perform such a function— it is so for those engaged in conventional discourse because they act with a corresponding determination (*adhyavasāya*), since otherwise action would be impossible; thus, by virtue of its performing that causal function...

Because it appears [as such], it seems as if distinct from those things that do not produce it; yet we shall demonstrate that this is not its true nature, because it is not a factor for critical investigation.
Those objects are [mere] cognitions—
Those [particulars] which reside [in the cognition] are grasped as being "similar" because they appear through an exclusion from certain [other things];
it is not the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) that appears there, because it does not appear therein.
And those very [particulars], from certain...
Furthermore, [particulars], though excluded from others and possessing exclusions themselves, appear as non-different;
because they are thus presented by cognition even while being non-existent in themselves,
the linguistic usage of "universal" and "co-referentiality" is performed with a false object.

And this entire [cognition] is a distortion produced by the latent impressions deposited by the perception of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) themselves. Therefore, even though conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—which arise in dependence upon those [particulars]—do not have those [particulars] as their objective appearance, they are non-deceptive regarding the real object, just as the error of a gem [is non-deceptive] regarding the luster of a gem; but this is not the case for others.

Even though it arises from a distinction between those [two], just as in the case of the cognition of a jewel in the light of a lamp, one might— setting aside the pursuit of a specific unseen factor— superimpose another particularity by grasping some general feature.
Therefore, there is no capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) in objects that are the domain of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
nor is there an absence of impermanence and so forth in the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because:

There is no such thing as "impermanence" distinct from the moving entity itself; because that entity, being of such a nature, is perceived as having the property of manifesting moment by moment, it occurs to us that "this is impermanent" or "this has impermanence."
Entering into that very dharmatā, conceptual constructions manifest various exclusions of one or many phenomena;
yet they are not without a basis, because they have as their basis the perception of those distinctions, nor are they without a real object.
This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*), because that which has such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) appears in that very way.
However, the apprehension of a thing as being multiple, single, or distinct would be an error (*vibhrama*).
Because that [cause], which produces one or many effects,
exists in such a state for the purpose of making known its existence in that way when there is a desire to know its existence in that way;
it is not due to a difference in the nature of the thing itself.
Because it is impossible for that which is one to be many,
and impossible for that which is many to be one.
And because that which is distinct [from them] is negated;

for if one accepts the referents of words according to the actual state of things based on the difference in their primary causes (*prakṛti*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be impossible. Therefore—
If it is argued that there is no fault because a single limiting adjunct (upādhi) is denoted by two [words], [we reply:
since dependence on another is impossible for that which provides no assistance, it is not a limiting adjunct.
And because of the relationship of producer and produced within dependence on another, since the two do not exist simultaneously, there is no designation of both; rather,
it is by means of the cognition of one.
If [the object] were supplied by mental projection (adhyāhāra), the word would not have a real entity as its object;
and if it has the appearance in cognition (buddhi-pratibhāsa) as its object, then let everything be exactly so.
Likewise, because there is no manifestation [of the object] when only one of those possessing distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is apprehended,
this applies even to the beneficiary and the benefactor, who are the possessor of the adjunct and the adjunct itself.
If it is argued that there is no fault because they exist simultaneously, we say no;
for that which is already established lacks dependence on another,
and thus cannot function as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Because that which is unestablished lacks its own essential nature (*svarūpa-asiddhi*).
In all respects, dependence (*pāratantrya*) is non-existent; having made it a conceptual superimposition (*kalpanā-āropita*), one engages in conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) in every way.
Why is that very [single cognition] not accepted as the intellect (*buddhi*)?

If it were made the object of a single word and a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, because all [entities] would be implied by the force of the thing itself (*vastu-bala*), there would be no point in anything other than that.
Since the appearance in cognition is devoid of a real object, there is no occasion for defects that arise from the causal capacity of real entities; thus,
even when it takes a single form as its object, it remains undetermined.

An entity that possesses one form, which is grasped by a cognition that expects another form, appears as non-different in the intellect even when associated with different words and meanings; thus, the relations of qualifier and qualified,
as well as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), are not contradicted according to how they are perceived.
Even the distinction between property and property-bearer belongs to this [object];
when there is the possibility of a distinction among multiple objects,
that very same entity is what is intended when one desires to know the affirmation or negation of a distinction regarding a single object among them.

Having prompted [the opponent] with the word "dharma" (property), which excludes other distinct entities, and because it appears thus to the cognition, another nature of this [subject], which is undifferentiated from the property as if it were a separate property,
is established as the subject (*dharmin*) and demonstrated.
And to that extent,
because there is a distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin), the cognition appears as if it possesses distinction; it does not arise from a real ontological distinction.
Because of the aforementioned fault; for,
by urging such a multiplicity of distinctions,
there would be a distinction in the statements and a distinction between the probandum and the probans, based on their respective intrinsic natures.
It is produced through various appearances of phenomena (dharma) for the sake of realizing its own intrinsic nature;
because it grasps that intrinsic nature, the cognition is as if directed toward that object, though it is actually devoid of an object.
Conceptual cognition arises, which is determined by the distinction between that [object] and its effects. //76//
In that [cognition], the form which appears as if it were a single external object, appearing as if excluded from others, is devoid of reality because it cannot withstand critical examination. //77//
Since those objects are established within cognition and consist of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they appear as if non-different [from one another], yet they are excluded from others. //78//
It is precisely by means of cognitions and designations that have as their object a commonality and a common substratum for those [particulars] that false discourse is extended. (79)
And all of that is based on the mutual non-existence of things;
therefore, it has the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) as its object and is the basis for the attainment of the real entity (vastu). //80//
Where there is a real connection with an object, as in the aforementioned inference, [the cognition is valid];
it is not so elsewhere, even if there is a similarity to error, just as the light of a lamp [is not the jewel] when [mistakenly perceived] as a gem. (81)

In that case, although many [entities] have a single effect, they are made to conform to worldly practice through designations and cognitions of unity, based on their exclusion from those things that do not produce that effect. (82)

Likewise, although it is a single entity that performs many functions, when its nature is fully revealed, it is perceived as possessing various properties through the distinction of those objects which do not constitute its effects. //83//

This meaning of words is stated according to common cognition; although it does not exist [ultimately], grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is not possible for it with respect to a real entity. //84//

The determination of property and its possessor, as well as their distinction and non-distinction, is of such a nature that it is understood in the world without having examined the reality of the object. (85)

Relying upon that very [conventional reality] in such a manner, the establishment of the probandum and the means of proof is conceived by the wise for the purpose of entering into the ultimate truth. //86//
Ultimately real objects are neither conjoined nor divided by themselves;
that they appear as both one and many is a cognitive distortion (*buddhy-upaplava*). //87//
Therefore, this distinction exists within the conceptual object (*bauddha-artha*); thus, there is both the universal and the particular.
And by means of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), a differentiation of properties (*dharma-bheda*) is conceptually constructed for that very [object]. (88)

Because the perception of the real entity is abandoned when there is a conceptual construction of the probandum and the probans, it is the particular (bheda) conjoined with the universal that is the object of apprehension here, not the specific individuality (svalakṣaṇa). //89//
That [object] cannot be apprehended in any way through forms such as "identical" or "different," because it is impossible for many distinct differences to exist within that single [entity]. (90)

That form [of the object] is distinct from everything else; likewise, there is no scripture or conceptual construction that expresses it, because [all such means of cognition] function solely by way of universals (sāmānya). //91//
These are the summary verses.
Furthermore, what is the reason that words are not applied to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? Because:
Words express that which has been conventionally designated; that [designation] is remembered for the sake of practical usage.
At that time, the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not exist; therefore, no convention applies to it.
For words do not reveal an object that has not been conventionally designated.
And a convention is established for the sake of practical usage, so that indeed from this word, once the convention has been made, [the object may be understood].
One might think that the word would apply to this object at a later time;
however, it is not logical for a word whose connection was previously established with one particular specific individual (svalakṣaṇa) to be used later [for another].

Because it is not apprehended as distinct by way of place, time, or individual manifestation, there can be no linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If that is so, then the universal (*sāmānya*) must be pervasive, whether it be distinct or non-distinct [from the particular].
It is expressed by words;
therefore, there is no fault regarding the absence [of the object] at the time of linguistic usage. This is not so, because:
A person would also act only after having recognized those things capable of purposeful action.
For the purpose of establishing that [object], denotative words are applied to meanings. //93//
Indeed, it is certainly not a calamity for the world that one should suffer pain because of not making conventions or not employing words; rather,
everything is indeed to be attended to by him.
An undertaking is for the sake of a fruit,
because an undertaking that is fruitless is to be disregarded. Therefore, one who employs even words in some context must have some fruit in mind.
It is proper to strive for that which is characterized by the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired;
therefore, having understood what is the means and what is not the means for achieving the desired and avoiding the undesired, one should act accordingly.
One would employ words such as "I shall engage in activity" or "I shall cause [another] to engage," or one would attend to the injunction;
otherwise, there would be no need for such dependence.
In that regard, a universal (jāti) is incapable of performing a purposeful action (arthakriyā). For a universal never serves for such things as carrying or milking;
nor is there any context [for its utility] of that sort.
Without [the genus], there would be no use of words in worldly transactions.
If it is argued that the genus is denoted for the purpose of characterizing the individual— which cannot itself be denoted— then:
Even if a relationship [between word and object] exists, how could one act when it is not indicated by a word?
For no one [acts] toward a staff...
When it is said, "Cut!", one cuts the person holding the staff;
nor does the application [of the word] occur toward the individual because of impossibility,
for in that case, one would be a speaker of incoherent nonsense.
There is no application [of the word] to anything other than that, like the injunction to milk a bull;
nor is there the indication of one thing by means of an injunction for another thing.
For even when a relation exists, there is no cognition of the possessor of the staff (*daṇḍin*) from the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*).
If it is argued that this is because the relation in that case is not fixed,
then that [lack of a fixed relation] is equally true in the case of the universal (*jāti*).
Furthermore, because the universal alone persists even when individuals have disappeared, whereas words such as "brother" and the like—
being relative terms— would imply another [related entity], the same is not the case for the auditory cognitions of universals such as "cowness," which do not denote a related entity.
Because even for universals that have departed from their particulars, there would follow the consequence of their constant persistence through those auditions [of words],
due to their eternal connection with them.
If it is argued that this is indeed desired because the capacity [of the word] is perceived,
then there would never be any application of the word "cow" at all.

Because there is no specific implication regarding the states of being accompanied or unaccompanied. If it is argued that there is no fault because the injunction refers to the universal (jāti) as related to the individual (vyakti),
then [the universal] must always be a qualifier of that [individual].
Since the individual (vyakti) as it exists would already be implied [by the universal], that which possesses it (tadvān) would have to be the denotable object;
however, there is no relation whatsoever between the universal and the individual, because they do not assist one another by way of being produced or producing.
Therefore, even the [application of] a characteristic is untenable.
Consequently, there is no application of a word to a genus because of the absence of a result. If that is so, then:
"Since that which possesses it (the universal) is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the word is applied to it;
and that [word]..."
Why is it not applied directly?
If the application of the word to the individual were fruitful,
why then is that word [not applied] directly?
It is not enjoined with respect to individuals alone;
what need is there for another intervention in that case?
If it is argued that this is due to their infinity, then this [objection] is equal [to ours]. //94//

It might be argued that because individual instances (*vyakti*) are infinite, it is impossible to establish a relationship between them and a word. But this infinity applies equally to the possessor of the universal (*tadvat*) as well; for even by means of a universal, only the manifested individual can be expressed, and thus that which has not had a relationship established cannot be denoted.
In that case, a connection must necessarily be established;
yet it cannot be done. If it is argued that by establishing [the connection] with that which is related to it, it is effectively established there as well, it has already been stated [in response].
In this case, even if there were a relationship, there would be no cognition of what is produced in one place in another; nor does such a relationship exist. Furthermore:
when those who produce that [effect] are identical to those who do not produce it in terms of their distinction from others, why is [the effect] not produced [by the latter]?

With reference to whatever purposeful action one intends when employing words for objects, since those objects that perform that action are distinct from others, why is the word not applied to them alone, given that they are non-different in that respect?
If it is argued that [the universal] exists because the defect is the same [in both cases], then let there be a further universal; enough [with this discussion]. //95//

It might be argued as follows: even if the referent of a word is the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), since it denotes that which possesses such exclusion (*tadvat*) as qualified by that exclusion, there is no difference from the position [that the referent is] that which possesses it (*tadvat*). For what difference is there here between "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*)...

Whether it be "the universal is that which possesses exclusion" or "the universal is that which possesses universals," let there be this fault of [the universal] being like that; let the universal not be something other [than the individual].
For even by one who accepts birth, a distinction between entities must necessarily be accepted;
in the absence of that [distinction], there would be no such thing as birth.
By way of this consequence, let there be the cognition of difference from one [entity] and non-difference from others among those objects qualified by that [one];
for it is impossible to avoid the fault in every respect.
Because it is impossible;
because there is no purpose in admitting a different object;
and because that object is established by another means.
And because the acceptance of that [distinction] is necessarily entailed;
moreover,
the word "sound" functions by excluding what is other than itself.
It is said: "Therefore, if this [universal] is not excluded from those [particulars], how can it [be established]? (96)
For when employing a word, one employs it with the intention that the listener should act toward objects by avoiding what is undesirable; thus,
in that context and elsewhere, there is the mention of its name for the sake of permitting such activity.

Because it would be redundant; and if there were permission for engagement and withdrawal, then due to the lack of regard for a single injunction, there would be no statement at all if there were no expression of the exclusion of others.
Therefore, necessarily...
Exclusion must be indicated by the word,
and since that [exclusion] is non-different from others [of the same class], it also possesses the characteristic of a universal (jāti).
To abandon that which is accepted as certain, that which is subject to certain censure, and that which establishes the meaning of a genus, and instead to postulate some other meaning,
is merely a stubborn adherence to what is useless.
Because it is not possible for this [exclusion] to exist according to its conceptual construction;
indeed, exclusion is not what is being performed. Rather, when those who speak of the object of engagement [in practice] state "universal" (jāti), they are referring to that very [exclusion].
If there is indeed this exclusion [of other objects] for it, then surely this much alone is the purpose of words; what need have you for another, separate universal in that regard? (97)
But was it not said that "the object of engagement is being demonstrated"?
This was indeed said; however, what was said is incorrect. For it has already been explained that this [object] is not fit for engagement.
By that same reasoning, activity toward what is not enjoined is also refuted; and likewise, there would be an intervention in the case of an injunction.
If the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) are accepted as the objects of linguistic application, why are the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and its possessor not likewise accepted?
If it is argued that this is because exclusion, being a non-entity (*avastu*), cannot serve as a means of proof (*asādhanatva*), then [the following applies]:
[The opponent argues: "The [objection] regarding the universal (*jāti*) is equal;

if it is claimed that there is no fault because one proves [the property] through its possessor (*tadvat*), then that [objection] is equally applicable to that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttimat*)."
Furthermore, for those who maintain the theory of exclusion (*apoha*), verbal cognition apprehends a non-entity.

Under the influence of error, it induces activity by determining as a causal factor that which is not a causal factor. However, correspondence with the real object occurs only when there is a connection between that [cognition] and the real object through the production of the object from that [cause].
Otherwise, it does not exist at all.
If it is argued that there is no error because the object has arisen, we say no; for [the cognition] does not manifest that [object].
Because of the determination of that [object],
and because of the deviation seen in the case of the illusion of a jewel in the luster of a jewel.
If it is argued that error possesses correspondence with a real object (*avastu-saṃvāda*), we say no;
for there is a deviation from this rule by what has already been stated.
Indeed, the definition of error is the appearance of what is unreal (*vitatha-pratibhāsa*).

However, because it is invariably concomitant with that [object], the correspondence does not depend upon appearance. But when one acts toward a real entity (vastu) with a mind directed toward it as it actually exists, there is no action toward the universal (sāmānya), which is the object of apprehension,
because it lacks the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā).
Furthermore, if it were to function otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension;
and if it were to grasp that [object] as possessing the property, the uselessness of the universal and other such faults have already been stated.

If it is argued that even when the universal (jāti) is not apprehended, cognition proceeds as if it were connected [to the object] due to a latent impression (saṃbandha), then neither the universal nor its possessor exists, because not even a single intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is apprehended;
thus, one would merely be relying on the opponent's own doctrine.
In that case, since there would be no persisting entity, there could be no recognition— such as "this is that very same thing"— regarding objects that differ from their original state.

This is not a fault, because: "Even though there is difference, one observes that objects perform this or that purposeful action such as cognition; [these objects] are then associated with sounds whose scope is the exclusion of what is other than them. (98)
One might even perform a recognition by connecting [past and present perceptions] upon seeing another [object].
This has already been stated: although there is a difference [between individual entities], things produce identical purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), just like the eye and other [senses].
For one who perceives that single purposeful action—such as cognition and so forth—among those [entities], it is due to the very nature of things (*vastudharmatā*).

In this very way, entities being differentiated from others produce a false cognition in which that [entity] itself appears as conjoined with a sound whose object is the exclusion of those [others], and which— through the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of one's own experience— is conjoined with a differentiation [that does not exist in reality].
Otherwise, cognition would not possess both distinction and connection,
as is the case with [the perception of] men carrying staffs.
For even when the same single staff is joined elsewhere, the cognition "this is that very same one" does not arise; rather,
the cognition is "that is here."
And recognition is not like this; rather, it is "this is that very same thing. Therefore, that [argument] is not [valid].

Even for one who perceives that single [entity] in many places, it is logical that there is both distinction and connection; however, there is no contradiction in such cognition occurring through the force of delusion (*vibhrama*). Yet, delusion cannot exist in the absence of a cause.
If it is argued that this is incorrect, [we reply:

those very entities, which perform a single function, are the cause by virtue of being, through the medium of experience, the cause for the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction—which has delusion as its fruit—due to their inherent nature. Thus, they are the efficient cause (*nimitta*).

For even in the case of mirages and the like, those two distinct entities— which, despite being different, produce the experience that serves as the cause for the cognition of a single, undifferentiated form of the illusion of water— are the cause;
for there is no other universal (sāmānya) whatsoever therein that exists in such a manner.
It would be perceived; or else, if it exists, a cognition grasping an existent object could not be an error.
If it is argued that it is an error because of the superimposition of an unreal form, then it is not [a cognition] of that universal.

It is apprehending; for indeed, whatever form this [cognition] superimposes, that alone is its object, because it is impossible to superimpose what has not been made an object, just like any other form. That...
And since that [universal] does not exist there, it is not a universal.
If it is argued that the superimposition of that [universal] occurs when a universal is perceived, and not otherwise, because otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
If it is the case that [the term] "performing a single function" is employed,
why is it not accepted?
And even for one who necessarily accepts it, the generality of individual instances must be [acknowledged].
The capacity to produce an effect must be admitted; therefore, it is those very [particulars] themselves, as distinguished from others,
that produce such a cognition— so what is the use of a universal (sāmānya) here?
If it is asked, "Why does one not perceive it exactly as it is, with its distinctions unconfused?"—
the answer is that this is due to incapacity.

Because conceptual constructions arise from ignorance (*avidyā*), errors do not necessarily depend upon external objects; rather, they may also arise from internal disturbances, such as the optical illusion of [floating] hairs and the like. Ignorance—

If [it were argued that] because it arises from [ignorance], the same consequence would apply even to visual consciousness and the rest, we say: no; for that [ignorance] is characterized by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and ignorance is indeed nothing but conceptualization.
That [cognition] is erroneous by its very nature;
sensory cognitions, however, are not conceptual in this way. Nor...
Or rather, we shall explain that this same fault applies even to those [Yogācārins] because of the appearance of duality within non-duality;
for even when all things are subject to cognitive distortion, the distinction between valid cognition and its semblance persists until the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*),
due to the correspondence with what is intended as capable of causal efficiency.
Even though it is false,
it is conducive to tranquility, like the perception of one's mother [toward a friend],
or like the cognition of water in a mirage.

Furthermore, although there is no distinction between the arising of a different state and that of an error, [cognitions] are [respectively] consistent with the object and otherwise because they arise as being capable or incapable of the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). If it is asked, "How can there be an arising from what is incapable? [the answer follows].
Because there is no necessary connection between conceptual constructions and their objects,
conceptual constructions do not necessarily arise in accordance with reality; for instance,
when one perceives a mirage.

It is said that "it is an error regarding water" because it arises from that [cognition], and not because it conforms to the actual nature [of the object]. This is because it is produced by an object that distinguishes [itself] from what is not water, by presenting a representation that imitates the actual nature [of the object].
However, due to a lack of proficiency in perceiving specific characteristics, that [error] depends upon its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and [other] conditions.
It is produced by awakening;
therefore, it arises from a conceptual error born of a distinct state of being.

This recognition that "this is that very same thing" does not arise from the perception of a universal (sāmānya) that is distinct [from the individual], nor from one that is non-distinct, because— like the individual itself— it would lack continuity. Furthermore:
Even for another person, that cognition does not arise from the universal alone.
For even another person cannot claim that this cognition arises from the universal alone;
for if it were always a cognition of that [universal] alone, it would follow that there is no cognition of the individual.

For if the universal alone were grasped by this cognition as something eternal, then the individual would remain entirely unperceived by this knowledge; in that case, how could there ever be a connection with the possessor of that [universal], which has not been grasped? (100)
There would be no certainty regarding its possession [of the universal], and how then could there be linguistic convention?
When, for a cognition grasping the universal, the particular is not employed as its objective support (*ālambana*), then those two are never grasped as conjoined; this is his [point].
Otherwise, there would be no cognition of the form "this is the universal" or "this possesses that [universal]"; and thus, through the cognition of that [universal],
there would be no cognition of the possessor of it, just as in the case of a different object.
If individual manifestations, accompanied by a single entity, are the cause of cognition; //101//
It might be argued that these individual manifestations (*vyakti*) are the cause [of the cognition] by way of being its objective support (*ālambana*), but not in isolation; rather,
when they possess a single auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*), then they are perceived together with it.
Does that single object remove their diversity?
And because of their diversity, it is not accepted that they are the cause of a single cognition.
How indeed is the plurality of those distinct things refuted by that single [cognition]?
For it is said that their plurality consists in their not being the cause of a single cognition.
Even if there are many things, if they produce a non-differentiated cognition with respect to a single [object], [they are one].
We do not say that a plurality does not produce a single cognition because of its diversity. Diversity is not opposed to production;
what then?
Isolation [is achieved].
Thus, accompanied by that one [cause], they indeed produce [cognition]. If this is so, then [regarding] the cognition produced individually even without them: //103//
Because even by that single [universal], they lack the capacity [to produce the cognition], there is no apprehension of them by the intellect.
[Objection: How, then, is the capacity of the individuals understood in that cognition? [Response: Because that [cognition] occurs even in the absence of each of those [individuals].
This fault does not apply, because [the cognition] would be absent if the universal were non-existent, whereas otherwise it exists;
just as in the case of blue and other colors, even when one is removed, visual consciousness [still arises].
It is so;
even in their collection, they lack that capacity.
Likewise here too, since it occurs even when each one is individually absent, there is no capacity at all times.
This is an unequal comparison; for it is thus:
because the distinct capacity of blue and so forth is observed in visual cognition. (104)
