The establishment of causal capacity (śakti) does not exist even in a collection in this way; how could it possibly exist in an individual?
For it is observed that blue and other [colors] each possess the capacity for visual cognition;
thus, capacity in a collection is not contradictory.
Likewise, individual instances never produce a continuous cognition independently of the universal;
therefore, they are incapable [of doing so].
In that case, since the individuals themselves are not present there, they would not be apprehended by it;
if it were capable [of apprehending them], that capability would depend upon one or another of those individuals, and not exist independently.

Furthermore, it might be argued that a weaver does not produce a cloth in the absence of the loom individually; even when the loom is absent, the weaver still acts, yet the cloth is not produced from him alone. Likewise, even when individual instances are removed one by one, the universal persists in the production of cognition.
That is not the cause. What then?
Cognition arises in dependence upon some one among the individuals. This being so:
How could those [particulars] assist that single [universal], yet not assist a single cognition?

For it is contradictory for distinct objects to perform a single function; this is the entire point of the present undertaking. If those manifestations, though distinct, do indeed assist a single universal—
But what offense has been committed by these [elements] against consciousness that they do not assist it? What is the use of an internal, redundant "universal" (*sāmānya*),
as if [dealing with] things that are not distinct?
If they possess the power to assist through a single commonality, let them thus produce that very same single cognition.
Furthermore:
"And their effect is obtained; for that which is assistance is indeed production. (106)
For indeed, there can be no so-called "benefactor" for that which, like before, maintains its own nature without any excellence;
otherwise, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Even if it produces a different object, what does that have to do with it? If that [object] were its substratum, what kind of relationship between substratum and dependent could there be for something that provides no assistance?
Or else, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Since that very [cause] is the obstacle to it even when there is assistance,
what other [factor] could be its benefactor by producing it?
[It would be so] only for the substratum that depends upon it.
If it provides no assistance when that [cause] is employed, what is this so-called "dependence"?
A phenomenon whose nature is to arise from that [cause] is said to depend [on it] because of an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), not because its excellence can be added to it.
It is contradictory to say that "the self depends on others. Therefore,
whatever relation exists between anything and something else, it is entirely subsumed under the category of being produced (*janyatā*),
because there can be no assistance toward the production of an already existing entity from another.
And because that which is ineffective provides no assistance;
therefore, it is the universal, assisted by the individual, that produces cognition.
In the case of production, its status as an effect of that [cause] is clearly established;
however, even if the individual [manifestations] were alone capable, since their capacity is not established anywhere in this context, they would be ungraspable.
If it is argued that individuals are capable [of producing cognition] because they appear in consciousness,

then how can there be an appearance of those whose assistance is unestablished? This very point must be considered when accepting a universal (*sāmānya*), because that which does not provide assistance cannot be an object, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
That which is not an object does not appear in consciousness.
Since that which provides no assistance cannot be an object,
past, future, and other such things would not be objects because non-existent things lack the capacity to provide assistance.
If this is argued, let it be granted that those [cognitions] have no objects;
even in the absence of an object, there occurs an appearance that conforms to it, because it arises from a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of that form.
It is indeed the very self-nature of consciousness;
moreover, its capacity follows from existence and non-existence,
not from mere appearance.

Because a universal exists apart from the individual even though it does not appear [as such], and because there is an absence of appearances such as [illusory] hair and the like despite their appearing;
if it is thought that a cognition with a non-differentiated appearance does not [arise] regarding distinct things.
We do not say that multiple [causes] do not perform a single effect;
rather,
we say that a cognition which has been impressed with the forms of distinct objects does not appear as non-distinct.

It cannot be so; for there is no appearance of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) in cognitions that grasp universals (*sāmānya*), because those [cognitions] occur even in the absence of that [particular], and because it appears in its own cognition through a different form (*ākāra*). Furthermore, it is impossible for a single thing to possess multiple forms, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, this [cognition], which arises from that [object] and does not manifest as that [object], does not appear as non-different even though it grasps distinct objects.
It does not manifest as such.
Even so, due to the delusion of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), it causes the world to engage in conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). However,
that form appearing therein does not exist in external objects,
except for the non-difference [of the universal] from the particulars.
And that [object] is formless;
it was stated previously that this [cognition], while grasping that very [object], thus undergoes such a distortion. Furthermore:
For even for those who maintain that there is a real universal (*vastu-sāmānya*), the individuals (*vyakti*) are indeed distinct;
thus, the objection—"How can there be a cognition of a non-distinct form regarding these [distinct individuals]?"—is equally applicable.
It is not equal, because in that case a non-distinct universal actually exists. But is it not so in that case?
Its appearance is not perceived even though it exists;
for that [appearance] is manifested as possessing the manifestation of color and shape.
And there is no such universal;
nor is there any non-different form that is distinct from it.

Even for one who maintains that the universal is the form (ākṛti), because that [form] is non-distinct from the particular, it does not subsist in other objects; thus, due to this difference, a non-different appearance is not tenable. Or, let it be so.
The appearance is distinct from the cognition; they are said to be "identical" because of the apprehension of that [appearance]. //107//
There is no undifferentiated appearance in those [individuals] based on the apprehension that "they are similar. For it is not logical that they be called "similar" when there is a single appearance;
rather, it should be "that very same thing."

If it is argued that there is no fault because both are apprehended, even so, one would have to say "that is here," rather than "it is the same. If it is argued that their very identity constitutes their similarity, [we reply: no.
How is there mutual similarity? If it is argued that this is due to their connection (*sambandha*), we say no; for a connection belongs to that which is dependent.
Because it is illogical and because it would lead to an over-extension [of the definition].
If those [particulars] are identical, how can they be apprehended by distinct cognitions?
Is it not the case that there is indeed an undifferentiated appearance in them simply because they are apprehended as "identical"? No, indeed.
In the perception of that [object], because both the distinct and the non-distinct appear, there is the cognition "they are similar.
What, then, is it?
It is the state of having a single effect.
[It is] similarity.
For we do not perceive two forms in the cognition of an object; and not perceiving [them],...

Why do we deceive ourselves by imagining two distinct objects? Rather, individual instances that perform a single function come within the scope of conceptual construction; thus, they are blended through this error, and this is faultless.
But surely cognition is their effect, and that [cognition] is differentiated. //108//
[It is] for each individual manifestation;

for likewise, there is a distinction even in the consciousness that manifests as that [object]. How, then, could they have a single effect? For that which is their effect is itself divided. Whatever...

Even a single effect such as a jar, including its function of carrying water and so forth, is indeed differentiated according to each individual substance because they are distinct; thus, there is no single effect common to all particulars.
This is not a fault, because:
Because it is the cause of a single unifying cognition, the intellect is non-different;
and by virtue of being the cause of that single cognition, the individual manifestations are also non-different. (109)
It has been explained that there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) or conjunction of entities;
in that regard, the cognition possessing a conjoined form is nothing but an error. However, those [entities] which are distinct...
And [it is said]: "Objects, becoming causes for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in succession, produce [them] by their very nature.

Yet, this non-differentiation among them is called the "differentiation" (*bheda*) of cognition and so forth, because it consists in the exclusion (*viveka*) of that which has a nature not capable of producing a certain single effect. That too—
Although it differs with respect to each individual substance, being by its very nature the cause of a single reflective awareness that transcends difference, it appears as non-different;
for it is the cause of such a reflective awareness.
Because objects such as cognitions that appear as non-distinct are the cause [of that appearance],

it has been stated more than once that even individual instances (vyakti), by their very nature, produce a single cognition whose form is integrated, despite having as their ultimate reality a distinction of intrinsic natures (svabhāva-bheda). Therefore...
The non-difference of entities consists precisely in their having a single effect,
and that [non-difference] is simply the exclusion of what does not have that effect.
Because no other persisting entity is observed, and because [such an entity] is negated.
For it has already been stated that there is no visible object that does not appear through differentiation;
or, if such a thing existed, how could it, being unestablished anywhere, be a cause of cognition? This is the refutation.
And because it is established [otherwise], the postulation of that [intrinsic nature] is incorrect. Therefore,
it is merely a convention (*saṃketa*).
One who seeks that knowledge. //110//

This alone is logical: this mutual distinction (*viveka*) among entities, for the sake of which even a convention (*saṃketa*) is established, would be appropriate because it serves the purpose of activity through the exclusion of what does not perform that function. For if the convention were not for the sake of cognizing that [distinction], its application in practical discourse (*vyavahāra*)—
Even at that time, because there is no contact [with the excluded objects], one would not proceed by means of the exclusion of others;
for their distinction from those [others] has not been signified by the word.
And that is the [nature of] the hearing [of the word].

The cognition that appears as having a form similar to that which performs the action and that which does not perform it has as its seed merely the distinctness of things [from one another], and is thus devoid of [external] objects. (111)

Even though they produce [a cognition], they are considered non-deceptive regarding the object, because they serve as factors for the exclusion of what does not perform that function and because they rely on a distinction among real entities. (112)
Therefore, because it has as its object the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and because it depends on that which produces it, [this cognition]—

arising by superimposing that [exclusion] upon objects that lack a single inherent nature (*svabhāva*)— is a false appearance; thus, although it does not produce that effect, it determines [the object] as if it were producing that effect.

Although the scripture generates a false cognition— one whose seed is merely the distinctness of things and which possesses a uniform conceptual determination— it is said not to be non-concordant with respect to those entities that are ultimately distinct from it, because it lacks the capacity to exclude anything other than them.
For that distinction among them is real,
because it cannot be transcended in any way.
It is neither one nor distinct, for either [of those] is entirely untenable in its case.
In the case of an object that is being entered [into cognition], the object would indeed be left far behind by both word and cognition,
because that which is intended as their object does not exist, and there is no other object.
Because no [positive] entity whatsoever is contacted [by it],
for that very reason that scriptural statement is said to have "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) as its object.
Because it is applied without distinction by taking up the specific differences of exclusion among objects excluded from others,
even in conventional usage, it functions through the exclusion of what is other.
Because it functions [to exclude others], when the meaning of "tree" is apprehended by way of its exclusion from non-trees, there are two [aspects]. //113//
"It is a mutual dependence: in the absence of the apprehension of one, there is no apprehension of the two;
therefore, the application of convention is impossible"—so some declare. (114)

If a tree is the exclusion of non-trees, it cannot be apprehended without the apprehension of non-trees; for one who has not cognized a tree does not fully understand the nature of the exclusion of non-trees. Since there can be no linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) regarding an object that has not entered the mind, [the tree cannot be established].
Some say that it is possible [to establish a convention].
For them, are non-trees excluded from the convention or not?
Thus, having accepted a single real universal (*vastu-sāmānya*), they fall into the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
They raise the objection that convention is established through the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*).
To them, [the response is]: even when establishing a convention in that regard, are non-trees excluded or not?
If [they] are excluded, how could they be known prior to the apprehension of the tree? //115//

For at that time, the cognizer does not know the tree nor the non-tree, since he approaches [the object] out of a desire for that very knowledge. Being thus ignorant, how could he [know] the exclusion of the non-tree?
One would understand [the meaning] through convention;
and in the absence of such understanding, from a word that does not exclude others and does not apply to them, [no comprehension would arise].
If those [particulars] were not excluded from the linguistic convention, then for those engaged in practical activity,
there would be no engagement by way of avoiding them, just as in the case of specific trees.
For it is not reasonable that, when a word has been applied during convention by way of excluding others, there should be activity in actual usage toward those [excluded objects] while avoiding them;
just as in the case of the various distinctions such as the *śiṃśapā* tree and so forth.
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"Without prescribing one thing or excluding another, having pointed out a single object standing before one, the convention 'this is a tree' is established; that [object] is what is understood."

If it is argued that there is no fault in this regard even within conventional usage, we reply: No; for one who maintains that the universal is a real entity does not, through the exclusion of something, establish anything at all. What then?
Having pointed out a single object standing before one,
the convention "this is a tree" is established;
at the time of the convention, it was perceived in that manner.
In this way, one understands this very object or its related property even in conventional usage;
thus, the objection is not the same.
It is not the same.
Because even in that case,
the undesirable consequence— that "this is a tree" and "this too is that very same [tree]"— does not cease.

Having pointed out one [tree] and saying "this is a tree," even if one says "this too is that very same [tree]," one does not transcend these two alternatives; and in both cases, that same fault remains. It is not without fault.
Because that which is the opposite of what has been seen is easily known:
for one who sees something as a single entity and experiences a cognition elsewhere that distinguishes it from that form, [it is known] as "other than that" in accordance with that experience.

The ascertainment of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-niścaya*), which discriminates that [object], arises. For this very person has been instructed by being shown, "This is indeed a tree," [and] where that [tree] does not exist...
One sees that very treeless [space] and realizes it for oneself;
this is not possible for one who maintains the doctrine of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

Because a form perceived in one place does not persist anywhere else, there would be no such cognition of it even when another individual is seen. If that is the case, then this [objection] applies equally there as well; for:
For when the cognizer is established in a single cognition called "unitary reflective awareness," he himself distinguishes between objects that are causes of that [awareness] and those that are not.
This has already been explained: although these entities differ in their intrinsic natures (*prakṛti*), some produce a single effect such as cognition, while others do not;
this [person] himself [perceives] them therein.

Thus, having distinguished between those things that are causes of it and those that are not, one understands them. For that person, the entities appearing within that cognition appear as causes to the mind;
though they are themselves devoid of the nature of being a cause, they appear as if they possess a single, uniform nature. (120)
The statement "one should apprehend [the object] through its differentiation" is intended to enjoin differentiation;
yet the cognition that perceives this [differentiation] of that [object] views it, through delusion, as if it were a single entity. //121//

Because of the persistence of those [objects], which by their very nature serve as the causes for such conceptual constructions due to the influence of conditions, they appear in the mind of the observer; and because they are the cause of that cognition and are excluded from others, they are determined as being "thus" (tathā), even though they are not actually so.

The cognizer, following his own cognition, perceives these trees— whose internal and external distinctions are undivided— as having a single appearance within his own and others' conceptual constructions; thus established in that conceptual consciousness, he would perceive the causes of that consciousness as distinct.
Thus, [the word] enjoins the exclusion from those things which are not its causes;
the conceptual cognition that apprehends this [exclusion], by the power of error alone, appears as if it were grasping a single entity.
It appears [to the mind],
yet there is no single object perceived therein through whose perception and non-perception this distinction between "tree" and "non-tree" would occur, even though the perceptions are distinct.

One should not do so; for, due to the distinction between the appearance of the branches and so forth, the universal is not perceived in the same way as a staff-bearer is perceived by means of his staff. Furthermore, that which is not perceived cannot be characterized through its further distinctions. Moreover, a form observed in one instance cannot be seen in another.
In the case of being a tree or a non-tree for that which possesses those [properties] and that which does not, the individual would be the only tree;
let it be so for a jar and the like.
In the case of words, there is the exclusion of other referents (*arthāntara-vyavaccheda*).
Now, how is this the case with words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) and so forth?
For there is nothing whatsoever that is unknowable, from which [the knowable] could be distinguished.
Since that [object] is indeed knowable only when it is apprehended through differentiation (*bheda*),
this fault does not apply; for:
In some cases, for the purpose of settling [the mind] upon a certain object, a word is employed by turning the intellect away from something else, in order to ascertain that specific object.

Otherwise, the employment [of words] would be useless; therefore, even in the case of terms such as "knowable" and so forth when they are brought into common usage, there is something that is to be excluded.
For everyone employing a word does not transcend positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*),
because its purpose consists in the engagement with or the withdrawal from [an object].
For if this [word] were not [connected] to anything from anything...
One should either withdraw or engage the intellect according to the knowledge of things as they truly are;
in all conventional dealings, one should not say anything that contradicts [this],
for such speech would constitute a definitive assertion [of error].
Because of the invariable concomitance [of the means with the end],
just as in the case of the command, "Bring water with a jar. If [one were to say] "with a jar" or "with cupped hands,"...
Or, if the fetching of water were intended in any manner whatsoever,
one should simply have said, "fetch water," and not "with a jar."
Likewise, [the command] "Bring an object by means of something brought— be it dust or this or whatever else"— would likewise have its instrument and object unexpressed.
Thus, if bringing [the object] or any other such desired performance were [already established], then one would not even say "bring it," because the statement would be purposeless.
Likewise, even for terms such as "the knowable" and so forth, which are brought into common usage, there must be something from which they are excluded; otherwise,
there would be no suspicion of them being anything else.
Because of the impossibility of its application there, for in that case, precisely that which is a point of doubt for one of deluded intellect must be refuted;
or else, if one does not have such a doubt, why would one [seek] it from another?
He depends upon instruction;
and how is one who speaks without refining his audience not insane?
This is because linguistic conventions are established solely for the purpose of refining that [cognition];
furthermore, there exists no word such as "knowable" (*jñeya*) that is not presented within the context of conventional usage.
Because one considers the meaning of a word occurring within a sentence;
for where, indeed, are these words employed?
In the consideration of the object of application (*prayoga-viṣaya*), "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is stated; however,
regarding the word "knowable" (*jñeya*) when its application is not specified, if one asks "what is its meaning?", there is no [specific] meaning at all.
Consequently, there would be no comprehension in some cases;
the same applies to words such as "jar" and so forth.
Furthermore, even when a cognition arises from hearing a word in isolation within a certain context, because it follows observed usage and remains expectant of further information,
that cognition is merely an incomplete manifestation of that [cognition] as found in words such as "pot."

Such [a process] exists indeed even in the case of words such as "the knowable" (*jñeya*), according to how they are observed. Therefore, every employment of a word has the purpose of excluding [the object] from some [other] cognition and establishing it in some [specific] place; for only thus is it fruitful.
And when that upon which a mental placement (niveśana) depends is excluded, those things being differentiated from it appear with an identical form despite their difference. (124)
And this [object], through the exclusion of others, is understood; it is said that there is some "part" of that entity, yet even for that, there is no form whatsoever.
From words directed toward that very [object], the exclusion of others is understood;
therein, no further distinct entity is understood by anyone.
Furthermore, sound does not produce duality; mutual non-existence is non-existent.
To perceive that which is formless as possessing form is a distortion of cognition. //127//
Even when this word is being applied, having excluded that from which it differs, it is applied while excluding others,
as a common form appears in the difference among those things that differ. Thus, the exclusion of what is other than that is implied.

This very same point has been indicated by such statements as: "By means of the exclusion of other objects (arthāntara-vyāvṛtti), some part of that entity is understood; a word expresses entities precisely as qualified by the exclusion of other objects."
For when it expresses that exclusion (bheda), it functions only by implying the exclusion of other objects;
because the indication of an exclusion residing in one thing is necessarily concomitant with the implication of the exclusion of what is other than it.

That very distinction is the "attained portion" through the exclusion of that [other]; because it is its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), when that [exclusion] is attained, it is said that "the thing qualified by it has been attained.
However, the exclusion of other objects is not itself the qualifier.
It is the actual state of certain objects as qualified by which they are expressed by words, like [the word] "staff-bearer.

For when two things are being differentiated, since the distinction belongs to both, even when the distinction of one is expressed, there is an inseparable implication of the other; thus, of those two—
There is no relationship of qualifier and qualified;

for even when a single particularity is denoted, the exclusion of others is understood through the indication of positive concomitance and negative absence, whereby words serve as a constituent part of linguistic usage.

He says that [the object] is understood either by showing [it] through the exclusion of that [other], or as qualified by that [exclusion]. For this very reason, a word does not have two functions: the exclusion of others and the denotation of its own referent.
Because the exclusion of others is understood precisely from the expression of its own meaning,
since the own-meaning consists in differentiation;
for there is no positive concomitance that is not negative, nor any negative concomitance that is not positive.
Or there is the absence of exclusion (vyatireka), because if there is no object to be excluded for a single positive concomitance (anvaya), the injunction would be fruitless;
likewise, if there is no persistence anywhere for a single exclusion.
And this distinction is formless;
its appearance as if it possessed form is merely a cognitive distortion.
Therefore, this [exclusion] is not the ultimate reality; for otherwise, the exclusion of an entity would itself become a real entity, because it is expressed as "this is distinct from that. //128//
For form is the ultimate reality;
if difference were form,
it would be of that nature.
Or it might have a nature other than that;
if it had that very nature, it would be that [entity] itself, and thus it would not be distinct from it.
For the nature of one thing cannot belong to another.
That very thing is not the nature of difference; rather,
its nature would have to be something else entirely,
and consequently, the entity would be excluded from that [nature].
Consequently, there would be no such thing as "its difference from this";
for that which is excluded from something due to a difference from it becomes that very thing itself, and thus it could not be said that "this is its difference. It is not so.
For there would be no mutual distinction [between them],
due to the absence of a relationship; or, if such a relationship exists,
it must be a cause-and-effect relation, and thus, because there is no difference, the form would be that which is produced by that [cause] and the distinction would be that [effect].
All effects would be the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) of their own causes; and if difference were a distinct form (*rūpāntara*),
then because it would possess difference as its limiting adjunct (*bhedopādhitvāt*), this [difference] would also be different from that [cause], just like a separate substance (*dravyāntaravat*).
There would be no difference [between them],
for this is not merely a difference consisting in an adventitious attribute (upādhi), since there is a specific designation [to the contrary].
Consequently, in the absence of a substrate (upādhi), there would be the non-existence of difference itself.
Therefore, it is not distinct [from the thing].
And because there is no other way of understanding it, it is not a real entity (paramārtha) in its own right.

How, then, could other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) not be rendered useless in that case? For when an undifferentiated entity is indicated by a word, since it is differentiated from others, all its differentiations would be understood through the indication of even a single partless differentiation; thus, other means of valid cognition would become redundant. Why is this so? [Because...]

In the case of the interruption of a single-sense pun (*eka-artha-śleṣa*), a single *dhvani* operates; there, no indicated (*vācya*) object whatsoever is interrupted, nor is there any indicative mark (*liṅga*). //129//

Because there is comprehension of the entire object through its denotation by virtue of the object's own capacity, a single word thus possesses manifold fruits while having a single substratum. //130//
It has been stated previously that cognition, having determined its own manifestation— which possesses internal and external distinctions,
is the object of linguistic convention, and is capable of causal efficiency— presents it as the referent of a word.

And in that very [single] locus, those words, through various causes of error, appear as if their forms were mixed together; they function to effect an exclusion according to convention, yet one word does not perform the exclusion that another accomplishes. Convention—
Because of their specific restriction, no disconnected entity whatsoever is implied,
such that by the expression of one [entity], there would be a comprehension of the whole through the power of the object; for words [function] according to the mind—
Because it is the object of an error,
and because in that case there is an absence of causal efficacy in a non-entity,
such being the case—

By way of perceiving the object, this conventional practice— which follows the cognitive distortion (*viplava*) of the appearance of various and unitary properties as being distinct or non-distinct— is non-deviant provided that it is connected to that [object].
Therefore, even in the case of that which is unreal, there is a correspondence with cognition regarding the object as it actually exists at the end;
however, this is not the case for cognitions and words that apprehend different aspects.
Because they have a single entity as their object, a word that has multiple effects would have a single substratum, which is a contradiction.
However, according to the explanation given, there is no fault when the basis is the appearance in cognition (*buddhi-pratibhāsa*).
Indicating a distinction while not rejecting its unity, it exists; when it is pervaded by another, it appears as one with that other. //131//

In that case, there would be grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) by virtue of conforming to the cognition; however, there would be no contact with the actual property of the thing when the sound brings about a distinction [between them]. //132//

It might be true that "he indeed exists there," yet [the word] does not denote a single entity, because the absence of the visible object—which does not appear in the cognition—is ascertained. //133//
These are the intermediate verses.

Therefore, it has been stated that words and cognitions have the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as their object and the universal (*sāmānya*) as their domain, because these [two] are impossible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*). (134)
For if objects were indeed made the objects of words or conceptual constructions by way of positive affirmation (*vidhi-rūpeṇa*), then this [absurdity] would follow:

the cognition of all objects in all their aspects, as well as the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) and other such faults. Thinking thus, the author of the *Nyāya-śāstra* [proposed] *anyāpoha*.
He states these two as the objects [of the critique]: for indeed, since the nature of a real entity is unitary, how could there be a cognition of diverse forms?
Furthermore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) cannot both have a single object as their domain. (135)
How can that single, partless entity be made an object by cognitions that possess diverse forms?
For difference is based upon the diversity of forms.
And because that [particular] is non-different [from it],
the universal, which has that as its essence, shares the same fate (*ekayogakṣema*) as it; thus,
since there is no occurrence of two things with mutually exclusive meanings in a single locus, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity that is the nature of a real thing to both exist and not exist in that very same place, because that would involve a contradiction.
Nor can a universal be something that does not exist elsewhere.
It might be argued that the occurrence belongs to the universal (sāmānya) and not to the particular (viśeṣa). This is not so, because there is no difference [between them].
For that which has a single form must be either the universal or the particular.
For if there were no difference in form (*rūpa*), this distinction would not be logical; or, if it did exist, it has been stated that there could be no non-distinction (*avyatireka*).
Therefore, this undivided [entity] must either persist or not persist.
Furthermore, that which lacks positive concomitance (ananvaya) cannot be a concomitant (anvayin). Even for one who asserts that the universal is indeed distinct [from its instances], for him as well:
"And if there were difference, the linguistic conventions of non-difference would be without basis."
How could words, which denote distinct objects according to their respective natures, serve as the basis for a single cognition of an object? Furthermore,
those denoting different objects would not imply [the presence of] one another.
Since [the cognition] is free from expectancy, how can it be based on the relationship between qualifier and qualified?
These faults do not apply here, because exclusion (vyāvṛtti) exists everywhere. //136//
For just as one [individual] is distinct from that [universal], so too is another; thus, the fault of the universal being non-distinct does not apply.
As for the remaining absence [of a universal], it has already been stated previously. Moreover:

When distinct entities perform a single function, a common term is applied to denote that function, because of the cumbersomeness, incapacity, and futility of expressing each individual distinction. (137)
This [exclusion] has been formulated by the elders based on the exclusion of what does not perform that function;
it does not apply to existence itself, because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all things is established. (138)
That form which belongs to the brindled cow (śābaleya) does not belong to the black cow (bāhuleya); nevertheless, the exclusion of what does not produce that effect exists in both of them. (139)
And without non-difference of the object, non-difference of the word is not tenable;
therefore, even its being an effect of that [object] is desired only as a distinction from what is not its effect. (140)
Just as, in some cases, the eye and so forth have the single fruit of visual consciousness.
Since it is possible to enjoin that effect without distinction, [the injunction would apply to all]. //141//

In order to convey the understanding of everything at once, someone might create a conventional term even in the absence of a real universal (*sāmānya*) that is distinct from those [individuals]. (142)

Furthermore, one might think: "How can there be a single designation (*śruti*) for many things without a single underlying object (*artha*), since those things are not identical? For a single occurrence [of a word] does not produce a cognition in other [things], and if a cognition were produced without such a connection, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, [if it were based on a universal], there would be a single..."

Because the application of a word would be futile [if applied to many], because there is no single injunction regarding a single object, and because when things of distinct natures are enjoined separately,
their distinction cannot be fully understood when they are thus commanded; therefore, even for that [universal],
the world must apply the word by thinking "this one exists."
Or that this single scriptural statement causes [the meaning] to resound by the very power of the thing itself—
this is not so.
Rather, certain words are employed in certain places for some specific purpose.
In that case, if multiple [factors] were to be applied to a single [object], they would necessarily have to be enjoined therein;
for if each were enjoined separately, there would be excessive prolixity.
And it is not the case that this [object] is non-different [from them].
A common form can indeed be challenged;
yet there is no fruit whatsoever for this exertion of his.
Only those objects suitable for that [purpose] should be indicated by this [word];
whether they are indicated by a single word or by many is a matter of the speaker's autonomy in this regard.
Thus, this single scriptural statement, being applied to many [subjects] by virtue of the speaker's intention, does not deserve censure;
nor is it impossible.
It is an instigation,
because it is dependent upon the desire [of the agent].
For if there were no desire of the one who employs [the word], how [could it occur]?
This [cognition] would then function even with respect to a single [object];
or, if it is by desire, who is able to obstruct it even from functioning toward many?
If it is argued that there is simply no engagement because of a lack of purpose, the purpose has already been stated.
It has been stated that when things are distinct, there is a cognition of them as one due to a difference in their purposes,
and not because of the oneness of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), each according to its own [character].

It has already been stated previously that since things with established natures do not possess a mutual admixture of forms, how could a word based on a single nature apply to diverse things? [The answer is:
It is through the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what does not serve that purpose.
Since those that are distinct are not contradictory, let that very non-difference of meaning be the cause of the non-difference of words;
therefore, these [words] have that as their purpose, and thus they are distinguished from those whose purpose is not that.
They are indeed stated to be distinct;

moreover, their status as effects of those [causes] is nothing other than their difference from one another. This is just as in the case of the eye, form, light, and attention, or the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object.

Alternatively, when there is contact with those [factors] which share the single effect of visual consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna*), and when it is possible to designate that commonality of effects, someone might establish a conventional term (*saṃketikī śruti*)—such as "ya-ra" or "śa-so"—for the sake of linguistic brevity, [thinking], "From this comes visual consciousness. Why? Because these are the causes of visual consciousness.
Or rather, [the intention is]: "May there indeed be a simultaneous cognition of all those causes. And yet, there is no single recurring form here;
it is merely for the sake of that [cognition].
Those entities are distinct from things that do not possess that meaning; thus, their very difference is their non-difference.
And all such terms—whether denoting a collection (*samūha*), a continuum (*saṃtāna*), or a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*)—are used collectively in this manner.

Since they perform some single effect and there is no distinction among them in that regard, a specific injunction would be purposeless; therefore, for the sake of applying [a term] to all of them at once, people in this world apply a single word, such as "jar," to them.

Although they are no different from others in terms of their distinction from both their own kind and other things, because they serve as a factor for that specific purpose, they are distinguished from others;
thus, due to this non-difference [from that purpose], they are perceived without distinction from it.

In that context, even the expression "the color and so forth of the jar" means that the color and so forth possess the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the jar, insofar as they are capable of performing specific functions such as holding water;
[this is stated] by way of the self (ātman) established through the accomplishment of its general function. Color—
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), those things well-known as being distinguished by the specific quality of accomplishing particular effects are thus referred to;
however, there is nothing else here that possesses the characteristics as previously described.
There is no such substance, because it is not perceived.
Furthermore, the use of the singular number is either for the purpose of indicating its single capacity or is dependent upon linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). Likewise...
Those things which, being specific causes and effects, accomplish or are accomplished as some single entity,
are likewise— having been assigned a convention by words such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth— spoken of for the sake of a single conceptual object (*pratyaya*),
as should be stated as before.
Even those things which, whether individually or collectively,
are employed in some context, are expressed for the sake of cognition by words denoting specific states all at once—
such as "visible" or "resistant"— in order to distinguish them from others.
By way of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) from what is different;
just as, for example, things that have a single effect are designated by words such as "jar" through an agreement based on their exclusion from what is other than those that produce that same effect.
Likewise, even with respect to the cause, the manifold is treated as one merely for the sake of conventional usage,
just as in the case of a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow).
For example: "Sound is produced by effort, it is non-eternal, or it is created.
Likewise, by negating its effect: "Sound is not visible, it is impermanent, or it is without self.
And by negating its cause: "It is ownerless, or it is empty."
In this manner, other [terms] should also be stated as appropriate;
regarding words such as "empty" (śūnya) and "impermanent" (anitya), [the object] is intended according to conceptual construction (kalpanā).
Having superimposed the form [of the object] upon the cognition, a designation is made by means of its exclusion;
for every verbal referent possesses a division manifested through the intention of the intellect.
Objections such as the introduction of faults that lack a counter-argument are merely the fluctuations of a dull-witted mind and should be disregarded.
Now,
if even multiple things that subsist in a single locus were to possess a single designation,
then it would not be only those things with a single function that are denoted by a single word; for there is no distinction between them and others [that share the same locus].
But even by means of a single occurrence, could many things be expressed by a single word? What contradiction would there be?
It has been stated in this regard: because that which is intended to be perceived is not perceived, it does not exist.
Or, if [the universal] were unperceivable, then designation, recognition, and so forth—which depend upon the perception of that [universal]—would not occur, and so on. Furthermore:
"Subsistence is being contained; manifestation is [the universal's appearance]"—this is not tenable in its case. (143)
Regarding this [universal] which, existing in many places, causes a single word to apply:
what is its mode of existence (*vṛtti*)? Is it perhaps the state of being contained (*ādheyatā*)?
Just as jujube fruits exist in a bowl,
or because the individual instance (*vyakti*) is manifested by them.
If it is the state of being contained (*ādheyatā*):
because that which is eternal cannot be assisted, there can be no substratum (*ādhāra*). For a universal (*sāmānya*) is held to be eternal.
Because in the case of impermanence, there is the arising of successive [moments], there is multiplicity; thus, like a distinct [object], it is impossible for there to be a single cognition [of it].
And what could an eternal [entity] possibly do?
It would be the substratum.
If it is argued that it is the substratum because of its inherence (*samavāya*) therein, what is this so-called "inherence"?
The relationship of locus and located belongs to things that are inseparably established (*apṛthak-siddha*).
We do not admit that this status of being a locus can belong to something that provides no assistance,
for fear of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), and so forth— these relations between entities do not differ from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*),
because there is no mutual or external restriction among things that do not provide assistance to one another.
And because there is no connection for that which is unconnected;
even though [there may be] mutual [connection] among those things inhering in the same object.
There is no assistance [provided by the cause].
Therefore, there must be an assistance from that single [cause]; for if it were non-existent, the aforementioned logical fallacy would ensue.
Therefore, by means of its own benefit alone, it is explained as being connected to another through the intellect;
thus, even in that case, there exists a causal relationship.
The connection has indeed already been established.
Therefore, this claim that the substratum is the support of the universal while providing no benefit to its own nature— being [thus] independent— is merely a borrowed ornament.
[Objection: How then is a bowl, which is currently not producing [the fruit], the support for jujube fruits? [Response:
Because they are spreading out [into it].
The capacity [of a locus] is the production of its own effect in that very place, as in the case of a pit and so forth [producing] jujube fruits and the like. //144//
By its very nature, a heavy substance possesses the property of producing an effect in a different location;
its state of producing an effect in the same location is brought about by the substratum.
Therefore, that [state] is preceded by—

The bowl, acting as a simultaneous auxiliary (*sahakārin*) at that very moment, is called the "support" (*ādhāra*) because it produces the effect of the jujube fruit right there. Otherwise, even the designation "the jujubes are here in the bowl" would not occur. Indeed, this designation is not produced by the assistance rendered by that [bowl].
What then?
It is produced by conjunction.
But is that conjunction between those two alone?
Because it is produced from those two or because it inheres in them, why does it not inhere in only one [of them] or why is it not produced [there]? Because of its lack of capacity.

Since that [entity] is incapable when separate, it remains exactly the same even when conjoined; thus, because there is no assistance rendered, it would not become possessed of that [capacity] through conjunction.
For what is conjoined receives assistance from something other than itself.
The capacity [of the cause] consists in the production of a specific quality.

What kind of assistance can there be for those things that are neither produced nor producers? Since their own nature is already established, they cannot be effects; therefore, [assistance would consist only] in the performance of an action characterized by another form.
Furthermore, because there is no assistance rendered therein;
for it has already been stated that in either case, the agent is ineffective and thus provides no assistance.
Therefore, all relations between entities are established as causal relations through a specific distinction based on the particular functional capacity of the producer alone.
Therefore, this capacity for production in the jujube fruits and so forth, which constitutes the status of the bowl and other vessels as their substratum,
is not possible; that too is absent here.
For this nature of being a substratum, characterized by the act of producing, is not possible for a universal that resides in a universal,
because the latter is unproduced.
Because it persists even in the absence of that [cause],
there is no stability.
Furthermore, it might be argued that the substratum is the stabilizer of the universal, because it is the cause of its persistence.
"The support [of a thing] does not exist because it produces [it];
that is incorrect, because [the thing] remains even in the absence of that [support]."
For indeed, in the case of entities subject to falling, something might be a sustainer even if it is not a producer, by virtue of obstructing their fall;
however, in this case as well, if someone were not to inquire into the nature of that obstruction, [the argument would fail].

For that obstruction to falling is not indeed something distinct from the object itself which would be produced by the agent who establishes it. If it were a distinct entity, its utility would lie solely therein; what, then, would constitute an obstruction to the falling object?
Even if there were no falling due to such an obstruction, the same objection would apply, leading to an infinite regress.

Or rather, the absence of falling is the prevention of falling; how could that be produced by anything? For it is not the case that "one produces an absence," since there is no such thing as an absence that is an effect.
If it were to have the nature of an effect in any way, it would follow that it is not an absence.
Therefore, this is an instruction regarding the negation of the activity of an entity; that is to say, it does not produce an entity.
And thus, this [negation] is not...
Since it performs no action whatsoever, what non-agent could possibly be the establisher of anything? Therefore, being unconnected with anything, this [moment] would never remain;
hence, its falling—

Furthermore, "obstruction" (*pratibandha*) refers to the production [of subsequent moments] in the same location as their material cause (*upādāna*) among momentary entities. Let it be granted that for things subject to falling, there is non-production due to such an obstruction.
Because it causes motion, let there be some sustainer for a substance that possesses movement; but what kind of "staying" could a sustainer effect for a universal, which is devoid of action?
For its staying is simply the non-deviation from its own nature.
And that [cognition] does not depend upon a substratum because it is eternal;
furthermore, it is simply untenable when subjected to the analysis of its difference or non-difference [from the object]. //145//
Granted that the persistence of a universal is caused by its substratum;
is that [persistence] different from the universal,
or is it non-different?

If it were something else, then that [other thing] alone would be its substratum; and since that [universal] is unattached, what would be the use of a substratum for the universal? [This applies] if it were attached.
Or else, it must be stated what the restriction is;
if it is the act of causing stability, then the same consequence applies there as well, and there would be an infinite regress.
Consequently, because no assistance is being rendered, there is no cognition that "this is the state of this [entity].
If [you claim] it is a production, what is the use of a substratum that is required yet provides no assistance?

For "dependence" means a connection with that [cause]; and since it is illogical for a universal (*sāmānya*)—to which no specific quality can be imparted—to have such a connection, [the cause] could only produce it. There is no other cause for its persistence.
Or, if non-difference from the universal is established, then that [particular] is simply its own nature; and since that exists eternally,
its persistence is not brought about by anything else.
Therefore, there is no substratum for the universal;
thus, its occurrence does not consist in being located within something else.
Furthermore, even if the universal exists, its manifestation (*vyakti*) may constitute its occurrence therein, because that manifestation is the cause of its cognition.
It is not logical for it to be so, because:

That which conforms to another within the self for the sake of making consciousness capable of arising is considered the manifestor; and with respect to that capacity, the cause is considered the producer. (146)
Even if its capacity [to produce cognition] were already present, dependence on that [cause] would not be logical;
for how could that [capacity] belong to the possessor of the universal, since the universal itself is unchangeable? (147)

Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between a producer and a manifestor. [The manifestor] is either capable of producing a cognition of its own object while depending on another homogeneous material cause (*upādāna*), or it is independent [of such a cause].

Alternatively, that which produces an entity is called a "manifestor" (vyañjaka). However, in the case of another [type of cause], the capacity to produce cognition is not necessarily implied by the produced effect; thus, its status as a causal factor (kārakatva) consists merely in its act of production.
For if that which acquires the capacity for the production of consciousness from something were not its product,
then that capacity, being its very nature, would have existed there already even prior to it.
Thus, it would not depend upon that [cause] for the production of consciousness; and if this [consciousness] were something other [than its cause],
the consequence would follow that it exists eternally, just like the [cause's] own state.

Therefore, since a manifestor neither produces that [object] nor anything else, it is contradictory to claim that something which performs no function at all is nevertheless required. But surely even things that are not producers— such as smoke and the like— are manifestors because they are effects?

It is true that manifestors [do not produce cognition]; however, fire does not produce cognition of itself by depending on smoke, because such fire is not a direct producer [of its own cognition]. Rather, cognition arises therein solely through the power of the material cause (*upādāna*), and not through the power of the object, since [the object] is non-existent [at that time].
Nor does it exist in that [object] through a succession following the mark;
nor do cognitions appearing as general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) have a proximate object as their domain.
It has already been stated, and will be further explained, that [cognition] arises through power (*bala*). Therefore,
regarding those objects which produce cognition by means of direct application (*sākṣāt-upayoga*), in that case...

They necessarily depend upon that [cause], and from it they obtain their own self-nature. Furthermore, this acquisition of self-nature cannot arise from anything for that which is universal and eternal;
therefore, it is not manifested by anything.
We certainly do not say that the manifestation of a universal is its acquisition of fitness;
what then?
"Inherence in its own substratum.
For that [cognition], whether in itself or elsewhere, is the cause of consciousness when it is inherent in its own substratum.
Regarding this, it has been stated: "What is this relationship characterized as the state of substrate and superstrate between that which is not produced and that which produces?"
Regarding the term "inherence" (*samavāya*):

since it depends on inherence in its own substratum, it would necessarily be produced by cognition as its cause; for that nature [of inherence] did not exist previously, and subsequently arises from that [cognition].
Because [the universal] exists [eternally], if its own nature were always present, it would follow that cognition would arise even prior to the inherence [of the individual]. Indeed,
the manifestation of the universal does not result from the refinement [of the individual].

What, then, is the manifester? It is the sense faculty that perceives it. Furthermore, like collyrium and the like, this refinement pertains to the manifestation [of the object], not to the sense faculty.
Because the cognition is non-different at the times of its presence and its absence. //148//
The sense faculty, when refined by ointments and the like, acquires some degree of excellence in its apprehension, because there is a distinction between clear and unclear perception;
and that which does not produce such [perception] cannot be its refiner.

In this way, there is no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sense organ through its manifestation, because there is no difference in the cognition [of the object] during the times of its presence and absence;
however, the refinement of the object [does affect] the sense organ.
Even if there is no distinction [in the object], it might be beneficial by imparting a specific quality to it;
however, it is not the refinement of the sense faculty.
If it is argued that it is beneficial because it imparts the power of vision to what was previously invisible:
Thus, while demonstrating an object that transcends the senses, how could it not differentiate between cognitions?
[This holds] when there is a restriction to a single [cognition].
Furthermore, there would be no perception of other universals;
and since the sense organ is refined by the individual instance,
when that [instance] is perceived, there might at times be no certain determination regarding the universals manifested by it.
Or else, there would be no certain cognition of it as one;
for that [universal], being undivided, lacks any distinction among those [particulars].
Whether it be the manifestation [of the universal] or the refinement of the sense organ, [it remains the same] regarding the universal.

If it has the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of producing consciousness, then because it does not deviate from that intrinsic nature, it would produce consciousness independently of the refinement of the sense faculty (*indriya-saṃskāra*),
since it [already] possesses the assistance of a refined sense faculty.
If it is argued that [the cause] is merely incapable,
what is this meaning of "auxiliary" (sahakāra) for that which cannot have any excellence (atiśaya) added to it?
For entities are impermanent; they would depend upon auxiliary causes because of the acquisition of a specific nature.
For that very nature which is their producer arises from those [causes] at that very moment.
Thus, their mutual dependence consists precisely in this state of being produced [from one another].
But why should a universal, which is eternal and possesses that very nature, depend upon a sense faculty, given that it does not depend on anything else?
For that which is not of the nature of that [manifestation] alone— namely, the refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*)— cannot possibly arise from it; rather,
it is the universal (*sāmānya*), acting as its auxiliary cause, that produces the cognition.
Even if it is said that the universal is the cause, it would effectively be stated that the universal is merely the effect of manifestation through a causal succession. Furthermore,
if it is maintained that universals possess the quality of being possessed of a genus (jātimattā) by virtue of their manifestors:
Just as a lamp or similar object, being a manifestor, is apprehended as possessing "lamp-ness" and so forth, [so too is the universal apprehended as possessing its own nature]. //149//
For that which is the cause of the cognition of a particular object is the manifestor of that object.
The state of being a cause of cognition exists even in the case of lamps and the like with respect to universals such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth.
Because the visual organ perceives an object in dependence upon the refinement of light,
lamps and the like possess [the universal] "cowness" and so forth by virtue of that [refinement].
There could not be [any such manifestation]. For there is no manifestation of a universal other than its being a cause of cognition;
this is because it is impossible to impart any excellence of nature (*svabhāva-atiśaya*) to it.
If it is argued that "inherence (*samavāya*) is the manifestation," [we reply:]...
This has already been answered:
"Because its inherence is impossible" (07504).
For what arises together with the individual is merely its inherence; there is nothing else.
If there were no specific distinction,
then as before, it would not be the cause of cognition even afterwards.
If it were the cause of cognition solely by virtue of inherence (*samavāya*), then other things inhering in its own substratum would also [be causes of cognition].
[Otherwise,] there would be the consequence [of its being perceived].

Therefore, the very fact of being a cause of cognition is what constitutes manifestation; and since that is equally present in the case of a lamp and so forth, the same undesirable consequence follows.
Therefore, neither being the locus of inherence (*ādheyatā*), nor manifestation (*vyakti*), constitutes the subsistence (*vṛtti*) of a universal.
Since it does not so subsist, it cannot be the cause of cognition in multiple locations; for this very reason.

For those who maintain that the universal (jāti) exists [as something] either different from or non-different from the individual (vyakti), how can there be cognitions of a commonality with respect to individuals that have never before existed? (150)
The word "tu" has the sense of emphasis, meaning "it indeed exists. For an existing entity,
by its own capacity, produces in another a cognition that conforms to its own nature.
It requires a relation to that [particular],
otherwise there would be the fallacy of over-extension;
and that [relation] belongs to the universal.
It is not possible for that [cognition] to belong to either the position of identity or difference;

for what is perceived in one place cannot possibly be seen elsewhere. Indeed, that cognition, being produced as a single entity, would have to extend to another individual instance, which is impossible.

If that which grasps [the object] were to see something there and then see it elsewhere, that [seeing] would have to be of an existing thing; for if there were non-difference [between the two locations], there would be no persistence [of the object], and if there were difference, there would be no dependence [of the one upon the other]. //151//
It is not possible;
for an intrinsic nature does not transcend being either identical to or different from its own nature.
Because that which is not of the nature of form does not transcend otherness.

Indeed, this very thing is the otherness of form: namely, that it is not without distinction like another aspect. If that [aspect] were not other than the universal, then it would be that very [universal]; if it were not so, [it would be other].
Because it would follow that it is a different entity, like any other distinct thing;
nor can there be an entry of one individual into another individual, because it would follow that the latter ceases to be an individual.
Therefore, there could be no inclusive cognition (*anvayinī buddhi*) from a universal that is non-distinct [from its particulars],
nor from one that is distinct.

In some cases, even for other relations such as that between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), there is an absence [of the relation] because there is no assistance from anything else and no restriction;
this is due to the lack of a connection.
And because this consequence would apply even to the arising of cognition; therefore, one who—
by means of perceiving a single object— desires the occurrence elsewhere of a cognition that occurs in one [place], must [account for its] identity or difference.
It is unreasonable to say that [cognition] does not transcend [the object];
therefore, this uniform cognition regarding objects is nothing but an error, arisen from the latent predispositions of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-vāsanā*).
It has been thoroughly analyzed that the differentiation of states, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) are its substratum;
how then [is this so] now?
Words such as "primordial matter" (pradhāna), "Lord" (īśvara), and "effect" (kārya) function non-differently with respect to entities that possess distinctions not inherent in them;
they do so because they are embellished by latent predispositions (vāsanā) deposited according to convention.
Because the continuum of consciousness determines objects in that manner— even without depending on their actual differentiation—

through the exclusion of imagined entities that do not exist as such, [these cognitions] arise as conceptual constructions produced by the power of grasping, appearing within conceptual consciousnesses regarding objects.
They function [in this way];
for when those [particulars] are not as they appear, there exists no universal (sāmānya) whatsoever, whether distinct or non-distinct from them.
However, through the conceptualization of such an existence, the distinction from other things may arise by virtue of the cognizer's intention;
it is precisely due to that intention that there is a universal.
If it is asked, "Why not?"—

then a distinction must necessarily be admitted there, because [the universal] is invariably concomitant with it; and since that [distinction] alone is sufficient for the function of the universal, [the universal itself] is purposeless.
Regarding the conceptualization of a universal (*sāmānya-kalpanā*):

if this cognition of a universal occurs whether entities exist or do not exist, it is not based on a real object but is merely a cognitive distortion (*viplava*); thus, for us, it has no objective referent.
There is some degree of regard for its conceptual determination (*nirūpaṇa*) and non-discrepancy regarding this object in certain cases;
however, this is due to the constraint of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), not because of its actual inclusion within such an apprehended object.
We shall demonstrate—and have already demonstrated—that it occurs even when things are not as they appear, just as in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, its having difference as its object occurs frequently because, through the force of perceiving distinct entities, one determines their existence within those [entities].
Thus it is when there is the conceptualization of existence.
Because it exists elsewhere as well;
furthermore, this person who postulates a universal as a distinct entity must postulate it either as residing solely within its own substratum or as being omnipresent, like space and so forth.

In that case, if [the universal] resides only in its own substrate, then when a jar or the like arises in locations devoid of "jar-ness" and so forth, how could there be the possibility of a universal residing in a substance located in a different place? For that [new] substance is about to arise from a previous substance.
It does not go,
because it is admitted to be devoid of activity;
for an entity that exists in another substance does not move from that [original] location.
A connection with an entity located in a different place— which does not pervade the space between those two—
is not logical; for it did not exist there previously, yet it exists there afterwards.
And since it has not arisen there, nor come from anywhere, who— other than one possessed of dullness— is capable of bearing this burden of contradiction? Furthermore,
it is not possessed of parts.
It does not abandon its previous substratum; rather, it exists in a location different from the place where it was about to arise. And it exists in both of those [locations].
Alas, what a succession of calamities! //152//
For the relationship between two entities existing in different locations must be of two kinds: either by way of having multiple parts,
through their connection with each other's respective parts— as in the case of light— [or otherwise].
It is like a rope, a bamboo pole, or similar objects;
for it is not logical that something could simultaneously be in contact with two distinct locations without possessing parts.
Because that [space] lacks a second self-nature;
and because a single self-nature consists in the form of a relation residing in those locations; otherwise, a relation with them would be impossible.

It is illogical for a single substratum to both abide and not abide in that same place at that very time by means of that very same nature, because there is a contradiction between the natures of abiding and non-abiding in one and the same thing.

If it is argued that its nature exists as all aspects everywhere and at all times, then the cognition based on the perception of that intrinsic nature would itself be present everywhere in all aspects; and in that case, one would perceive even a cow as a horse.
Because it is connected with the substancehood of the self abiding in the horse, and because it is ascertained as such through the apprehension of its own nature,
and because that single [substance] lacks any other unperceived aspect.
Therefore, that which is partless cannot be simultaneously placed in multiple locations; however,
if it were to abandon its previous substrate, it could indeed occupy a different location.
It would have to exist [there], yet that is not accepted.
For something existing elsewhere to arise in a place other than that, while not moving from its own location, to be said to "exist" [there] is utterly illogical. (153)
Wherever that entity exists, it is not even connected with that [place]; yet it pervades that which occupies such a location—this is truly a great marvel! (154)
These are the intermediate verses. But for one who holds that the universal is omnipresent, even for him,
if that [universal] is omnipresent because it is non-different from a particular in one place, then it must be manifest only in that [particular].
The universal would be perceived everywhere;
however, it has been refuted that there is any manifestation of an eternal universal.
Therefore, [the universal] is eternal.

It would either be seen or not seen at any time without depending on any external embellishment, because it is established in that very nature and because no other nature can arise from anything whatsoever.

Even if one were to admit that the universal pervades the individual, since there is no difference [in the universal] due to its presence in one individual, it would be manifested everywhere; consequently, it would be perceived even in those locations devoid of individuals.
And that [cognition] does not depend upon an individual instance. //155//

For if it were dependent upon the individual instance (*vyakti*), then in the absence of the manifestation (*vyañjaka*), the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) would not be perceived. Why, then, is the opposite—that the universal (*sāmānya*) and its possessor (*tadvat*) [are related as manifestor and manifested]—accepted? (156)

For even one who might offer this rebuttal— that a universal, whose cognition depends upon its connection with its own substratum and sense organ, is not perceived in locations devoid of that substratum— [we reply that] for him too,
the connection with the substratum and sense organ certainly exists as a contributory factor; therefore, the observer of it [perceives it] accordingly.
One would perceive it as persisting;

for while that [individual] is being perceived, it is not logical that its [universal] aspect remains unperceived, since the universal is manifested by the individual and cannot exist in the absence of a manifestor.
The claim that there is no perception in certain locations is also false,
because such a relationship between the manifested and the manifestor does not exist there.

For a manifestor, such as a lamp and so forth, is the cause for the cognition of another by means of its own cognition; it does not reveal its own manifested object in a place devoid of its own form. Manifestation is not like this, because the reverse is the case.
For how could that [individual] be the manifestor of the universal? And how could it be visible by means of the cognition of that [universal]? It would be the manifested.
And that very same [fault] follows, as in the case of a lamp and a jar;
for [the object] is invisible in nature without some manner of its cognition.
Moreover, having perceived what impossibility has this [author] relied upon such a laborious theory of a universal (*sāmānya*),
given that there is mutual difference?
Because a uniform cognition is impossible with respect to individual instances that are mutually distinct,
how is it now that [words] such as "cook" (*pācaka*) are expressive even without a single, underlying referent?
Even among cooks, readers, and the like— who do not possess a mutual underlying connection— there is a recurrence of the same word and cognition,
such as "cook" or "reader.
For there is no other single, undifferentiated [entity] present in them.
There exists that by which they, being distinct, might be perceived as such;
if there is an action, [it must arise] from the individuals.
In that case, let that very cognition be [the basis for the notion of oneness].
What is the use now of a separate action or anything else?
Since a distinct thing cannot be the cause of a non-distinct cognition, a single universal is postulated.
If, even though it is distinct, the universal were to produce a cognition that is non-distinct,
what offense has been committed by the individuals such that they are not accepted as being so [i.e., producing a non-distinct cognition]?
If it is argued that because those [cognitions] are of a single form,
there would be no cognition of distinction such as "this belongs to that," nor would there be a cognition possessing a specific aspect other than that [single form].
It has been stated here that exclusion (*vyatireka*) and the specific cognitions [of objects] arise from the differentiation of each [object] from other things;
therefore, it is like the individual (*vyakti*).
Because of its difference [from other actions], action is not the cause of this cognition of non-difference regarding "the cooker" and so forth; rather,
the genus (jāti) residing in that action is the cause because it is non-different.
If this is argued, [we reply]: No, because a universal (jāti) depends upon action (karman). //157//

For a genus that is related to one object cannot be the cause of a cognition regarding another object, just as the genus "cowness" is not [the cause of cognition] in respect to white horses and the like;
nor is the genus "action" [the cause] in respect to the actions of cooks, for those [actions] are not [of that genus].
The actions are not denoted by the word "cook.
What then?
It is the substratum of those actions [that is denoted].
It is a substance. This is because that action-universal (*karma-sāmānya*) is caused by another [verbal] root;
for from that [action-universal], there would arise the forms "cooking" (*pākaḥ*, *pākaḥ*), but not the form "cook" (*pācaka*).
Its being the cause for action has already been stated; furthermore,
because there is an absence of stability in action.
For impermanent action does not exist at all times;
and if that condition were to have action as its cause, then once the action has ceased, one could no longer be called a "cook."
Since the action of cooking itself exists, and precisely because of that lack of connection, it is not the case that the universal is an improper cause for the word. //158//
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For when the action has perished, that universal (*sāmānya*) exists neither in the action nor in the agent;
thus, even though there is a connection with what was previously connected, it does not exist [in the present], and therefore, due to the lack of connection, there can be no verbal cognition.
This is the reason; otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the argument].
If it is argued that they arise by taking the past or the future as their objective cause (*nimitta*), [we reply:]...
Furthermore, karma is not the cause for non-existent cognition and designation; for otherwise, those two would result in being without a cause.
For that which is non-existent and devoid of any designation— how could it be a cause?
Because the nature of a real entity (vastu) is characterized by being an effect or a cause.
That which has neither fallen away nor yet attained its form— the past and the future—
is the cause of action;
furthermore, other factors such as individual manifestation (vyakti) and so forth are not accepted [as causes].
In that case, those two [cognition and designation] would be without a cause;
and thus there would be no establishment of the universal (jāti) for that [universal], because it is not accepted as being the cause of cognition and designation.
If it is argued that "capacity" (śakti) is the basis for words such as "cook" and the like, and that it is neither an action nor a universal (sāmānya), we reply:
no, for capacity lacks [the required] co-inherence (ananvaya). //159//
