For there is no such thing as "power" (śakti) that is entirely distinct from the cook and so forth; otherwise, it would follow that the substance itself is useless, since its utility for the purposeful action (arthakriyā) of cooking and so on would reside in that power alone.
If you say that the substance is useful in relation to that power, then what is the use of the power?
If one were to admit a distinct power for the sake of the employment of a power, it would lead to an infinite regress; therefore, it must be stated that the substance itself is what is employed.

If it is employed for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) itself, why is it not accepted that it is employed in its capacity (*śakti*)? What is the use of an intermediate capacity that serves no purpose?
Therefore, "capacity" is simply the substance itself; and that [substance], being its effect, does not persist [throughout]. Consequently...
There would be no positive concomitant word.

If the universal such as "cook-ness" and so forth were already present [in the individual] beforehand, it would be manifest like "existence" (sattā) and so on; if not, it could not become so later, because there is no difference [in its status]. //160//

Furthermore, "cookness" (*pācakatva*) might indeed be a certain universal (*sāmānya*), because its inherence (*samavāya*) in the object [the cook] is not occasional, just like existence (*sattā*) and so forth;
this has already been made clear.

It would be so; for it is the established doctrine (*samaya*) that as many universals (*sāmānya*) as possess the property of inherence (*samavāya*) in an object, they all inhere in it simultaneously with its production. If there were a deviation from that [doctrine], then for that [object]...
Furthermore, because there is no difference [in its nature] afterwards, there could be no inherence (*samavāya*) of that [effect] in it; for,
due to a deficiency in the nature of being related to that [cause], it did not previously exist in that very nature.

To say that [the manifestation] occurs "after" [the entity] has already existed is difficult to reconcile. If the manifestor depends on an auxiliary action, then for that which is unchanging, there can be no action even if there were an excellence in its dependence, because it is momentary. (161)
If it is argued that the state of being a "cook" is manifested by the substance in dependence upon the assistance provided by the action (*karman*), [we reply:

for that which possesses a stable intrinsic nature (*sthira-svabhāva*), there can be no excellence (*atiśaya*); therefore, what need is there for dependence on something that produces no distinction? Or, if there were an excellence, then because the action is momentary (*kṣaṇika*), there would be a different [excellence] arising at every moment as its very intrinsic nature.
Since an excellence (*atiśaya*) arises [in it], that too would be momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
Therefore, for something that perishes at the very place of its own arising, how could there be an action (*kriyā*) depending upon which a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) might exist? How so?
In that case, there is now the application of two concomitant cognitions and words toward a single, undivided entity, as in the case of "cook" and so forth.
But is it not precisely this very point that is being considered: how [is this] with respect to those [entities]?
"Moreover," [it was] thus considered: since that [arising] is not possible in those [two],
how then could they exist in the signless?
Not in the signless;
what then? Not in the sign of external reality.
Conceptual constructions arise from the awakening of their respective latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
from these, words [arise].
It has already been stated that the existence of a real entity (*vastu-sattā*) is not the common basis for conceptual construction and verbal expression.

This is as follows: due to the force of their respective habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), even when there is the perception of one thing after another through the occurrence of contradictory forms, those two [entities] are perceived as recurring; yet, in that case, there is no inherent nature (*svabhāva*) based upon them that could exist simultaneously for two mutually contradictory things.
Because it is impossible for them to coexist in one [locus],
they would then occur without restriction; for there can be no such thing as a causeless occurrence.
It is logical that there should be a restriction such that [an object] exists in some cases and does not exist in others;
for it is certainly not without a cause, since its cause is a specific latent predisposition (*vāsanā*).
We maintain, however, that no such external object of perception exists.
And it is not the case that when that [object] is absent,
there should not be [cognition]; for instance, in the case of objects perceived by one who is asleep or suffering from ophthalmia, which are non-existent.

Furthermore, because conceptual constructions arise in that manner with respect to specific forms superimposed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic convention, and because those [forms] do not arise when they are non-existent, [the object] does not possess all aspects in every case;
for it is not so perceived when there is a distinction [between existence and non-existence].
Because of conceptual construction.
And regarding this, we have already stated something: that some things, even by their very nature, produce a single cognition due to a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore:
Since the difference [between individuals] is equal, let that very same proximity by which a universal extends to some [individuals] and not others be the basis for words and cognitions. (162)
Thus is the intermediate verse:
If there were no other continuity of existence apart from cessation, then the effect of one thing would not belong to another, because of their absolute difference. (163)
If these entities were devoid of any inherent nature that is concomitant [with them], apart from their exclusion,
then there could not be a single effect for these many [entities].
For whatever is its [the effect's] own nature—
It is not a producer; for that which belongs to another is not a producer,
because it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) due to its distinctness.
That very thing which is the producer of a certain effect is not present elsewhere as that producer; therefore, it would not produce another [effect].
For that which is the producer is indeed its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
If it were to belong to another as well,
it would be non-different from that [other] by virtue of that intrinsic nature; thus, there is a continuity of intrinsic nature.

If a plurality [of causes] were the producer of a single effect by virtue of having a single nature, then since that [single] nature exists even in one [cause], the auxiliary factors would be useless. //164//
If, because they possess a single nature, multiple [causes] are the producer of a single [effect], then that non-different nature of theirs exists even when only one [cause] is present; thus,
due to the non-deficiency of the cause, the single [effect]—
It might also be the producer [of the cognition]. Why?
Because that non-different form does not depart; indeed, it is the specific qualities (*viśeṣas*) that depart.
For there is no distinction within that which has a non-different nature when another object is present.

A distinction [would be impossible] because there would be no abandonment of non-difference; and since that [non-difference] exists even there, there is no loss of it even when one [particular] is present. As for those particulars, there might be their loss because there is no rule for their simultaneous presence; yet they are not [the same as non-difference].
The producers are desired [as being momentary],
because it is admitted that the auxiliary causes possess the nature of producing [the effect] through a single inherent nature; therefore, the producer must abide [only for a moment].
And because that which is non-abiding does not possess productive capacity, the effect would have to arise even while [the cause] remains as a single entity;
yet it does not so occur. Therefore—
Because there is an absence of the effect when even one [of the causes] is removed, its production must arise from the specific [causes]. //165//
That effect, which is common to many auxiliary causes, does not arise even when a single particularity is absent;
yet it arises again when all the particularities are once more complete,
provided they are not incomplete.
Even when the form is non-different,
an effect that does not arise from a certain thing due to its nature as an existent must be because of the deficiency of that very [cause].

And there is no deficiency in a form that is non-distinct even when it exists in a single location; for if [the effect] does not arise even while that [form] is unimpaired, then that [form] lacks the nature of being its producer.
It indicates that because an effect exists or does not exist according to the completeness or incompleteness of its causes,
it arises from those very causes;
for when those [causes] are present, the effect necessarily occurs, whereas it does not arise from anything other than them.
Because there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in [assuming] conceptual construction (kalpanā).
Therefore, only particulars (viśeṣa) are productive, not the universal (sāmānya); consequently, only those [particulars] are the real entity (vastu), because:
That alone is an ultimately real entity which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).
For we shall explain that this indeed is the defining characteristic of a real thing and a non-thing: namely, the capacity for or incapacity for causal efficiency.
And that object capable of causal efficiency does not persist; that which persists cannot produce an effect from it. (166)

Therefore, every universal (sāmānya) is a non-entity because it is incapable of causal efficiency; however, only the particular (viśeṣa) is an entity, precisely because [causal efficiency] arises from that alone. [Objection:
But in that case, since there is no continuity of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-ananvaya),...

The nature that produces one thing does not exist in another; therefore, the latter would be a non-producer. Or, if it were a producer, then because there is no distinction between them in their difference, everything would be a producer.
This is not the case, because:

For even when there is a difference [between things], some may be the cause [of a certain effect] while others are not; this is their very nature (*svabhāva*). All things that differ from the productive nature of one thing are either equally productive or not at all.

If there were no distinction among these, it might be argued that "someone [is the producer]. However, since a distinction is indeed possible, then even given a difference, due to some specific excellence of its own nature (*ātma-atiśaya*), one [entity] is the producer and not the other; for that is its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), and not that of the other.
For the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of things do not admit of questioning, such as "Why does fire burn or is hot, while water does not? At most, one might ask:
"From what does this intrinsic nature arise?"
Because there would be no restriction for that which is independent due to being causeless, there would follow an over-extension;
therefore, its intrinsic nature is said to arise from its own cause.
The fact that even this [nature] has its production from that [other cause], and that from yet another, constitutes an infinite succession of causes.
For there is no subverting argument against the claim that among distinct things, a certain cause exists and nothing else, other than their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
But if there were no difference [between them], destruction and arising would occur simultaneously. //167//

Because there would be no distinction; by its very nature, the universe—like its own self—would not undergo division, origination, persistence, cessation, and so forth, since non-difference is thus observed. For this indeed is the definition of difference and non-difference: that even for that which has a single form, there is both exclusion (*vyatireka*) and non-exclusion (*avyatireka*).
Because two contradictory [properties] cannot exist within a single essence,
difference also does not exist in that way. If it is argued that this is not so, we do not indeed assert a non-distinction from all aspects such that this [consequence] would follow.

If it is argued that its self is neither different nor other [than the body], then because they are distinct, there can be no such things as simultaneous arising and so forth. If that is the case, then when one [of them] perishes...
The self persists; it has no differentiation. If both persistence and non-persistence were based upon the same single self, what other property could serve as a differentiator?
Thus, there would be no diversity whatsoever anywhere.
It has been stated that because one accepts two objects— one characterized by separation from all aspects and the other not so characterized—
only the name [of the object] would be desired, but not the thing itself; therefore,
these entities do not share a common fate (ekayogakṣema) and are indeed distinct.
Therefore, there would be no cognition of both the universal and the particular. //168//
Therefore, this distinct entity, being independent because it is not produced [by anything else], does not deserve the designation "this is its universal" or "this is its particular.
This same logical consequence applies equally even in the case of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
If this is argued, it is not equal [to our position], because:
Since cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva), there can be no conceptualization of its persistence or non-persistence.
For that which is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is nothing at all, and [consequently] there are no properties associated with an intrinsic nature for it.
Conceptual constructions regarding the persistence, change, or destruction of intrinsic nature are not applicable;
therefore, the error [of momentariness] does not vitiate the cognition of universals. //169//
Indeed, this false cognition which perceives a single form in what is manifold is entirely without an object;
therefore, there can be neither the establishment nor the non-establishment of its object.
As for that which was further stated:
For that which produces it is its very nature;
how could something other than that which is its productive form be a producer?
In this regard, we do not say that another thing lacks the form that produces it; what then?

That which is the producer of one thing is not [the producer] of another; thus, another entity is also a producer by its own nature alone, and not by the nature of another, because it is not that [other] entity.
Therefore, they are distinct according to their respective natures and are producers of those [effects].
And since it exists by way of its own nature, what contradiction is there here? That which lacks a single form would not possess that [specific] nature, nor would it be the producer of that effect.
And what logic is there in the claim that the effect must be produced by that [universal] alone? Furthermore, it is the distinct particulars (*viśeṣa*) that are the producers.
Thus it has been said. And those particularities do not follow one another through that nature;
for that which is the productive form of one does not belong to the other, yet this does not [constitute a fault].
Even if there were non-difference among them, they would still be non-producers. //170//

It might be argued: "It is true that the specific features (viśeṣa) are the producers; however, it is not their distinct form alone that produces, but rather they are producers even through their non-distinct [form] by virtue of being connected to that single capacity (eka-śakti). Therefore, they were described as non-producers [in that respect]."

Even though a common form exists, those [causes] are not the producers of that [effect], because since that [common form] does not depart, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the effect being produced even when only one [cause] is present; this was stated previously. Furthermore, the manifestation (*pratibhāsa*) itself is also a differentiator.
Not partaking of anything else;
by the word "also" (*api*), it is meant that there is no distinction such as arising, abiding,
or perishing for this [entity] which is undivided.

If one considers all objects [to be identical], then for that person, this differentiation of the appearance of cognition regarding objects and the superimposition of contradictory properties would not exist;
even if that [identity] were present, despite the lack of difference.
There would be no distinction whatsoever;
and thus, this differentiation would not exist, just as in the case of a single self.
Therefore, this [phenomenon] consisting of distinct appearances and so forth is indeed a specific difference.
And we do not perceive any other non-distinct appearance here by virtue of which there could be a cognition of non-difference; therefore, it is indeed a distinction.
That very object is its [the word's] referent; the others are its exclusions (vyāvṛttayaḥ). //170//

That which is the effect and that which is the cause has been described as the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). All human activities have the avoidance of the former and the attainment of the latter as their fruit. //172//
It has been stated that whatever performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*) is alone a real entity (*vastu*).
And that [performer] is precisely the particular (*viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, that which is called "universal" (*sāmānya*) is simply the exclusion of that very [particular] from others.

For if that [universal] were the object [of the cognition], it would not be logical for the form of the perceptible [particular] to be unperceived; because the non-differentiated cognition regarding particulars is produced by the perception of that [universal]. Moreover, just as there is no lack of distinction between them as universals, yet not everything is the means of accomplishing everything.
Likewise, even though there is no difference in their being distinct, not everything is a means of proving everything. //173//

As for what was said: "How could that which is distinct from the nature of producing it be its producer? Or, if it were a producer, then because there would be no distinction, everything would be a producer"—this has been answered here:
this [consequence] would hold true only if there were indeed no distinction.
And just as for this proponent of non-difference, even though there is no distinction of non-difference, it is not the case that everything is the producer of everything,
so it will be even though there is no distinction of difference. Or alternatively:
For if there were a distinction, some factor would exist as an inherent property of the entity;
but if there is no distinction, it is contradictory for that single [entity] to both act and not act. (174)

Even though there is no difference in their mere distinctness, because their intrinsic natures are determined by their own specific causes and conditions, only certain things would be causal agents and not others; this is because the latter lack that nature. In this regard, there is nothing at all contradictory.
But if it were a single entity, then its being both an agent and a non-agent in that very same respect would be a contradiction.
If you argue that there is indeed a distinction [between the two states] due to the absence of activity [in one], then the auxiliary causes would not produce [the effect].
We certainly do not assert that there is no distinction in every respect, because difference also exists. Therefore,
although something may be a non-producer [in some respects],
it nonetheless acts as a cooperative cause due to its difference [from others] in some way.
They would be non-agents; or else, if agency occurs in turn, does that [agency] belong to that very same entity? (175)
Furthermore, it might be argued that there is no such thing as a non-agent,
because everyone is employed in every [action] by turns, or because a capacity, having undergone transformation, enters into that [action] under another form.
Because of its utility. Indeed, how can this very same alternative, which relies on differentiation, belong to a single entity?
Or how can there be transformation for that which is non-distinct [from it]?
Or, in the case of some distinction, how could there be unity?
This argument regarding "loss" (hāni) is trivial. Furthermore: there would be both absolute difference and non-difference in the entity possessing those [qualities];
or else, there would be a mutual difference between those two, which consist of a similar and a dissimilar nature. (176)
If entities possessing distinctions were to possess those [distinctions] by means of a non-distinct nature that constitutes their own self,

then, because the distinction would also have that same non-distinct nature as its essence, how could there be any mutual distinction among them? Alternatively, if that [nature] is not the common self of that [distinction], [then it cannot be the cause of their identity].
That being the case,
it is not logical for that [entity] to exist even as that [nature]; for if it were not so, it would not be that.
It would follow that there is no dharma;
for it is not logical that this nature, which possesses both activity and cessation, should be a single [entity].
Nor is there absolute non-difference in every respect.
Even between those two, there would be a distinction,
for nowhere is there an absolute distinction or non-distinction, since they are established through differentiation as "the universal" and "the particular."
If that by which the difference between those two [is established]—namely, "this is the universal"—is itself a difference, then [the universal would be nothing but difference]. //177//
It is indeed a difference.

If the distinction between the universal and the particular is established based on that very nature by which it is designated as "universal" or "particular," then, insofar as it exists through that nature, it is simply a difference.
For those two are indeed their own natures; if they were distinct, then there would be a distinction between the universal and the particular due to the difference in their intrinsic natures.
For if an intrinsic nature were itself an entity,
then there would be a lack of both generality and particularity,
just as there is between the differences and the generalities of jars and other such things.

Furthermore, if there were a separation between particularity and generality, then the particular would not arise from the general, nor would the general [arise] from the particular, because of the absence of a relationship between them, like a jar and other such objects; this has already been stated. Moreover:
That self (ātman), having placed which before him, this person proceeds—desiring the fruit to be accomplished by that [self]—is the substratum for both difference and non-difference. (179)
Difference is conceived through its own nature, while similarity is conceived through exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
A real entity certainly exists, yet it does not persist [as a single universal], because that would lead to the absurdity of [indiscriminate] activity and so forth.
Thus, every cow is either different from or non-different from a horse; one must consider this difference or non-difference.
When one inquires about the specific [property] of an entity, it proceeds by referring to that which is called its "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva);
for it is precisely that which is so designated.
However, categories such as "substantiality" (dravyatva) and the like are not what is signified by the word in that context.
Because each [word] denotes its own respective object separately,
and because the object is not deviant from that [denotation], there would be comprehension [of the meaning] from it.
And this has been thoroughly investigated by the Teacher;
therefore, he who asks whether the object presented by words such as "cow" and so forth is different or non-different [from the universal]—
Why, by introducing a different object, is a dual-aspect cognition produced therein?

Therefore, that which is its own nature, unique and not shared with others, which a person takes as the primary focus when seeking specific purposeful action— such as the carrying or milking of a cow— is not anything else.
In the case of a possible object, such as entering a battle, it is that very same specific nature which is indicated by its respective word,
and not a universal such as "substantiality" (dravyatva) and so forth;
for [the word] indicates that [specific nature].
Because at that time it is not intended to be attained;
because [the universal] is included within the cow and so forth, and because there is no continuity for those things that have become its very self, it possesses neither form therein.
And he subjects that very entity to inquiry through various modes;
when there is a distinction in it, there is no non-distinction of its substantiality and so forth.
This is indeed not a contradiction,
because in all cases difference is admitted by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and because the universal is characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and is itself of the nature of intrinsic nature.
It has also been stated regarding non-difference:
"But if there were non-difference by way of its own nature, then one who seeks purposeful action based on that intrinsic nature would proceed toward both equally; even a single [entity]..."
It performs that causal efficacy precisely because it possesses that intrinsic nature;
since this is equally true for anything else as well, why does that other thing not perform it too?
By this very [argument], whatever indecent and confused ravings the shameless ones utter are also refuted, because they are possible only in isolation. (181)
If this [proponent] were shameless, he might utter some indecorous and improper thing— such as "the camel would be curd"—
which, due to its lack of finality, is confused and involves neither rejection nor acceptance;
that too has been refuted by him through the absolute difference of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Or, if that [nature] were inherent in its lineage:
since everything would possess both natures and their specific distinctions would be negated, why would a person commanded, "Eat curd," not run toward a camel? (182)
For in that case, even a camel would be curd, yet it is not that very same camel which would not also be another camel; likewise,
even curd would be a camel, yet it is not that very same curd by which another curd would also exist.

Therefore, since neither of these two lacks the absence of that nature, nor lacks its own nature which does not become something else and is restricted to itself, there is no distinction whatsoever between them.

If one who is commanded to eat curd were to eat even a camel, [one might argue] that there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) by which it exists as a distinct entity. That very excellence is the curd; since it does not exist elsewhere, the ultimate reality is neither [the universal nor the particular]. //183//
Now, if there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) in these two by which this [milk] is thus impelled to proceed as a transformation of milk alone and not otherwise,
that very excellence is the object of the activity of one who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Curd is that entity whose intrinsic nature is characterized by its being the material cause of that [sour taste] fruit;
and such an intrinsic nature does not exist elsewhere.
Because there is an absence of activity for one who seeks an object, that [cognition] does not possess both forms; thus, this is an extremist position.
Furthermore:
And if all things were identical with the universal self, then cognition and verbal expression would not be distinct;
consequently, because that distinction would be absent, the doctrine of the synthesis of differences would be impossible.

Thus, this shameless person, not perceiving even a single fixed form anywhere because there is no distinction among entities, how could he resolve upon objects with a cognition possessing unmixed forms, or how could he designate them?
Then, because of the non-apprehension of difference, there would be no doctrine of their synthesis, such as "the camel might be curd" or "it might not be.
However, if they are indeed unmixed...
Having apprehended the two forms, one should withdraw [the mind].
Because the cognition that is associated with a single form is restricted in certain respects, the distinction between those two forms is produced solely by the difference in their appearance.
There would also be a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because the determination of one or many is the object of appearance;
and thus, that which is one could not possess both forms— this is a false doctrine.
This is it. It is established that there is no continuity of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) among entities;
rather, the universal (sāmānya) is characterized solely by difference.
Nevertheless, by their very nature, some [entities] produce a single cognition.
Some [hold that] certain things do not have initial results;
let it be granted, then, that there is a distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) among entities, which constitutes their commonality (*sāmānya*).
But for those things which are indefinable and possess no intrinsic nature at all, how could words have as their object a distinction of intrinsic nature?
Regarding them, [words] must necessarily...
The application of words must be established;

for when things are not determined in any way, injunctions and prohibitions are impossible. And thus, in all cases, this linguistic convention relies upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Fire would not have heat as its intrinsic nature, nor would it be non-hot,
because an alternative intrinsic nature that does not exist cannot be established in any way whatsoever.

Because there would be no cognition whatsoever, the world would be utterly deluded, since there would be no cognition of the nature of fire. This might be argued: "In that case, there is no negation of anything non-existent; rather, it is simply another entity that is not hot."
"It is negated. How, then, can there be such a thing as "existent-nonexistent"?
We do not say this with respect to everything.

In the statement "that which is non-existent does not exist there," it is only the negation of place, time, and properties that is performed with respect to all entities, and not the negation of the substratum (dharmin); for if that were negated, the application of words referring to it would be impossible, since a negative particle (nañ) cannot be employed without a specified object.
In that case as well, how is there a negation of place and so forth?
Because even there, there is no negation of place and the rest.
If it is argued that the relation of the object is not being negated,
then [we reply]: surely, in the negation of that—

Furthermore, the same fault applies to the negation [of a non-existent], namely that a word does not apply to what is non-existent, and so forth; or else, if this [non-existent] is negated, the subject (dharmin) would likewise be negated.
It is certainly not a negation that the relation does not exist;
what then?
When it is stated, "There is no jar here," "Not now," or "Not thus," there arises the cognition that "there is no connection with this" or "these are not its properties"; and in this way,
the connection is negated.

Nevertheless, how can it be negated so long as the cognition "this has neither a relation nor a property" does not arise? And this [cognition] cannot possibly occur in the case of non-entities, because it does not exist in that way for them.
Therefore, because of the cognition of the absence of a relation, there arises the cognition "this is not here" and so forth;
that [cognition] occurs when that [relation] is absent.
It would not exist; or else, if it were perceived, its non-existence [would be established].
Just as it is according to perception, who can prevent words that arise from it?
For that alone which is not an object of discursive thoughts (vitarka) is not an object of words;
if those [thoughts] have arisen, who could prohibit speech?
For cognitions do not strive toward an object that cannot be expressed;
however, it has been stated that the relation itself is not denoted by its own intrinsic form.
Because when [a word] is denoted, it is presented to the mind as being related [to its object],
there is no comprehension [of the object] according to the intended meaning.
Therefore, although this [relation] is being perceived, it is perceived only as having the nature of its relata; thus, it is not denoted by way of its own intrinsic form (*svarūpa*).
Consequently, the same logical consequence that applies to non-existence (*abhāva*) does not apply to the relation either. Furthermore, this...
How could one who does not speak provide a rebuttal against someone who asserts that "non-existence" is the denotable object? Or, if he were to speak, how could non-existence remain unexpressed?
Now, if one should not even desire non-existence, then there would be no statement; how, then, could that very thing [be established] now?
"It is not that non-existence does not exist.

Furthermore, regarding the point that because a meaningless word is not employed when negating an object, the negative particle (*nañ*) cannot be used without an object, the answer will be stated hereafter. Therefore:
There are words for non-existents;
how, then, can there be a distinction of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-bheda) among them?
To this also [it is replied]:
Since non-existence lacks the nature of form, words that denote form cannot even be suspected [to apply] to it; thus, they are established as denoters of exclusion (vyavaccheda). //185//
One might wonder whether the referent of words that function according to the nature of real entities is their form or rather their differentiation; however,
non-existence (abhāva) must be taken as the cause precisely in its character as a distinction.

Because no form [of existence] whatsoever exists, and because it is impossible for non-existence to occur when that [existence] is present— since existence is characterized by the presence of that [nature]— this alone is the primary distinction.
It is entirely out of place to raise the doubt as to whether words that express such non-existence have differentiation (*viveka*) as their object;
therefore, it is established that all words have differentiation as their object.
And these conceptual constructions,
although they rely upon a single entity,
appear in the intellect as if they were distinct, due to the various distinctions imagined according to their respective limits.
Because they are perceived in distinct isolates (*viveka*), their objects are indeed different.
Therefore, even when the essential nature itself functions as the probandum and the probans, there is no actual conjoining of the probandum and the probans.
Those two are not the reason (hetu) because they constitute only a part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā). And this very [reason], when adduced as a reason,
is either an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) that depends on a distinction of conditions (upādhi), or it is the intrinsic nature alone.
It is said: for the sake of establishing the probandum, [the reason is stated] like "being an effect" or "existence" in relation to destruction. (186)

For an entity whose own nature (*svabhāva*) is brought to completion by depending on the operation of another is "produced" (*kṛtaka*). Therefore, this term "produced," although denoting an intrinsic nature, implies that this [nature] has an external condition (*upādhi*).
By this, [the properties such as] "being differentiated by a difference in conditions" (*pratyayabhedabheditva*) and so forth are explained. Thus...

In some cases, an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is stated as a reason in dependence on a distinction of conditions (*upādhi-bheda*); in other cases, it is independent. Generally, for example, existence (*sattva*) is [the reason] for impermanence alone; in some cases, it is through the inclusion of a specific property that constitutes the essential nature, as in the case of "origination" for that same [impermanence]. By this [method]...
In this manner, other classifications of essential-nature reasons (*svabhāva-hetu*) should also be understood.
If existence (*sattā*) as the essential nature is the reason, how can existence not be proven?
For there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) among particulars, which would contradict [the requirement for] the reason and the probandum. (187)

If existence (*sattva*) were the reason for impermanence or anything else, why is the probandum (*sādhya*) not also accepted as such? For that [probandum], when being established in this way, becomes a specific instance (*viśeṣa*); and a specific instance cannot be proven because it lacks positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).
As it was said: "Because of the lack of knowledge regarding the specific qualification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This very qualification is contradicted precisely within that which is to be proven (*sādhya*).

What then? Because the same fault applies even to the reason (*hetu*). For a reason that lacks positive concomitance (*ananvaya*) is not a factor for establishing [the probandum], because it gives rise to doubt.
This is not a fault, because:

"But when existence alone, based on its substratum, is to be proven with respect to a subject that is a general property (sāmānya-dharmin), no specific [positive] object would be established, and such [a mere negation] is not prohibited. (188)
In no way does the specific characteristic become established by proving mere existence;
for one who seeks to establish that "there exists some subject (dharmin) qualified merely by its being an entity" has not specified the particular nature of its specific characteristic.

Since there is no contradiction in the mere existence of something, there is here no negation of its existence; rather, what self-interest does one serve by speaking while failing to consider any particular distinction of it, such as "it exists in such a way"?
Therefore, by this [reasoning], only that which has its distinction already included is to be proven;
when the probandum is thus one whose distinction is included, your reason is devoid of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*).
Therefore, when existence is the probandum, a specific property would be proven. //189//
For that subject (*dharmin*), whether characterized as the primary [Pradhāna], as one, as eternal, as consisting of pleasure and so forth,
or as something else— however it may be qualified— is established as having that very nature;
yet it does not persist in that way.
Even if it follows mere existence (*sattā-mātra*), nothing is established by that which is already proven. [Objection:
But in that case, would this not lead to the same consequence for fire and other such things? [Response: That too...
There is no dispute regarding the mere existence of fire; however,
because the specific, intended locus lacks positive concomitance (ananvaya), it remains unestablished.

Indeed, that substratum does not qualify it; for it has been stated, and will be stated again, that [the qualification] is by way of excluding its non-connection (*tad-ayogavyavaccheda*). Therefore, in that case, it is the universal alone that is established by way of excluding its non-connection.
In this case as well, existence (*sattā*) is not established anywhere in that manner;
because the object denoted by terms such as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*) is absent in some instances, it [existence] is indeed without qualification.

How can non-existence [be established]? It is indeed established by way of being an object of cognition (*jñeya*), an object of designation (*abhidheya*), and an object of valid cognition (*prameya*). What then [is the point]? Now...
Let it be established that "the object of knowledge exists";
nevertheless, what would be established by that? For elsewhere, it is precisely that universal fire (*agni-sāmānya*) which is unestablished there and is thus what is being proven.
But is it not the case that even there,
a positive concomitance with a universal that is devoid of connection to that [specific instance] is simply not established?
Indeed, no one [accepts this].

Likewise, one establishes a positive concomitance (anvaya) through what is not [actually] the case; for when demonstrating it to another, one must show that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire, such that "wherever there is smoke, there is fire."
Thus, being established as pervaded by fire alone, it produces the cognition of fire precisely where it is itself perceived.
And in that case, there is no purpose in stating the probandum (*sādhya*),
because the desired conclusion is established merely by explaining the connection with the observation;
and furthermore, if it were not stated, [the following would occur].
How is there a positive concomitance (anvaya) with that which is qualified by it?
This [reason] is established as being inseparably connected (avinābhāvī) with fire;
by its very nature, it excludes the possibility of fire not being present in that location. Thus, it is [the reason].
In that way, the probandum (sādhya) is stated;
however, there is no subsequent positive concomitance (anvaya) preceded by its formal presentation here, because such a statement of the probandum is not a constituent part [of the proof].
Or, if it is preceded by that [thesis], who would refute the thesis by means of the proof?
And so he said:

The non-deviation of the logical mark (liṅga) from the property (dharma) is demonstrated elsewhere; being well-established therein, that [mark], when conjoined with it, will cause the subject (dharmin) to be known. Therefore, like the proof of fire and so forth, the proof of existence (sattā) is also faultless.

But when the object of proof is the mere thing (vastu-mātra) itself, unqualified by its distinctions, there is no obstruction to the positive concomitance (anvaya) of the probandum that pervades that very [mere thing]. //190//

Furthermore, when existence (*sattva*) is the probans (*sādhana*), provided that no specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) is grasped, there is no contradiction with the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) regarding the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) which pervades the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*).
For it is not necessarily the case therein that—
A specific qualification must be adopted,
because the capacity of the proof resides in its dependence on mere existence,
not in its being the probandum itself.
Because it would be fruitless. Furthermore:

"A property of an existent (bhāvadharma) does not exist in what is unestablished; a property that is deviant has both as its locus. A property that is contradictory belongs to non-existence (abhāva). How, then, can that existence (sattā) be proven? (191)
For when existence is the probandum,
everything that serves as its reason does not escape the threefold class of fallacies:
unestablishedness (asiddhi), inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra), and contradiction (virodha).
In that case, if the reason is stated to be a property of an existent entity (*bhāvadharma*),
how could it belong to something whose existence is unestablished? For indeed, [it cannot].
If one accepts that the property (*dharma*) exists therein [in the substratum], how could one not accept the existence of the entity (*bhāva*) itself? For it is the very nature (*svabhāva*) that,
through some particular perspective, is called a "property" (*dharma*), appearing as if it were distinct from the substratum (*dharmī*).
It is explained as follows:
for it has already been stated that there is no distinction whatsoever between the expressed objects of two words denoting a property (dharma) and its locus (dharmin).
Alternatively, one might state both properties [positive and negative],
because there is no contradiction even in the absence of a mere negation (*vyatireka-mātra*) through the non-exclusion (*aparyudāsa*) of a non-dependent entity,
just as "not being corporeal" (*amūrtatva*) applies even to that which is indefinable (*nirupākhya*).
If it is argued that because that which is indefinable (nirupākhya) is non-existent, it cannot be the object of negation, then should it now become the object of affirmation?
If you say that this too is not the case, [we reply:]...
How, then, is it not the object of negation?
Because negation consists in the cessation of an affirmation. Therefore...

How could this mere exclusion (*vyavaccheda-mātra*), which is possible for both [the proponent and the opponent], appropriate to itself the capacity to prove (*gamakatva*)— which is obtained by excluding the suspicion of its occurrence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)? And he himself, while stating through his own words that [the reason] possesses the property of both [the subject and the similar instance], [is speaking of it as] being existent...
How is he not insane to claim that its occurrence exists elsewhere as well and that it is non-deviant with respect to existence (*sattā*),
while [at the same time] asserting it to be a property of non-existence (*abhāva*) that pervades mere existence (*bhāvamātra*)?

For one who asserts that the exclusion of an object is the reason for existence, this would be a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*); because its presence is impossible in any instance, while its absence constitutes the very exclusion of existence.
Therefore, although this property (dharma) is of three kinds,
it does not possess the characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*) for proving existence (*sattā*), nor is there any other alternative; consequently, existence is not proven.

Furthermore, regarding its status as a means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) when it refers to a property of the thing (*vastu-dharma*) that, by its very nature, pervades only that [subject] and whose existence is established in the locus (*dharmin*). And if its pervasion (*vyāpti*) by the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) is somehow ascertained through that [reason], there is no contradiction.
Since there is no deviation [between the reason and the property], this undesirable consequence does not arise.

However, when the pervasion (vyāpti) is not ascertained, or when it is restricted to the locus of the subject (dharmin), nothing can be a prover by virtue of being of that same nature (tat-svabhāvatā).

Therefore, an established essential nature (*svabhāva*) that is pervaded by its own property (*svadharma*) is the indicator; this is what must be stated. For a lamp, while illuminating by means of its luminosity, does not [function as an indicator] if that form [of luminosity] is not apprehended.
It performs its own purposeful action;
its pervader is ascertained,
and it is the nature that is to be understood.
Precisely because that property has been ascertained, the property of that subject which is ascertained as its pervader is what is to be understood;
and when the latter ceases, it causes the former to cease. //192//
This pervading property (vyāpaka-dharma), which itself ceases to exist, is the negator of that pervaded property (vyāpya-dharma);
for it is in this way that it is established as its pervader.
It occurs if it were not to exist in its absence;
by this, it should be understood that the definition of the capacity for comprehension (*gamakatā*) of both types of formal proof (*sādhana-prayoga*) has been stated. [The proof is] of two kinds.
For the formal argument (prayoga) is indeed twofold: by way of similarity (sādharmya) and by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya). As some have said:
"It is both positive (anvayin) and negative (vyatirekin).
In reality, there is no difference between these two, except for [the distinction of their formulation].
Because of the difference in formulation (*prayoga*).

For even in a formulation by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), there is an understanding of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) by implication; for in its absence, there would be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason with the probandum. Likewise...

Even in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there is an understanding of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); for in its absence, there is doubt regarding the absence of the reason (*hetu*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent. We shall explain this in detail later.
For example, in the case of impermanence, [the reason] may be either an effect (*kārya*) or a non-effect (*akārya*), provided it is not subject to destruction.

By this, he demonstrates the examples for these two [types of inference]. Among them, the positive concomitant (*anvayin*) is as follows: whatever is produced is all impermanent, just like jars and so forth; and sound is produced.

Thus, having demonstrated that being produced is pervaded by impermanence, when the fact that sound is produced is stated, it follows by implication alone that "sound is impermanent. Therefore, the explicit mention of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not strictly necessary here.
This is the formulation based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as well: "In the absence of impermanence, there is no state of being produced; yet sound is produced. Because its nature is established [as being impermanent], it does not exist in the absence of that [impermanence].

Since the existence of "being produced" (kṛtakatva) in sound is established by implication from the statement that it exists as having that nature, the proponent does not state the proposition (pratijñā). However, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
For that which is not restricted to being of that nature does not necessarily cease when that [nature] ceases. Therefore, having established that restriction, the cessation must be stated.
If that [cessation] is established, it implies by implication the restriction to that nature; thus, the positive concomitance (anvaya) is established.
How, then, is it to be understood that what is produced is necessarily impermanent, such that this is stated? Because:
"Since destruction has no cause, it follows from [the nature of the thing] as its very essence. (193)

For entities that are perishing do not depend upon a cause for their existence as such; this is because they arise from their own causes as things already subject to destruction. Therefore, whatever is produced is by its very nature [perishable].

It is indeed perishable. For instance: the necessity of existence is not observed in things that depend on other factors; however, a thing that is independent [of external causes] exists in its destruction.
For if [things] were dependent, some things such as jars might even be eternal;
because, despite the abundance of their causes, there would be the possibility of non-arising in certain cases. //194//

Even though causes of destruction are numerous, because their presence depends upon their own respective conditions, their proximity is not necessarily guaranteed; thus, it may happen that something does not perish at all.
For causes do not necessarily produce their effects, due to deficiencies or obstructions.
By this, the inconclusiveness [of the reason] has been stated for all those who assert that destruction possesses a cause, because of the lack of fixedness regarding effects. (195)
This is the intermediate verse.
Therefore, this entity, with respect to its own existence, is independent and necessarily determined to exist; it is like a complete causal complex for which no obstruction is possible.
Regarding the production of an effect:
[one might object] that even for certain things that are independent, their presence is not necessarily [guaranteed] in every case—
for instance, because a sprout is sometimes not produced despite the completeness of the conditions consisting of earth, seed, and water.
Even in that case, it is because of the dependence upon the transformation of the continuum (*santāna-pariṇāma*).
An entity does not have such a dependence at all. Even there, it is the final causal totality (*kāraṇa-sāmagrī*) which is immediately contiguous to the arising of the effect.
That [final transformation] alone possesses the fruit;
it is that very [transformation] which is the cause of the sprout there,
while the preceding transformation is something else.
It is for that very purpose;
and no one is able to obstruct it there,
because no modification arises within a single entity.
Or, if [the effect] were to arise [from it], its unity would be lost;
and since that [cause], whose nature remains unaltered, lacks the deficiency toward the production of that [effect], the obstructing cause cannot function as an obstruction. Is this not so?
Even barley seeds and the like are not dependent [on anything else] for the production of a rice sprout,
because the conditions for its arising are sometimes present even in that case.
How is it that they are not dependent?
To what extent does that very nature which produces them not exist in the case of the rice seed? It is because they depend upon that [specific] nature.
If that is the case, then even among certain produced things or existent entities, there would be no such intrinsic nature (svabhāva) as that which is perishable; therefore,
[the argument] depends upon that intrinsic nature.
They are not perishable;
for even rice seeds and the like possess that very nature by virtue of their own causes. Therefore, whatever is not the cause of that [perishability] would necessarily lack that nature.
And that cause, possessing a fixed capacity, is indeed perceived in its own nature;
nor is there a restriction [on its capacity] by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The accidental occurrence of objects is not logical,

because for that which is independent, there can be no restriction regarding place, time, or substance; likewise, in this case as well, a cause for such restriction must be stated, by virtue of which these [objects] are only certain ones [and not others].
Those things born from a perishable nature do not have any determiner of their inherent nature (svabhāva) here, because the destruction of all that is born is established.
If it is argued that "the nature of what is born is to perish," [we reply: certainly not.
That which has the nature of being subject to birth and destruction cannot have a cause, nor can there be a determination of intrinsic nature for that which is causeless.
Therefore, in this case, there is no differentiation of the intrinsic nature of any cause; because such a thing does not exist.
It is not the same case with the result, for which [non-existence] does not exist;
this independence of destruction,
being in contradiction with existence at some place and at some time, brings about its absence by its very nature.

It establishes this: for if an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is independent were to exist at some time or in some place, it would necessarily depend on that time or substance; thus, as has been stated, it would not be independent at all.
In that case, if that perishable nature were independent, it would be causeless.
It is not causeless, because it exists precisely due to the cause of its existence, since it arises in such a manner; for when something exists, it exists as exactly that which it is.
If it is argued that existence does not necessarily arise from anything,
then existence must be accidental.
This [suffering] would never cease for anyone, anywhere, or at any time;
for it would either adhere to something or not, depending on what and where it might belong.
Whether it be dependent or independent,
if this existence (*sattā*) were non-restrictive,
it would not possess necessity.

Therefore, this [destruction] is not accidental in any case. How, then, has it been stated that destruction is now causeless? Because once something has arisen, its existence does not depend on anything else.
And it has been said in this regard: "Destruction is not something other than the entity;
indeed, destruction is its very own nature (svabhāva). For that [nature] itself is born as persisting for only a single moment.
Yet, dull-witted people determine this nature of his only subsequently, and not even upon its initial perception.
"Due to a lack of proficiency," it is subsequently established by that [lack of proficiency], just as poison is [misidentified] by the ignorant through the observation of its effects.
Therefore, this is nothing other than existence itself.
Since destruction does not depend [on anything else], it pervades that [entity].
But how, then, is it understood that destruction is independent?
And because that cause lacks capacity (asāmarthya),
and because there is a negation of action by that which produces non-existence— this is indicated by the word "and" (ca).
How is it that [the cause] lacks capacity?
For when an entity is already established, an agent does not produce it;
nor does he do anything for it in the production of another [entity].
And because it does not produce the form of either that [thing] or its opposite, it is ineffective and thus not required. For you consider the negation of activity to be destruction;
therefore, it follows that this cause of destruction produces non-existence (*abhāva*). In that case—
If non-existence were some kind of effect, its very nature would be existence;
thus, it would not be non-existence.
Therefore, "to produce non-existence" means "not to produce existence."
A negation of its activity would have been established;
nevertheless, since this [negation] is ineffective, why is it even considered? Thus, the independence of an entity with respect to destruction is proven.
Therefore, this [effect] exists by way of its own nature; indeed, wherever it exists, it exists there by way of its own nature even apart from that [cause]. //196//
This very [entity], being observed to exist in some instances, exists by its own nature (svabhāvataḥ) because it is independent;
likewise, it must exist by its own nature in other instances as well, since there is no difference [in its nature]. Therefore, any inference regarding an existent object is of only two kinds.
Because of the restriction of the relationship between those two [the cause and the effect] with respect to their own respective probanda through both presence and absence. //197//

Therefore, inference regarding a real object is of only two kinds: that based on the mark of effect (*kāryaliṅga*) and that based on the mark of essential nature (*svabhāviliṅga*). This is because, depending on the respective case, there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between those two marks and the probandum (*liṅgin*), which is all-pervasive [in relation to them], as was stated previously.

Since activity is preceded by cognition, when that [cognition] is not perceived, it is said that one should not act; thus, non-perception possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). //198//

The third reason, however, is non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), which is said to be a means of cognition for some object without distinction; for in the negation of the verbal usage based on the ascertainment of existence, every instance of non-perception is indeed a logical mark (*liṅga*). This is because verbal usages proceed from the ascertainment of existence.
These have been called "occurrence" (*pravṛtti*).
For it was stated previously that non-apprehension itself is non-existence (*asattva*).
And that [non-existence] is due to the power of the cognizer, not due to the power of the object;
for as long as there is no cognition of it, that entity does not exist for him.
Even if it were existent, those [entities] do not perform that function [for him].
In reality, however, that which is not perceived is neither existent nor non-existent;

for even among existing things, there are occasions when they are not perceived due to the remoteness of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, since this [non-perception] is equally possible even in the case of non-existent things. Thus, the existence [of such a thing] is negated for the cognizer due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Non-apprehension, characterized by its own causes, excludes linguistic conventions involving words;
therefore, this non-apprehension of things that have reached the conditions for apprehension is,
in reality, of the nature of non-existence, because it is unfit for [cognitive] activity.
For her as well, this same validity applies regarding this object;
even though she results in the certainty that [the object] is non-existent.
Even in the case of non-existence, this is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for it is impossible that [an object] capable of being perceived [should not be perceived].
It would not be perceived while all other causes are present; however,
prior non-existence is not a means of proof for that [non-perception], because:

Many objects beyond the reach of the senses are not connected to the subject matter of the treatise and lack any inferential mark; how, then, can their non-existence be established through non-perception? (199)

Thus, this person, seeking to establish non-existence by means of mere non-apprehension, would have to establish it for all objects through the cessation of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, the cessation of a treatise (*śāstra*) is not a prover of non-existence.
Because it does not apply in cases where one lacks the qualification;
for a treatise, when it proceeds, does so by relying upon a means that accomplishes some human goal.
Otherwise, it would be mere incoherent chatter and thus lack authority;
furthermore, in such a context, many points need not necessarily be set forth.

Just as certain mental states of individuals, which are restricted to each person, arise from indeterminate causes, or as specific substances that are separated by space and time or irrelevant to the context do not [produce cognition], so too [is it with those objects].
It takes the treatise as its object;
however, it does not possess the power to produce knowledge regarding remote things through the application of its own capacity.
Furthermore, their effect is not necessarily perceived such that they could be inferred;
nor do they [cease to exist] even when the three means of valid cognition have ceased to function.
It is not possible to determine that "they do not exist.
Therefore, non-apprehension of everything is not the means for establishing the certainty of cessation. Thus, this [is the case].

[The opponent argues: "It might be that this [non-apprehension] does not have the result of determining existence or non-existence, and thus it would lack the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatā*);
or else, this non-apprehension is simply not a valid means of knowledge at all, because the results of valid means of knowledge consist in definitive ascertainment (*vyavasāya*).
For even when there is a prohibition of activity, this [non-apprehension] does not effect a decisive determination free from doubt."

The mind acts [in this way], because even from doubt people sometimes engage in worldly activity. If that were the case, it would be faultless provided one acted preceded by certainty; thus, this is non-engagement.
The result has been explained;
there may also be some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that arises from an excellence of the inferential mark (*liṅga*). //200//
In this regard, not every non-apprehension is a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*);
rather, some [non-apprehensions] are indeed means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), arising from specific characteristics (*liṅga-viśeṣa-bhāvinī*), as was illustrated previously.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that non-apprehension is not a means of valid cognition—
this principle has been cited regarding the non-cognition of an intrinsic nature that makes [something] known;
it applies to any case where an intrinsic nature is not perceived due to remoteness of place and so forth.

That [object] is indeed non-existent merely because it is not perceived, as was stated previously. Furthermore, even an object that is beyond the senses, or a specific nature, which is rejected due to the absence of a probative mark (*liṅga*), such as "there is no dispassionate mind" or "there is no particular deity."

It might be argued that the volitions of generosity, non-violence, and abstention from harm do not possess the quality of being causes for higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*), because even regarding an object that is perceptible, the fruit does not arise immediately;

thus, due to a resemblance with things that lack such a fruit, one might be mistaken and deny their causal efficacy. However, one cannot conclude their non-existence merely on that basis, for [causes] may be separated by an interval.
Because one observes the arising of effects from causes, just like the transformation caused by the poison of a rat or a rabid dog;
since there is no contradiction in their existence, mere non-perception here is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
If it is asked, "What is the proof for their existence? [the answer follows].
Therefore, let there be doubt, or let it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no rejection [of the possibility].
In this regard, for certain objects...

Alternatively, there might be a failure to establish the indicator [of non-existence] due to either the lack of clarity in perceiving the intrinsic natures or the absence of a necessary rule for causes to produce their effects; however,
its non-existence does not follow from this alone.
Furthermore, because for some [things] there is manifestation by way of succession, the non-cognition of the causal agent regarding the effect is indeed the proof of its non-existence. (201)
When the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is to be proven, only the non-apprehension of that [nature] is said to be a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*);
however, the non-apprehension of the causal factors (*kāraka*) is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it is not possible that...
If the cause were absent, the effect would exist.
But is it not observed that sometimes the effect persists even when the cause has perished? We do not say that the effect exists at the same time as the persistence of the cause.
However, it is said that there is no arising of an entity devoid of a cause;
nor does an entity persist in such a manner as having that [cause] as its material basis.
However, because it indirectly benefits the continuum, it is designated as its effect.
If its non-existence were established in some way, it would be certain that its result does not exist.
Furthermore, the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the intrinsic nature of the object.
The non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāva-anupalambha*) is indeed a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that which possesses the mark (*liṅgin*),
provided that its pervading essential nature (*vyāpaka-svabhāva*) is established as being unperceived.
Just as "treeness" [is perceived] in a *śiṃśapā* tree;
its absence would be cognized by some reason [if it were present]. //202//
If the absence of this [subject], whether it be a cause, an essential nature (*svabhāva*), or a pervader (*vyāpaka*), were established by some indicative reason (*gamaka-hetu*),
then that very absence would itself produce its own effect.
Or, it [the non-perception] negates the pervaded;
for as long as its own absence is not established, there remains doubt even regarding that which is to be negated.
How, then, can there be an absence of an entity simply because the entity itself is not perceived?
10405 Proof: 10406 When there is no possibility of a cause for the non-perception of a perceptible object, 10407 the absence of existence is cognized for that entity which is not perceived. //203//
For if an entity were to exist, it would necessarily be perceived by its respective perceiving instrument;
it would certainly be perceived when there are no obstructions or other factors that hinder its vision.
However, that which is not perceived is determined to be non-existent.
Such [a reason] is [valid],
because its apprehension is non-deviant;
this very reason [applies] in the absence of both the probans and the pervader.
It should also be understood:
because the existence of a contradictory entity subverts the existence of that [other], the determination of non-existence occurs upon the perception of what is contradictory to it. //204//
For when a certain entity does not coexist with another,

because the two substrata of their respective material causes are in a state of mutual incompatibility due to a conflict in their initiation, there occurs the cognition of the absence of one when the other exists, as was stated previously.

This [non-existence] is not established separately from non-apprehension; for it is understood through that very [non-apprehension], and because of the contradiction [involved in its existence]. From this contradiction, there is non-existence.
[Objection: Let it be granted that such a non-perception (anupalabdhi) serves as a means for the cognition of absence. But how can that [non-perception] be an inference?
And why should it not be so?
Because it does not depend upon an example;
for there is no example whatsoever for this [non-existence]. Is it not the case that something indefinable, such as a sky-flower and the like, serves as an example?
How is that non-existence to be understood, such that it would be so? If you say, "Precisely through non-apprehension," then [the following applies] in that case:
How can non-existence be established without an example? Or, if there were an example, it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And in that case, there would be no comprehension [of the probandum]. Therefore, it is like the establishment of an indefinable (*nirupākhya*) absence.
Furthermore, because it does not depend upon an example, it is not an inference. Even while listening, the "Beloved of the Gods" is not adept at comprehension.
For the sign (nimitta) of linguistic conventions regarding non-existent things is the perception of what is not perceived; that [perception], by its own presence, [arises] from its own causes.

"Whatever brings these about"—this refers here to every instance where there is a proximity suitable for the causal complex of its own specific conditions. Furthermore, "non-existence" in this context is simply non-apprehension;
for this very reason, it [is established] from the cause.
Because it has the characteristic of an inference from an effect (*kārya-anumāna*),
we shall explain that it is included within the reason of essential identity (*svabhāva-hetu*).
This is also the case when negating the linguistic usage of the term "existent" (*sac-śabda-vyavahāra*) by means of the cessation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-nivṛtti*).

Sprouts and the like, which do not arise due to a deficiency of causal conditions (*nimitta*), serve as the examples; it is not only the "inexpressible" (*nirupākhya*) that is excluded. Even regarding the inexpressible, this very same process of activity is denied by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).

The non-existence of the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇā) is indeed established. This fool, having accepted either the sign (nimitta) or its absence, acts in contradiction to his own acceptance regarding engagement and withdrawal.
It is established as being either like that which is indefinable (*nirupākhyavat*) or like something else.
If it is asked: "How, first of all, is that very absence of apprehension established?"

We shall explain this further below. Furthermore, even in other forms of inference, one who maintains that the probans is pervaded by the property to be proven— why should such a person be convinced by an example, since the pervasion is already indicated by the statement itself?
If it is argued that the example is for the purpose of recollection even of an object already ascertained because [the cognition] is established as pervading [all things],
then that is the same in the other case as well.

Thus, although this person has already established the conventional usage of non-existence based on nothing other than mere non-perception, he is reminded here because he is confused. Now, regarding this [objection]: "The *pradhāna* and so forth do not exist, because they are not perceived."
Thus, in that case, how can there be the affirmation of the conventional usage of "non-existent" or the negation of the conventional usage of "existent"? And why would it not be so?
Because when that object is negated, the term expressing the substratum (*dharmin*) is not employed.

Because it is impossible for there to be a negation that lacks both a referent and a subject, this fault does not apply; for [the object] is established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The referent of a word is a threefold property (dharma) based on existence, non-existence, or both. //205//

When that non-apprehension of it is to be proven as the non-appropriation of its existence, such non-apprehension is the logical reason; it is not the non-existence of the thing itself, because of the employment of the word [to express it]. //206//

This has been explained: these words do not have the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object; rather, they appropriate as their object that thing which appears to a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from beginningless predispositions (*vāsanā*), for both the speaker and the listener who possess that conceptual construction, according to how it appears.
Because there is no application of the desire to demonstrate the actual object, and because it generates a conceptual construction (vikalpa) bearing that form;
and because a nature that does not appear as a condition for its own material cause and effect cannot be determined as having that [external object] as its domain.

That conceptual construction, however, arises from the latent predispositions (vāsanā) deposited by cognitions of existence, non-existence, and both; and by virtue of its determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the form appearing therein,
it is said to possess the properties of existence, non-existence, and both.

Thus, those established regarding this subject (dharmin) deliberate upon its existence or non-existence, [asking]: "Is this object appearing as the word 'pradhāna' based on a real entity (bhāva), or not?"

When its state of not being based on a real entity (bhāvānupādānatva) is to be proven, that very object— which, because it is personally experienced by each individual, is not subject to denial— is the subject (dharmin).
Nor can it be said that this very object is a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Because that [cognition] does not lose its nature even when the objects have neither been attained nor ceased,
it is directed toward aspects that are contrary to the actual reality.
Furthermore, because [words] exist even when there are conditions such as those belonging to other schools (*tīrthāntarīya*),
if words were restricted solely to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),
their application toward objects that differ according to various philosophical systems would be impossible. (207)
Furthermore, there would not be any statement whatsoever that lacks a real referent regarding the past or the unborn;
therefore, this [speech] is considered to have the objects of cognition (*buddhy-artha*) as its domain. (208)
These are the summary verses.

Furthermore, when it is to be proven that [the subject] does not have the form as intended by [the opponent] as its material cause (*anupādānatva*), this non-perception (*anupalambha*) exists as its property (*dharma*); thus, there is no lack of proof regarding the probans-property (*sādhana-dharma-asiddhi*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that the object appearing here as the conceptual construction of this very word is being denied; for a word is employed in order to present that [object] to the mind, and it would be impossible [to employ it] if that [object] were absent. Moreover:
When the existence of the word and its object is denied as the thesis to be proven, the substratum of the property is rejected;
thus, the composite whole cannot be the probandum, and the property alone would already be established.

For if only the meaning of the word were to be excluded, then because the very substratum (dharmin) denoted by the principal term would be negated, the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) would be without a locus. Therefore, this [exclusion]—
which does not depend on the exclusion of a substratum— is not the basis for the dispute and should not be put forward.
It must be so. Furthermore:

"By those who do not deny the referent of words, through the distinction between the positions of existence and non-existence, it is the real entity (*vastu*) itself that is investigated here, for the arising of the result is dependent upon it. (210)
What is the use of investigations for those who seek effective causal action regarding that which is capable of such action?
What is the use of a lustful woman examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch? //211//
For the referent of a word— whether it be non-existent or existent— neither obstructs nor accomplishes any human purpose,
because it does not correspond to reality in accordance with one's attachment.
Just as that which is not reality is not intended [as an object],
so this person, while proceeding in the constant investigation of what exists and what does not exist,
takes as his very basis only the real entity (*vastu*), having disregarded the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibhāsa*) upon which he [otherwise] relies.
Human purpose is obstructed [from being fulfilled], just as, for example, the remedy for cold and so forth [is obstructed] in the case of fire.

For in this case, the meaning of the word is not capable [of fulfilling that purpose], because even when there is the attainment of its experience, that [purpose] is absent. Therefore, one who seeks purposeful action (arthakriyā) ought not to direct a question toward that which is incapable of it.

This is not tenable; for a woman in love does not pay attention to whether a eunuch is handsome or ugly. Furthermore, as for what was said—that "the non-perception of the imagined is its characteristic" (dharma)—what is the meaning of that?

The referent of a word is conceptually constructed by virtue of being the object of conceptual cognition; the proponent of logic has stated that its property [of being a real entity] lacks a foundation in reality. (212)
