Because it is an object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the referent of a word (*śabdārtha*) is itself merely constructed.
The intended meaning is that its property (*dharma*) is the non-perception of a real entity as its basis (*vastv-āśraya*).
As for what was stated— that even upon the cessation of the three means of valid cognition, neither the existence nor the non-existence of a thing is established—
let that not be the case regarding other means of valid cognition.
In the absence of cessation, there is cessation;
because those two do not have a complete range of objects, scripture, moreover,
does not fail to pervade anything.

As for the question of how its cessation does not lead to [the conclusion that it is non-existent], it has been stated here: "Not all matters are recorded in the Āgamas, because they do not fall within the scope of the subject matter.
Furthermore:
Because words lack an invariable concomitance with real entities, there is no establishment of the object [of knowledge] from them; for they merely indicate the speaker’s intention.

For words do not function in accordance with the actual state of things, such that the nature of an object could be determined from them; rather, since they proceed from the speaker's intention to speak, being inseparable from it, they would convey that intention alone.
Furthermore, not all human intentions correspond to reality;

nor does an entity whose nature is not dependent upon that [intention] indicate anything else. As for the claim that scripture is a form of inference because it shares the common quality of being non-deceptive like the speech of a reliable person (āpta): [this is not so].
It has been stated that its validity consists in being an inference; how then is this so?
For this person is not capable of existing without relying upon scripture (āgama).

For in the case of certain [actions] whose results are beyond the senses, one hears of great benefits from engaging in them and of sins from desisting; and since no contradiction is perceived when those [results] exist, [the scripture is authoritative].

Therefore, since one must act when there is something to be done, he declares its validity through the investigation that "it is better to proceed in this manner. And that [validity] consists in being connected, having a suitable means, and expressing the human goal (puruṣārtha).
A statement concerning an investigation is therefore relevant; anything other than that is irrelevant. //214//
There is a connection among sentences that assists in the synthesis of a single meaning;
it is not merely a lack of synthesis, as in the case of sentences such as "ten pomegranates" and so forth.
Otherwise, one would point out the deficiency of the speaker;
furthermore, a person seeking results would not respect treatises whose methods are impossible or whose fruits are non-existent.
And it is not worth investigating those things which do not result in human goals,
being like the instruction on the ornament of the jewel on the hood of Takṣaka for the purpose of neutralizing poison, or like the examination of a crow's teeth.

By contrast, a treatise that possesses a conclusion, provides feasible means, and articulates the goals of human endeavor should be examined; for otherwise, it would be improper even to pay attention to it. Thus, if [it is not so]...
One who proceeds while being subject to contradiction during investigation would not be praiseworthy. What, then, is its non-contradiction?
It is that which is not sublated by either of the two kinds of valid cognition: direct perception or inference.
There is no contradiction for this [person] regarding the objects seen and unseen, because those two objects [correspond to reality]. //215//
Non-sublation by perception is the existence of those objects intended as perceptible in that very way,
such as the cognitions of blue and so forth, pleasure and pain, their causes, and the observation of passion and so forth;
and the non-perceptibility of those not intended as such, such as the form of sound and so forth.
And [this applies] to pleasure and so forth as they are situated, as well as to substance, action, generality, conjunction,
and so on; likewise, there is the existence of those things intended as the objects of inference that do not depend on scripture,
such as the four noble truths.
The existence of those things that are not inferable is as [in the case of] the self (*ātman*) and so forth;
even in the case of inference dependent on scripture (*āgama*), it is as with passion (*rāga*) and so forth.

Having accepted that form [of suffering] and its origin as unwholesome (*adharma*), there is no instruction regarding bathing, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and so forth, for the sake of abandoning them;
this is because their objects are exhaustively determinable.
Purity is non-contradiction.

Because there is a commonality of non-contradiction with the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*), the cognition [of the Buddha] is designated as inference even regarding its object that is beyond the senses, since there is no other way [to know it]. (216)

And because this very person, being thus established as authoritative (*āpta*), possesses the quality of non-deceptiveness (*avisaṃvāda*) common to all his statements and has never been observed to err, his non-deceptiveness is inferred even regarding objects accessible only through perception and inference; for his cognition of those objects is based upon that same [authoritativeness], just like his cognition of other things.
Therefore, although it originates from sound, it does not necessarily communicate the speaker's intention in the same way as a verbal expression;
thus, because it is non-discrepant with the object, it is also an inference. Alternatively, [this applies] to the speech of a reliable person (*āptavāda*) in another sense.
It is called inference because it is non-deceptive, due to the establishment of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means [thereto];
or else, it is inference because it is non-deceptive regarding the primary object, as in the case of another [inference]. //217//
Non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the non-perversity of that which is to be abandoned, that which is to be adopted, and the means thereto, as taught by him;
for example, in the case of the Four Noble Truths according to the method to be explained.
Because this [teaching], which serves human goals and is intended for application, is non-contradictory, [it is authoritative] with respect to other objects as well.
Furthermore, the acceptance of suchness is not for the sake of deception, because it is not obstructed [by reality] and because a speaker’s purposeless or false statement would be fruitless.
Thus, this [acceptance] occurs in both ways only out of necessity.
It has also been described that scripture possesses the nature of inference; for it is better to act in this manner based on scripture than to act otherwise.
Indeed, it has already been explained that inference is not thus free from error, because words do not possess an invariable connection (*anāntarīyakatva*) with their objects;
others, however, maintain that [inference] is correct when it depends upon a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*).
Others maintain that a person endowed with qualities such as seeing things as they truly are is an authoritative person (*āpta*), and that his composition [of a work] constitutes non-contradiction;
however, this point could be accepted if that excellence were possible to know. (218)
Every person who acts with foresight, desiring to engage in an activity, investigates whether it is based on tradition or not; they do not act out of mere whim.
This is so that, having understood what ought to be performed from this [tradition], they may proceed accordingly.
Thinking, "May I be successful," he proceeds toward other things as well by means of a cognition that is capable of being observed and is non-deceptive.
Since worldly convention is of such a nature,
if one were to proceed by means of an investigation into the person, there would be no engagement at all.
Because it is impossible to know such a person as they truly are, [the objection] does not arise from a lack of desire [to know].
For such persons speak without falsehood; for instance:

Others, however, maintain that [the truth of] "this is thus" or "it is not," as well as its being either faulty or faultless, are difficult to understand because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are hard to obtain. //219//

For it is from these internal qualities and defects that persons engage in correct or erroneous conduct; and since these [qualities and defects] are beyond the reach of the senses, they must be inferred from the bodily and verbal behavior produced by them. Furthermore, such behaviors can generally be performed otherwise even with deliberate intent.
Because they function according to human desire and because those desires are diverse,
how could this person, failing to determine [the truth] due to the confusion of logical marks (*liṅga-saṃkara*), arrive at a conviction? Or rather,
does such a faultless person not exist at all?

Since all [phenomena] possess opposites and are subject to decrease and increase, those outflows (āsravas) might eventually be eliminated through the internalization of that [remedy] by means of its repeated practice. //220//
But he whose outflows (*āśrava*) have been abandoned is difficult to comprehend.
For defects, possessing the nature of decrease and increase, establish the superiority and inferiority of the overcoming of their opposites, like a flame and so forth; for they—
Arising from conceptual construction, even though the substratum of grasping exists, they are subject to diminution through the cultivation of certain mental qualities;
when that [cultivation] reaches proficiency, they are of a nature to perish without leaving any trace.
They would be like flames and so forth;
therefore, it might indeed be faultless. How is it faultless?

This is not a fault; for even though the antidote has become one's own nature (*sātmya*), just as the antidote arises in one whose nature is still characterized by faults, so too will faults arise according to their respective conditions (*yathāpratyayam*). Why is this so? Because:
Of that which has as its intrinsic nature an object that is real and free from affliction, [there is no sublation] by means of errors.

Even if there is effort, there is no sublation [of the cognition], because the intellect has a partiality for that side. For an intrinsic nature cannot be turned back without effort, like the aversion of a Vedic scholar toward a Kāpālika.

And effort would be exerted through the perception of qualities and defects regarding the two natures— that which is to be attained and that which is to be averted— and this [effort] belongs to a person whose self is oriented toward the opposite side.
It is not possible for faults to exist [in that state], because it is free from affliction due to the abandonment of all faults without exception.
Because it is free from the suffering bound to the outbursts [of the afflictions] and to birth, and because it does not cause aversion to the flavor of the bliss of tranquility;
for even though its object is unreal, it arises through the power of grasping.
It would not [occur] because of the appropriation of a perverted continuum; however, it does [occur] with respect to the reality of things,
because it arises through the power of the objective entity.
Furthermore, defects whose objects are unreal do not obstruct that which is concordant with the antidote;
therefore, there is no further arising of defects,
even when effort is applied toward the side of the qualities of the intellect.

Because one who possesses discernment and an undisturbed mind applies effort specifically toward the antidote itself through the elimination [of faults], what, then, is the source of these defects from which they are abandoned by the cultivation of their antidotes?
The origin of all classes of defects arises from the view of a self-identity.
That is ignorance; therein lies attachment to it, and from that arises aversion and the rest. //222//

For indeed, for one who perceives "neither I nor mine," there is no attachment in the absence of grasping; and for one who is without affection, there is no aversion toward anything that does not obstruct the self or what belongs to the self.
And because that [view of self] is absent in that which obstructs and opposes it,
the vision of a self born from the practice of a similar kind gives rise to the grasping of "mine."
Both that affection and that hatred and so forth— all these defects arise from the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
and that very thing is ignorance.
Thus it is said:
"Delusion is the root cause of the defects; for this very reason, it is so designated."
The view of a self-identity is [abandoned] elsewhere; it is abandoned through the abandonment of that [view]. //223//

They say that delusion (*moha*) is the primary cause of the afflictions (*doṣa*), because the afflictions do not arise in one who is free from delusion; alternatively, [they say] the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the cause. And this would be so when there is a primary designation.
Because it is contradictory for many defects accumulated over numerous lifetimes to arise simultaneously,
and because when two factors are equally predominant, the designation of only one cannot pertain to the other part.
In either case, there is no contradiction in the designation of a single [entity];
moreover, its predominance is due to its being the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [designation].
Because through its abandonment, the defects are abandoned;
therefore, it is possible for the defects born from the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to be eliminated by practicing the realization of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is their antidote.
[This is] abandonment. But that one whose faults are exhausted is difficult to follow, such that one might practice based upon his instruction.
Let it not be the case that a word based on a person is scripture, because the author is difficult to follow.
Because the defects that cause the falsity of words reside in the person.
Some declare that [the Veda] is of non-human origin and possesses true meaning. //224//
Indeed, not every scripture is necessarily subject to deception;
for since the defects that cause deception reside in persons, that which is non-personal (apauruṣeya) must have a true meaning.
Some [say]: "For it is the absence of the cause that establishes the absence of the effect.
It is precisely with reference to those who speak thus [that this is said].
Because words whose meanings are true and which possess excellences depend upon a person as their locus.
Others declare: "Why should that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) not have a false meaning? (225)
Just as a person overwhelmed by passion and the like is seen to be a speaker of falsehood, so too is one endowed with compassion, the nature of dharma, and so forth,
a speaker of truth. Thus,
just as the falsity of speech depends upon the person as its basis, [so does its truth depend upon such qualities].
Likewise, since the state of having a true meaning [depends on the word],
when that [word] ceases, it also causes that [meaning] to cease;
thus there would be either meaninglessness or a contradiction.

For words do not possess meaning by their very nature; rather, the manifestation of meaning arises from convention, just as in the case of bodily gestures, designations, and so forth. This refers to non-contradiction.
However, suitability [for the purpose] exists at that time because of the formulation of his will;
for it is impossible to bring about things established by nature through the power of will.
Those [words], being initially meaningless, would become meaningful through human refinement;
and it is precisely this state of being refined by that [human agency] which is logically consistent with their being of human origin.
There is no arising;
for that very reason, because of the deception regarding the object,
even what has arisen is otherwise established.
It does not obstruct [the cognition], like the qualities of other persons. Therefore, this [word], when being withdrawn,
withdraws the manifestation of the object that arises from its own established convention.
How, then, could it possess truthfulness through the cessation of that [human agency]?
Furthermore, if "being of human origin" (pauruṣeyatā) means simply the act of production,
rather than the communication of a convention (samaya), [then the Veda would not be considered human].
For convention, which is based on human beings, is the cause for making an object known.
Therefore, even if words were not of human origin, the possibility of falsehood remains. //226//
For what is gained by its being authorless? Since the comprehension of meaning arises from convention (*samaya*), that [convention] is a human product and could even be false;
for instance, the statement regarding heaven as the result of practicing ethical discipline (*śīla*) would otherwise be otherwise.
At that time, one might cause [the cognition] to be erroneous;
because it is possible for it to manifest even what is not in accordance with reality,
that very same fault remains.
If the relationship were not of human origin, there would be cognition even for one who lacks consciousness [of it].
It might be argued as follows: words are indeed unrelated to their objects;
they are not erroneously misapplied by persons to those objects in other ways.
"Therefore, there is no fault.
But what, then, is the purpose of convention? For that [convention] is the relationship from which the cognition of an object arises.
If it were not of human origin, it would not depend upon convention;
or else, how could there be a relationship without a basis for cognition?
If that [universal] is manifested through convention, then the postulation of something else [a real universal] is untenable. //227//
Indeed, a relation, even if it exists, is not a cause of cognition if it is unmanifested;
rather, it is convention (*saṃketa*) that manifests it.
In that case, what is the use of something that merely presents what is already established?
An irrelevant factor is being maintained [as a cause].
Is it not the case that the function of a relation consists precisely in the production of the cognition of an object?

If it is argued that "it was done at that very time," then a time is not capable [of producing an effect] with respect to what is unfit; for if [the capacity] consists in fitness and its connection thereto, [then the time cannot be the cause].
In that case, let the relationship indeed be the word itself;
for the form of the word is capable, as its fitness is the effect.

Like the capacity for causality. If that [capacity] were a distinct entity, then the relation must be stated as to what it belongs to—[namely], "of the word. If it is argued that it is "the assistance consisting of capacity," we say no.
Because that which is eternal is beyond all degrees of excellence;
for even in that case, there would be the fallacy of over-extension, since no benefit could be established.
Furthermore, regarding capacity, if the capacity were inherent by its own nature...
Why is it not accepted that the object itself [is the convention]?
In that case, how would there be a relationship between word and object as a convention?
Because [the universal] resides in individuals;
for there can be no relation between established entities that are unmixed, as that would entail their non-difference and because they would be independent of one another.
Speech, which is not prompted by the desire for a specific object, indicates to one who knows "this is that" an object that reflects its own cause; thus,
the relationship between speech and the intimation (*vijñapti*) of the form of cognition is that of the produced and the producer.

From that sound, there is comprehension because of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*). The communication of that [relation] is the convention (*samaya*). From that, the connection between the signifier and the signified is established through the communication of the relation.
But that very [relation] is not [the one in question].
Or, let there be some other eternal relation; by means of that—
If words were restricted to a single meaning, there would be no comprehension of other meanings.
For it is not logical that there should be cognition of an object that is unrelated by means of that [intended] relation,
because that would entail its futility; and indeed,
every convention is seen to be established by the power of desire.
It illuminates everything;
when there is a connection with multiple meanings, there arises the possibility of expressing contradictory [meanings]. //228//
Now, lest there be a contradiction with what is observed, [it might be argued that] all [words] are denoters of everything. But it is not so;
for everything is not the means of accomplishing everything, because the relationship between cause and effect is non-confused (*asaṃkara*).
In that regard, [the capacity is] restricted—

When a word that is common to all possible objects of proof and means of proof is intended for a specific object of proof, how is it that the author of the convention effects only the manifestation of the desired [meaning]? Since that [word] is unrestricted, it receives its restriction from a person. At that time:
Furthermore, the postulation of its being authorless would be rendered useless.
Thinking, "May I indeed understand the meaning without confusion," the cause of confusion is scattered by persons.
In that regard, those very same [words] which, when employed by persons in certain instances,
become confused, being common to all, are restricted by them in certain cases.
If it is argued that the Vedic [practices] are restricted by their very nature because of a lack of thorough knowledge of reality, we say no; they depend on instruction.

Otherwise, they would not depend [on convention], nor could they reveal [the meaning] through linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), and there would be no conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) in the explanation. Furthermore, since the correspondence with the intended object in an instruction cannot exist if conceptual differentiation is impossible,
the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatā*) is indeed useless.
And the reason [for this] must be stated: because a relationship between distinct things is established. //229//

For external objects are not the nature of a word, nor is a word the nature of objects; by virtue of which, even when there is a distinction in their formal arrangement, there would be an inseparable connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) due to their identity. [This applies to] "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—
Like impermanence itself,
these sounds are neither produced by the intention to speak nor are they manifested by that intention; nor are they dependent upon the object [meant].
Therefore, how could they now establish that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) which is to be proven by that specific restriction? For that which is not [logically] connected cannot be its proof.
Because it could not be modified by persons, it would be entirely useless.
If one accepts [the existence of] mental formations (*saṃskāra*), this would be like the "bathing of an elephant" in its primary sense. //230//
Thus is the summary verse.
Furthermore,
is the relationship between word and meaning eternal?
Or it might be impermanent;

if it were impermanent, there would be either the occurrence or non-occurrence of human desire. If it were not dependent on humans, then by the reversal of place and so forth according to the intentions of humans, [the result] would follow from that.
There would be no demonstration [of the object],
because that which is not dependent upon one's will cannot possibly be [demonstrated] at will,
just like a mountain and so forth.

This same fault applies even to the case of permanence, because for that which has a stable nature, transformation is impossible; thus, it is the same even when [the entity] remains in all its states, since there would be no intended restriction. Consequently, there could be no cognition of specific distinctions, and the aforementioned undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) follows.
Furthermore, since [the scripture] arises from the activity of desire, it possesses human authorship; thus, there is the suspicion of deception. Moreover:
"Because the related entities are impermanent, there is no permanence in the relationship.
For a relationship depends on others, and in the absence of a necessary connection between those two, the status of being related would be impossible."

And that substratum is impermanent; with the disappearance of this connection, its [the connection's] disappearance would also follow, otherwise it would be without a substratum. Therefore, it is not eternal.
Furthermore, the meaning of its being a substratum must be explained;
for that which is eternal cannot be assisted,
and that which does not provide assistance cannot be a substratum.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the universal (jāti) is what is expressed, we say no;
for it has already been thoroughly examined that there is no purpose in expressing that [universal].

This is so because a genus is impossible in all cases; it is therefore untenable [to claim that a word denotes] individual instances by chance, since if a genus were always being denoted by words for individuals, it would be impossible for them to function by excluding other specific particulars. Therefore, the relationship is the presence and absence of an entity that possesses positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Therefore, those objects of words must be refined by persons through their intellect.
Relying upon those very two— existence and non-existence— which, though unmixed,
appear to a person as if mixed due to the habitual tendencies of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-bhāvanā*), they are thus [conceived as] belonging to persons.
[It would be] a conjunction. Furthermore, since the relationship is destroyed by the destruction of its substratum, that sound— being no longer related— would not be joined with a new [phoneme],
and yet entities continue to arise one after another.
Because an established relationship would be absent, those things that lack a relationship would be inexpressible. Even in that case,
[if they were] produced together with the objects themselves—
When [the object] is being conceptualized,
a reversal of intrinsic nature is not appropriate in the case of words.
Now, lest there be a deficiency in the meaning of a word whose connection [to that meaning] has been lost,
and lest meanings themselves become inexpressible, if one were to claim that a produced object arises as possessing its connection,
even though that connection was produced later, it would not belong to the word.
Because it is impossible for that [object] to have the nature of that [word], which is by nature unrelated to it, without a reversal of its own nature; and because,
when [the object] has arisen together with the word and is established from another source, the word provides no assistance to it.
And because it lacks a common substratum:

even if that [substratum] were capable of acting as a cooperative cause for its production, there would be the undesirable consequence of its constant production, since a permanent entity is independent and cannot be assisted.
Even if there is incapacity, there is still inability because it does not later abandon its own nature;
this fault does not apply when [the relation] is considered conceptually constructed.
For a relation that appears through human conceptualization does not depend on the actual connection between entities, nor is it characterized by dependence upon them; thus,
even for eternal things, it does not alter their intrinsic nature.

If one were to construct [the world] by imagining it oneself from some source, those [beings] would likewise be so; yet they are not subject to the law of falling away (cyavana-dharma). As it has been said: "By the departure of the support, the supported..."

"In that case, it is impermanent because its connection [with a substratum] is destroyed. If it is argued that, like a universal (*jāti*), there is no destruction even when the substratum perishes because it is eternal, then what efficacy does a substratum have toward things that are eternal, such that it is accepted as their substratum? (233)
It is heard [in tradition] that the universal (*jāti*) is eternal and does not perish along with its substratum (*āśraya*).
However, we do not perceive any efficacy of a substratum toward things that are eternal, by virtue of which it could serve as such a substratum;
for there is no production of what has already been produced, and that which is not an agent is independent. Manifestation (*vyakti*)...
If it is argued that there is an assistance to the universal (*jāti*) and to the relation by virtue of their substratum (*āśraya*), and therefore [the manifestation] is the substratum—[we reply:

the production of that [cognition] through its fitness for producing it, based on the connection with auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) which are the causes for the arising of cognition, is what is intended by "manifestation" (*vyakti*). (234)

Even in the case of jars and other such objects, for those who know the reasoning, since there is no distinction among unchanging things, what purpose is served by their respective manifestors, and how could they be considered "manifested" by them? (235)

The manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of jars and other such objects is simply the production of a subsequent moment capable of generating cognition, arising from the auxiliary causes in dependence upon the material cause (*upādāna*);
otherwise, if it were not dependent on that assistance, [manifestation would be impossible].
Because it would follow that [the cause] produces cognition;
because that which possesses efficacy is a producer;
and because the [cognition] has that [efficacy] as its very nature.

Furthermore, if [the object] were a different entity, it would follow that it does not assist the cognition; and since cognition arises through the object's own capacity, it would follow that jars and other things could never be perceived,
as they would not depend on light, because there would be no assistance to their own nature by means of such dependence.

Therefore, these [objects], depending on another for the production of the cognition of their own object, acquire from it an excellence of nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*); thus, they are produced by that [cognition]. As for the knowable—

However, because form (*rūpa*) is not established [independently], things are manifested for the purpose of making their distinction known by means of a word that, through the power of cognition, expresses an excellence in the effect;
this is not the case for universals (*jāti*), relations (*sambandha*), and so forth.
Since it cannot be assisted in any way whatsoever, it is not logical for it to be manifested by that which provides no assistance.
Furthermore, if the relation were a real entity (*vastu*), there would be a diversity of cognitions due to its distinctness [from the relata].
And this relation, being a real entity, must necessarily [be distinct] from both the word and the object.
Difference and non-difference do not transcend [the nature of] form,
for form is a real entity; otherness is simply its lack of being that very thing.

Thus it has been said. And how could this [object], being perceptible by the senses, be such [as perceived] in its own cognition if it does not appear as distinct from other things? This concerns the non-perception of the distinction between the visible and the non-distinct.
Because it is the basis for the existence of discernment and its opposite;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that such a state could not exist.

If it is argued that there is no fault even when [the object] does not appear because it is beyond the senses, just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth— no, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of non-comprehension, since what is unestablished cannot be a signifier.
If it were to signify by mere proximity, it would follow that even those who have not mastered the linguistic convention would understand it.

There is no comprehension through inference because of the absence of a logical mark (liṅga) and because an example is unestablished; for even in that case, since the object is beyond the senses, it requires a means of proof.
If it is argued that this is the same regarding the sense organs and so forth, we say: no.
This is because they are inferred otherwise:

for knowledge, when certain [causes] are present, possesses both positive and negative concomitance; it thus establishes that [the effect] cannot arise from those alone and demonstrates its dependence on something other than them.
Therefore, the existence of the sense-faculties is established by way of their effects;
it is not so for the relationship [between word and meaning], because that remains unestablished.
Because there is an absence of cognition which is the effect of that [object].
For in that case, neither the form of the word nor the object serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*), since both are capable of being present everywhere.
Because its basis for the cognition of a particularity has not been communicated, there is no cognition of it;
for when a specific relation does not exist, [there can be no such cognition].

That [reasoning] is correct. Or rather, just as in that case of the signless (animittā), there is a rule regarding the cognition of its specific distinctions, why is it not accepted that for words, the communication of meaning is likewise signless? Therefore, a similar logical mark (liṅga) would lead to the understanding of all relations without distinction.
Consequently, there would be cognition of everything without distinction;
therefore, for the sake of establishing the relationship and the resulting cognition, no one would depend upon tradition.
If it is argued that [the Veda] possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) when accompanied by tradition (*sampradāya*),
then what is the point of this long succession?

Why does that very same [word], depending on tradition (*sampradāya*), not effect the communication of meaning? Furthermore, that word is seen to be employed with certain intended meanings and is not seen otherwise; thus, through its being seen or not seen—just like smoke and so forth—it generates the cognition of that [meaning]. Therefore, it is that very [word] which [effects the communication].
The relationship is that which is called inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
We do not perceive the efficacy of anything else here, nor do we perceive any means of establishing it.

Furthermore, there is no relation between word and object that is distinct from them; since it is non-different from those two, it is simply those two themselves. Thus, there is no other way for a real entity to exist. //236//
Since the establishment of another state is based on a difference in form, that very form would remain the same; however,
there would be a difference in attributes (dharma) according to the sequence previously stated,
and that is not contradictory.
Thus, there is no difference in the entity itself;
nor is there any other possibility for an entity apart from difference and non-difference, because its nature is defined by its characteristics.
And because this conceptual differentiation does not transcend the nature of form;
moreover,
since the nature of a real entity is distinct, its relation is constructed by conceptualization.
This was stated previously:
for a relationship characterized by conjunction (śleṣa) is not possible among things that are not conjoined.
Nor is their relation a distinct entity (arthāntara), because:
"How could that which exists as a substance be dependent on another, or how could it be the relation of something else? (237)
For that which is already established does not depend on another;
nor is a relation independent [of its terms].
Furthermore, "substance" (dravya) is said to be an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
How could there be a conjunction with another nature? For indeed, one thing is not said to be conjoined with another by virtue of the existence of a different intrinsic nature.

If it is argued that [the connection] may not exist with the unconnected, but must exist with the connected, we say no; for the very connection itself is not established by those two, and that which would effect their connection is itself unestablished. Thus, this—

If it were the case that two meanings are joined by another meaning, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because there would be no distinction [between them]. Furthermore: "The phonemes (*varṇa*) being themselves devoid of meaning, the word (*pada*) and so forth are merely conceptualized."
How can this relation, which pertains to a real entity, function with respect to that which is not a real entity? //238//

For that which expresses would possess [the object] by means of its expressive component; however, phonemes, even if they exist, are not expressive. Therefore, there is no relationship between the expressed and the expresser among them.

Because that would entail the loss of its own nature in its manifestation. If it is argued that the phonemes are the expressive [signs] by virtue of a specific sequence, we say no; for the sequence is devoid of intrinsic meaning.
Because it is internal and thus non-differentiating,
and because that form remains unchanged even in another sequence, the cognition would be identical.
We shall also refute the view that the sequence is a distinct entity.
Therefore, if the phonemes themselves were not expressive, then the word (*pada*) and so forth would have to be the expresser;
yet that is impossible, because it is contradictory for such a thing to be either distinct from or non-distinct from the phonemes.

Therefore, the locus (*pada*) and the sentence (*vākya*), which appear as a single manifestation, are indeed false; they are an error consisting in the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on the appropriation of homogeneous latencies (*sabhāga-vāsanā-upādāna*), which are themselves bound up with the specificities of sensory consciousness (*indriya-vijñāna*).
Because of the impossibility of being both one and many: for it is not one,
since it is impossible for a single [object] to be grasped sequentially by multiple cognitions.

Nor can that [word] be apprehended by a single [cognition], because it is apprehended as a sequence of phonemes; and because at the time of apprehending a single phoneme, multiple cognitions must pass away,
given the momentariness of cognitions.

Because a moment (kṣaṇa) is the time required for the displacement of a single atom (paramāṇu); for if there were more [time], it would be impossible for that which possesses division to reach its final limit.
Because the completion of the final phoneme occurs at a time equal to the displacement of many atoms and the blink of an eye,
[the cognition] arises from memory according to the manner of the experience.
Recollection also occurs at that very same time,
because no distinction is perceived between the sequence of experience and recollection;
nor is it many words and so forth.
Because there is no appearance of difference to cognition,
and because its multiplicity will be refuted, it is not a real entity. Of that...
Because this does not transcend conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
and because a real entity (*vastu*) is a relation, how could that [entity] be the substratum (*āśraya*) for it?
Because it would be impossible for it to have a basis;
for in that case, it would indeed be without a basis,
and thus there would be no connection.
Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is not inherent; rather,
it is produced and manifested through the employment [of words] with that intention.
Or, the word "vā" (or) implies that its essence is a relation that is non-deviant from that [object].
And whether that [relation] is origination or manifestation, since it is the basis for non-deviance and is of human origin, it is indeed human-made (*pauruṣeya*).
Since the relationship [between word and meaning] is established through that [convention], there is no restriction on words regarding the communication of meaning;
thus, even if [the Veda] were authorless, that same deception would persist.
Furthermore, its authorlessness is asserted, supposedly because the authors are not remembered.
Furthermore, as for this claim that the Vedic sentences are authorless because no author is remembered—even though there are those who recite them—fie upon this all-pervading darkness! (239)
Our minds are filled with both wonder and compassion at how such a lapse in wisdom could have occurred even for him;
that others as well repeat [this] makes us feel merciless.
Fie upon this all-pervading darkness that has overwhelmed the world!
What fault is there in one who desires the welfare of living beings, yet is deceived?
For instance, the followers of the Sugata remember the authors of the mantras, such as Aṣṭaka and others;
and the followers of Kaṇāda [remember] Hiraṇyagarbha. Of these—
If it is argued that this is false speech,
then who now [would say] that other human-authored works such as the *Kumārasambhava* and others— which teach of themselves or another as the author— are likewise [false]?
If it is argued that, since they would be refuted in this manner, there is a contradiction of what has been accepted (*abhyupeta-bādha*) in that refutation; [we reply: no.
But surely this very [point] is a constituent of one's own commitment (*abhyupagama*); so whose [position] is sublated?
This is exactly the same for the opponent as well.
If it is argued that there is no fault because it is accepted by him, [we reply: no.
From where did this person previously have such an unauthoritative conviction?
And why would he now suddenly become a grasper [of truth]?
In some cases, one requires a proof;
that which exhausts oneself with the deliberation over whether [a text] is of human or non-human origin.
Therefore, since there is no subversion by what is not accepted from that very [intended] object of proof, this same [fault] applies equally to anything else; thus, it is not a valid objection.
And this person perceives no distinction.

Thus, in these statements, since you have accepted some excellence in the properties of the effects— which serve as the means of proving the non-human origin [of the Veda]— the operation of this [proof] is simply untrustworthy. Furthermore,
there are observed cases where the tradition of performance has been interrupted, even though the works were created by human agency.
If it is argued that they are perceived through effort, we say no;
because there is no such restriction.
Because non-perception or perception [of something] other than that [object] lacks certainty due to the lack of conviction arising from another's instruction;
and because we observe even those who deny things they have themselves created.
Because it is impossible to reach the ultimate conclusion [of this matter],
just as this person, without having heard it from another, [could not produce] this sequence of syllables and words.
"Another person as well is capable of speaking in that same way"—so says someone. (240)
To that as well, the same answer applies: "Even if [the Veda] were thus non-human-authored, what then would be human-authored?
and so forth. For instance:
"Or another composed text, apart from traditional transmission, by others..."
Who has been seen and designated by whom that he too should not be inferred in this way? //241//
Indeed, there is no other basis for the claim of non-human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) than the present inability of people to teach or recite it;
and that [inability] exists elsewhere as well, in the case of a text composed by one person for another.
It is equal [to the previous case]. Following that, everything should be inferred in the same way, or rather, nothing at all;
for it has already been stated in the passage beginning with "because that is not desired by him," and so on, as well as "because the desired [object] depends upon that," and so forth.
Moreover:

Whatever kind of thing is established from whatever source, that [source] is understood to be indistinguishable [in its causal capacity], even if its cause is unperceived, just like fire and wood. //242//
A cause is not called "causeless" merely because it is not perceived;
for even those entities whose causes are unperceived are inferred to be of such a nature when they are experienced as being non-different in essence from others of that same kind.

Even if the form of the cause has ceased, its [resultant] form would not cease, because it would transcend the properties of an effect; therefore, no one should speak in such a manner. Or rather, a specific characteristic of the form should be shown which would conform to this cause, by means of which the desired—
For those things that are undesirable, there would be no reversal into their opposite;
and because the cause— the cessation of intrinsic nature— is undifferentiated, the differentiation of entities would be accidental, and thus it would never cease anywhere.

Therefore, whatever intrinsic nature is observed to arise from a particular cause does not, even when occurring elsewhere, deviate from its own nature as having that causal property, provided it is not differentiated [from that context], just like fire and fuel. In this regard, those who fail to demonstrate the distinction [between instances] based merely on the observation of a commonality in the effect—
All those reasons that are extensively propounded are fallacious. //243//

For example: even the fire produced by a traveler today is preceded by another flame, not by the friction of fire-sticks; because it is a traveler’s fire, like a fire [produced] immediately before. How so?
Furthermore, there is an inconclusiveness regarding the fire of a traveler;
for it is by relying on the capacity of the fire to produce flames that the existence of another cause for the burning is rejected.
For if it were to exist without the flame, it would also exist elsewhere; thus,
in that case, there would be no relationship of sublation and non-sublation between the flame and the other production.

One might suspect a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) on the grounds that the state of having its origin in a flame could occur otherwise as well; since two properties could thus possibly exist in a single object, it would follow that neither the traveler's fire nor any other object would be restricted to a single [specific] thing. This is the doubt raised.

Thus, even though these two properties are mutually exclusive, their occurrence within a common entity (*vastu-sāmānya*) is said to be non-contradictory, but not within a particular (*viśeṣa*) characterized by distinct states.
Because it is contradictory for the partless self to be either that [identical] or not that;
nor is there a relationship of sublation and sublated between the flame and the subsequent birth of fire in the case of a traveler's fire,
since that [fire] originates from a flame.
Because there is no impossibility [of its existence] apart from that,
such a traveler’s fire would be produced from a flame.
Not all [of them],
because it is impossible to formulate a specific exclusion (*viśeṣa-pratikṣepa*) in that case.
Furthermore, because there is no necessity for that which possesses potential for distinction to remain in its original state;
and as for the argument that "if it could exist without a flame, it would also exist elsewhere," this is indeed the case.
If that causal complex by which [the Veda] arises were present, one might demonstrate its arising and thereby show its absence, or there might be a flame in that case. Therefore,
the study of one person being preceded by another does not establish that it is so for everyone.
It establishes [the point], because otherwise it would be impossible for that [to exist]; however,
such a thing—
devoid of the manifestation of that activity— would be so [only in that manner].
Even if it were such [as you claim], it should be stated in this way; however, when stated without qualification despite the possibility of specific distinctions,
it does not sustain its own meaning.
How could there be the possibility of a distinction, given that even those persons possess no capacity whatsoever, just like persons of the present day? Furthermore,
since no contradiction is observed between capacity and personhood here either, this is not a case of a non-contradictory affirmation.
The application of non-perception is a means of cognition;
for it has been stated that there is no apprehension of contradiction regarding things beyond the reach of the senses.
And this does not differ from the previous argument:
if men were capable [of producing it], then those of the present day would also be so.
This might be argued if a distinction were impossible;
however, that is difficult to prove.
For where one person lacks the capacity, it follows that all persons lack it as well.
As before, [the reason] is inconclusive;
for even though contemporary people lack the capacity for the *Mahābhārata* and other such works, the capacity of some [ancient person] is established therein.

Therefore, when distinguishing between causes— even regarding objects that produce the cognitions of "that" or "not that"— a difference in their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) must be demonstrated; for in the absence of such a difference,
either everything would be of that nature, or nothing at all would be.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any difference in intrinsic nature between the worldly and the Vedic;
in its absence, there is only their commonality.
When someone, while analyzing a property (*dharma*) of a single perceived [object], raises a claim of possible deviation (*vyabhicāra*) based on that which is possible within its own nature—
[considering] the case of the Veda and non-Veda— is it not so?
There is indeed a distinction characterized by reality (*tattva*).
This is true; however, it does not belong to those two alone. What then?

This is also the case with the *Ḍiṇḍika-purāṇa* and others. Furthermore, a difference in names that merely illuminates a distinction in their own internal systems does not invalidate the human authorship [of those texts], as is seen elsewhere.
Furthermore, as a consequence:
if humans were unable to produce such a composition,
or if one could distinguish a produced [composition] from one that is not conventionally agreed upon, then it would clearly be non-human (apauruṣeya).
The Veda. Now, it might be argued that humans simply cannot compose mantras; we shall examine this point later. Furthermore:
That which is called "mantra" is not something entirely different;
rather,
it is the means for accomplishing desired objectives by those possessing the power of truth and austerity.
That statement is indeed observed even among persons today; for instance,
because we see the neutralization of poison, fire, and so forth through the power of their respective foundations of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*),
and because certain Śabaras even today compose mantras.
And because we observe the ritual manuals (*mantra-kalpa*) of non-Vedic traditions such as the Buddhists and others,
and because those [manuals] are composed by persons—

Regarding the [Veda] being composed: even if it were not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) in that regard, how could it now be non-false? For instance, in the case of the mantras and ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of both Buddhists and others, acts such as violence, sexual intercourse, and the view of a self—which are causes for the lack of higher rebirth (*anabhyudaya*)—are described in one way [by them], while they are described otherwise [in the Veda].

How, then, could two [statements] that express contradictory things be true in one and the same place? In that case, if one were to postulate a different meaning for one of them, the same would apply to the other; thus, because the meaning remains undetermined, there is non-comprehension in some instances.
And likewise, even if it were existent, that which is useless and not of human origin—
such as the non-mantra status of the Buddhists and others— would require that the ordeal of drinking from a vessel (koṣapāna) be performed elsewhere as well.
Even Buddhists are seen to be engaged in the practice of administering poison;
in that regard, even the absence of mantras is contradicted.
Even through mudrās, maṇḍalas, and meditations that are beyond words, activities are performed;
yet these are neither authorless nor eternal.

It is logical: when action is possible for them, what obstacle could there be for men in the composition of syllables? Therefore, nothing is impossible for them to do. How is it, then, that the two types of mantras—those originating from truth and those originating from [worldly] reality—are mutually contradictory? It is not so.
Indeed, in all cases, those two possess the power of truth;
they are also characterized by the promises made by persons endowed with such power.
That power might also arise from specific attainments regarding movement;
[but] if mantras were of human origin, why would not all men be makers of mantras? [The answer is:
because of a deficiency in the means for performing those actions.
If they were endowed with such qualities as truthfulness, austerity, and so forth, they would certainly do so;
moreover, it is a man who composes poetic works.
"Every person would be a poet;
or else, if they were not, no one at all would be like him"— this is an unprecedented mode of expression.
It is true that [people] do not produce mantras when they lack the ritual procedures and means for their application;
however, we do not observe such completeness in anyone.
Because humans share common characteristics,
it has been stated in this regard that what is called "mantra" is not something distinct from the conventional usage of speech by those who possess truthfulness and other such qualities.
And those [defects] are observed in some men; thus,
even the possibility that all men are devoid of them is [a matter of doubt].
Because there is no contradiction, there is no definitive conclusion; furthermore,
non-perception is not a cause for certainty regarding things whose nature is beyond the senses.
Furthermore, memory, intelligence, penetration, truth, and power are not present in all [beings],
just as there are differences in the traditions for achieving those qualities and other virtues.
There may also be means of proof [for its existence].
Nor is everything, even if it exists, capable of being seen; for this very reason, the unseen cannot be denied.
Nor is there anyone among men who can obstruct any quality that is about to arise;
for since no sublation is observed, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is not established. By this [it is shown].
The refutations of omniscience and other such positions have also been explained above;
in those cases as well,
the principle is that such a person does not exist, because there is no established tradition of means for proving it.

Nor can it be said that [an entity] which does not possess the nature of [producing] something is incapable of making it known if it has not been perceived; for even among existing things, there is the possibility of not initiating an effect, and because [an entity] may be impossible to perceive due to the remoteness of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, the argument that "recitation is preceded by another recitation because it is a recitation" is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), since this property exists even in the case of reciting the *Mahābhārata*.
[Objection: But surely [the reason is valid] because of the qualification "Vedic recitation."

There is no fault. What, then, is the excellence of the Vedic study such that it cannot be studied otherwise? For a qualification that is not contradictory with the counter-example does not exclude the reason from that [counter-example].
If it is argued that [the Veda is eternal] because two non-contradictory states can coexist in one thing, on the grounds that people of the present day are engaged in its study;
This has already been answered. If you argue that it is because [the object] is not seen, this too has been refuted;
for non-existence is not merely a matter of not seeing.
Since [the word] "causes to go" (gamayati) is indeed subject to deviation, the qualification "possessing excellence" (atiśayabhāk) is equivalent to being unestablished (anupāttasama).
Even the pervasion that "whatever study of the Veda there may be, all of it is preceded by another such study" is not established,
because it is not proven that all [Vedic study] is of that nature.
However, whatever that cause was seen to be like, it would be "just so";
for when a particular [feature] has been seen, by abandoning that [particular] as being the cause, [one grasps] the universal.
The apprehension [of fire] is indeed fallible, like the whiteness of a substance used to establish the presence of fire.
By this, speech and other such factors are refuted as means for establishing passion and the like. Let it be so.
The study of the Veda is established as being preceded by prior study;
in this way, its beginninglessness is proven in every respect, yet it is not independent of persons.
Therefore, even if it were non-human (apauruṣeya), there would still be another [cause] that is not non-personal. //244//
For it is the person alone who, having reflected for himself or having received [the instruction] from another, applies [the words];
these sounds do not themselves resound for those whose organs are inactive, by virtue of which they might be considered non-human (apauruṣeya).
Even if they were authorless, it would be so only if there were a beginning of persons;
even then, however, the fact that [the Veda] is preceded by another would not be established.
Due to the absence of a teacher,
the first student would himself be the author.
Therefore, this human activity— proceeding from successive prior perceptions since beginningless time— is like the dust-play of children;
it is not something that is non-human (apauruṣeya).
If [a work] is considered authorless (*apauruṣeya*) because it is beginningless, then there are currently many more such [authorless works]. For instance,
this applies even to the linguistic conventions of barbarians and the like, as well as to the words of atheists.
Because it is beginningless, there is such a state due to the continuity of prior formative predispositions. //245//
Even certain practices of the Mlecchas, such as the marriage of mothers and the like, as well as the festivals of Madana and so forth, are beginningless;
likewise are the words of atheism which deny the unprecedented existence of the next world and other such matters. Not [so].
For those [scriptures] are set in motion by others who have not instilled any latent predispositions (*saṃskāra*) in them;
for even those who follow conventions (*samaya*) composed of their own creative intuition proceed only by means of the withdrawal of conceptual constructions regarding meanings never before heard.
Therefore, because there is no single teacher through whose continuous tradition something could have come from somewhere,
it is said to be "without a prior [cause]," even more so than in the case of what is seen.
The "operations" (*pravṛttayaḥ*) are worldly transactions consisting of correct and incorrect activities. [Objection:
But surely, it is maintained that in the first aeon (*ādi-kalpika*), worldly transactions were not previously observed and only came into existence later.
[Reply: No; for even those [transactions] are awakened according to their respective conditions, having been deposited by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of others.
If it is argued that let all [scriptures] be of non-human origin, what benefit would there be even if such non-human origin were established? Indeed,
it is accepted that non-human origin consists in being non-contradictory.
Since some [scriptures] that are non-concordant with reality are also beginningless, what is the use of [asserting] the lack of human authorship?
Or, even if the Vedic sentences themselves were indeed without human authorship;
Furthermore, doubt arises from observing differences in both the objects and the mental impressions. //246//
If, even though it is not of human origin, it were to produce only a specific manifestation of its meaning, there would be confidence;
however, [in reality], one may impose or deny [meanings] according to one's own desire.
12610 Etymologists, Mīmāṃsakas, and others are seen dissecting Vedic sentences; yet their meanings do not fail to cohere,
because the assignment of meaning is primarily governed by convention (samaya).
For even a single sentence may give rise to multiple alternative interpretations,
because verbal roots and suffixes are recorded as having multiple meanings.
Because conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is not accepted as being absolute; because there is an abundance of words that have no established usage (*arūḍha-śabda*);
and because the meaning of such [words] depends upon human instruction (*puruṣa-upadeśa*).
Because his teaching follows his own will, there is indeed no certainty regarding the meaning of the Vedic statements. Furthermore,
when proving that [the Veda] is not of human origin, would he prove this by means of the phonemes?
Or [if it refers] to the sentence:
in that case, since there is no difference between [the letters of] other [words], what would be the fruit of proving the [eternality of] the phonemes?
For the phonemes are not different in the world and in the Veda.
Furthermore, because recognition remains indistinguishable even when there is difference,

it follows that oneness cannot be established; and because difference is not perceived, the letters of the Veda are not established, since it would follow that they could not be apprehended through recognition.
And because they are not accepted [as such],
and since those [arguments] are equal in every respect regarding the proof of their lack of human authorship,
what is left over by this [argument]?
And thus, all conventional usage would be non-human in origin;
yet, since not all such usage is non-erroneous, this effort [of yours] is in vain.
Or rather, it concerns the sentence (*vākya*).
The sentence is held to be non-human (apauruṣeya);
it does not exist as something distinct from the phonemes, because it is not perceived [as such]. //247//
For we do not perceive any manifestation in the cognition of words and sentences such as "Devadatta" other than the manifestation of the phoneme *da* and so forth,
just like the manifestation of a second phoneme.
Furthermore, it is impossible to determine that anything else exists as an object of apprehension when it does not appear in the act of grasping,
just like any other distinct form.
If it is argued that the effect, which is impossible for anything else, is the indicator [of the word],
this might be so even if those phonemes exist.
That effect would not exist.
If it is argued that it does not arise because [the word] is absent in other words and sentences despite there being no difference among them, we say: no.
Because their lack of distinction is not established.
If it is argued that their lack of distinction is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), we say no.
Because that [word] is subject to deviation and because it lacks demonstrability,
even though there is no difference in the phonemes (*varṇa*), there would be a difference in cognition and a difference in the effect due to the difference in sentences;
and that [difference] arises from the sentence.
And since that [cognition] is beyond the reach of the senses, how could it exist?
If it were produced by mere proximity, it would occur even for one who has not mastered the linguistic convention.
Therefore, there is no such thing as a "sentence" that is a distinct entity from the phonemes, whose non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) would need to be proven.
Because of its non-existence, the non-human origin of the phonemes— which are no different from those in the Veda— is also [established] from the outset.
This has already been refuted in the [previous] section.
Furthermore, let it be granted that a sentence is a distinct entity;
nevertheless, it must consist of multiple components or it must be partless.
If it consists of multiple parts, those [parts] would be individually purposeless.

If even those many parts of it were individually purposeless by their very nature, then the attribution of that form to what does not possess that form is merely a conceptual construction, like [the attribution of] "lion-ness" and so forth. (248)
The sentence alone is meaningful,
while its constituent parts are themselves devoid of meaning;
in those parts, that [meaningful] self would be merely superimposed through conceptual construction.
Just as [the term] "lion" and so forth [is applied] to a young boy and the like, [the word "self"] would refer only to that which is produced by a person (*pauruṣeya*).
Now, lest this fault should occur, [if one were to argue that] it applies to each [individual]...
Those parts are intended to have that single meaning;
even though each one possesses that single meaning, there is a false conceptualization of multiplicity.
Furthermore, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would occur through the apprehension of a single part alone. //249//
For a sentence is a verbal form whose meaning is complete;
and since those constituent parts are of such a nature individually, each one of them would be a sentence.
And thus, a sentence does not consist of multiple constituent parts;
for the meaning of a sentence is understood through the comprehension of a single constituent part.

There would be no dependence on other constituent parts, nor would there be any delay in time; for since that partless self is apprehended in a single moment, it is understood in its entirety upon the arising of a single cognition.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with its being a single entity; furthermore, if they were heard all at once, a difference in time for all of them would not be tenable.
Now, let it be that [the word] does not depend on other parts, but arises from a single part alone.

Since the meaning of a sentence is established [only when all parts are heard], the sentence cannot consist of multiple sequential parts; therefore, it is required that all its parts be heard at once.
Even in that case, a lapse of time is certainly not tenable.
Because all [the words] are heard at the very time one part is apprehended;
and because, even when they are heard sequentially, the meaning is established from just one [word] among those that possess distinct meanings, the other [words] are redundant.
Because it would be redundant; and when [the word] is heard only once, its meaningfulness cannot be established for those [words] whose capacity to convey distinct meanings has not been observed.
"There is no fault because one perceives a functional object (artha) in the collection [of atoms];
No, because a form that does not exist individually cannot possibly exist even in a collection,
since no distinct entity (arthāntara) has arisen.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that sound is produced [rather than manifested], this is not a fault at all; for even though the individual parts are individually incapable, they become possessed of excellence through a specific kind of assistance, thereby contributing to a specific effect.
If each individual constituent were capable [of producing the meaning], the postulation of anything else would be redundant;
furthermore, the sentence must be a single, partless entity.
In that regard: for even if there were unity, sequential movement would be impossible for that which is undivided. //250//
A distinction in time is not even tenable;
for it is not logical that a single [cognition] should apprehend [objects] sequentially, because there is no difference between what has been grasped and what has not been grasped.
Furthermore, the comprehension of a sentence is observed to occur sequentially,
because the duration required for hearing, recollecting, and [processing] all the utterances of a sentence is completed only through a succession of many moments and eye-winks.
Furthermore, [the word] does not appear as something untouched by phonemes (varṇa) and yet appearing as a single cognition,
because the essence of the word does not manifest [apart from them],
and because it is perceived only through the sequence of phonemes.
Even though there is no difference between them, because the distinction between sentences is produced by their sequence, the cognition of a sentence possesses that sequence.
If one were not dependent on the assistance of the sequence of phonemes, they [the phonemes] would function in whatever way.

Furthermore, no sentence whatsoever could be perceived even when those [phonemes] are employed, either with or without the phonemes themselves; for it is impossible for that which is sequential to assist that which is non-sequential, and it is impossible to utter [speech] in a non-sequential manner.
And because there is no other possible mode of transition:

if it is argued that phonemes do not exist in the sentence at all, but rather that single, unitary form of the word appears as if possessing sequence and as if divided into phonemes due to the influence of the sequence of its manifestors;

The manifestation of that which is without sequence by a manifesting agent possessing sequence has already been refuted; for there is a contradiction between the manifested and the unmanifested. Furthermore, regarding a sentence consisting of phonemes, one who hears it incompletely would not have a cognition of the incomplete sentence, because a single part lacks the whole; nor, conversely, would anyone hear the whole [sentence] [if it were merely a collection of parts].
The claim that "the apprehension of a sentence occurs through a final cognition possessing the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of all the phonemes" is also false;
for there is never any such thing that does not come into contact with the form of the phonemes.
Because there is no apprehension [of it],
and because letters are not apprehended without a sequence, how could there be such a thing as a sentence that is grasped by a single cognition and devoid of sequence?
Nor do we perceive any other, indivisible essence of sound after the apprehension of the final phoneme; nor does the speaker himself discern such a thing.

If it were only thus, [thinking] "it would be good for me" or "it would be well for me," then one whose intellect is deluded by the desire for what is auspicious would dream that the sound, having reached its final cognition, has completed its course.
For even in the case of words and sentences being remembered, the phonemes are not perceived without a specific sequence;
because in a cognition that lacks sequence, there is an absence of priority and posteriority.
For them, there would be no distinction between the various words and sentences produced by those [phonemes],
nor would there be anything other than the sequence of phonemes.
It has been stated that we perceive sound as a form.
If that [sound] exists, it must be either impermanent or permanent. If—
How can that which is produced through effort and is of human origin not be impermanent? For that which possesses origination necessarily arises from something;
for if it were accidental (ākasmika), [it would follow that it could arise without a cause].
It has been stated that there would be no restriction regarding place and so forth for a sentient being;
and that [restriction] is observed only when the instruments are impelled by effort and are free from defects, but not otherwise.
Since the observation of causal factors is due solely to human activity,
it would therefore be of human origin.
Even if [the self] were eternal, there would be constant perception, because there is no possibility of its being obscured. //251//
Now, if that nature of sound were eternal and its very essence were to be perceived,
and if that essence of it never departed at any time, then it would be perceived eternally;
for in this way alone could it be eternal, if it did not fall away from its capacity due to any cause whatsoever.
Because the capacity to produce cognition is identical with its nature,
and because the possibility of it being a separate entity has already been refuted.
Nor is any obscuration of perception possible for that which has the nature of being perceived;
for even if such an obscuration were to exist, it could not impair its very nature.
Because it is impossible for its capacity to be disregarded;
for in that case, something that does not produce an excellence (atiśaya) cannot be said to perform any function at all.
And what that which is ineffective could be an obscuration for another, or anything else? This has been almost entirely threshed out [in previous analysis].
What excellence (atiśaya) do walls and such things produce in pots and the like?
They either produce or obstruct [cognition], by which they are considered to be obstructions. We do not say that they surpass anything;
rather, it is not the case that all moments of a jar [are perceived] by every sense-faculty.
The causes of consciousness—namely, the object, the sense faculty, and light—are mutually concomitant;
they are the causes of consciousness because they give rise to a distinct, qualified subsequent moment.
This is so even for that which is not being assisted [by another].
Because dependence is impossible;
for it has been stated that if a thing possesses a potent nature, there would be either constant production or constant non-production by another.
And these, being unobstructed by any other obstructing entity, are mutually beneficial to one another,
because they possess the capacity for non-intervention, spatial proximity, and cooperative functioning.
Because of the production of mutual excellence among them, however,
when there is an intervention, due to the absence of a cause, there is no production of another capable moment, and thus no production of cognition.
Therefore, because of the cessation of a previously arisen capable [condition], when there is a wall, another [cognition] that is about to arise does not arise due to the absence of its cause;
thus, due to the deficiency of causes, there is no arising of cognition, and so walls and the like constitute an obstruction.
They are so called because there was no prior obstruction of that which was capable [of arising],
since its nature has not fallen away.
Alternatively, even though things are momentary, mutual assistance among them is possible.
Because the efficacy of causes and conditions is inconceivable to one who is not omniscient,

an obscuration situated within the range of the sense faculties may indeed surpass those two [the object and the sense organ] by means of varying degrees of impairment to the arising of consciousness.
Regarding the distinction of obstructions, [this is known] from observing the dullness or sharpness of hearing in the case of sound and so forth;
otherwise, that which is ineffective in any respect whatsoever [could not produce such effects].

Since proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) is equivalent to non-proximity, the application [of the notion] "this belongs to that" would be merely constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); it would not have a real entity as its basis. Nor...
Purposeful actions follow upon superimposition;
for a young boy is not employed for cooking merely because of the metaphorical application of the term "burner."
Therefore, even if conceptual construction exists, entities that do not exclude what they are not would function solely according to their own intrinsic natures; thus,
even though [conceptual construction] exists...
If the sense faculties and so forth were to make known the obstruction itself,
it would not be the case that they do so;
therefore, there must be a specific quality produced [in them] by that [obstruction].
Thus it is understood.
Indeed, for eternal words,
there is no loss of excellence or production of anything when something else exists.
Therefore, if their nature were to produce cognition, they would produce all cognitions of their own objects for everyone, at all times, simultaneously; otherwise,
if they do not, then nothing would ever be produced by anything— this is a certainty.
If it is argued that the non-hearing [of a sound] by someone is due to the deficiency of some auxiliary cause, this might be so;
however, it is not the case that all sounds are eternally unhearable because of an obstruction.
Rather, there exists for the apprehension of those [sounds] a specific, determinate auxiliary cause.
Since it sometimes occurs for someone at some time, their hearing [of it] occurs occasionally and in some place as a result of that.
Granted, let there be dependence on another; however, the restriction [of the Veda's eternity] is contradicted. //252//
We certainly do not deny that causes have auxiliary factors; rather,
causes indeed depend upon those factors that assist them in their particular state,
from which an excellence (*atiśaya*) is obtained.
Because of its utility for an effect.
Likewise, if sound were to produce an effect depending on something else, let it do so; however, it would not be restricted to its prior nature.
Because of its passing away,
and because it acquires another intrinsic nature through dependence;
for it has already been stated that that which cannot be assisted does not depend [on anything].
Furthermore, if that assistance were a distinct entity, the absence of a relationship such as "belonging to it" and so forth would have been stated,
as well as its being unknowable.
Since knowledge arises solely from assistance [provided by the word],
therefore the word itself— and not the sense organ,
nor contact, nor the self, nor anything else that serves as a basis for the arising of knowledge— is [the cause].
It depends on [the object] for the production of its own cognition,
because everything else is ineffective in that regard.
Furthermore, these sounds must be either all-pervading or non-all-pervading.
If they were not all-pervasive, there would be non-perception everywhere.

How could that which exists in one location be perceived by someone situated in a place devoid of it? If it is argued that there is no fault in the position that [the sense organ] perceives what it has not reached, we say: no.
In that case as well, it is because of the dependence on the degree of the object's location in a suitable place, just like a magnet and so forth;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between clear and unclear hearing.
There would be no distinction;
and since the conditions for perception are present, they would be perceived equally in all places.
