Therefore, if all [things] were pervasive, there would be a simultaneous perception of them all; thus, they are not non-pervasive. //253//
For it is not the case that some sound does not exist anywhere; otherwise, all sounds would be perceived simultaneously by everyone situated in all places,
because the sense organs are capable [of perceiving them], the objects are present, and there is no obstruction.
And if there is perception of the conditioned, who is the agent of conditioning for that which is unchanging?
It might be argued: "Even though it exists, not every sound is perceived by everyone."
Because the conditioned is perceived only by means of the conditioned;
in that case, there is no perception of the conditioned [by itself].
Because refinement is impossible for that which cannot undergo modification, [the following holds]:
For if there were refinement of the sense faculty, it would hear all of that [sound]. (254)
In that case, if perception occurs through the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), then the sense faculty would not perceive [objects] through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains unavoidable: that the sense faculty, for which the refinement has been performed, would hear all sounds simultaneously.

If it is argued that there is a restriction to a single object because [the word] is distinct due to the difference in mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), then how could there be the perception of hearing in a cacophony consisting of a multitude of words? (255)
Now, it might be argued:
those conditioned factors (saṃskāra) of sounds are specifically determined;
in that regard, by someone...
A conditioned sense-faculty is the apprehender of only a specific [object]; thus, there is no simultaneous hearing of all sounds.
If the restriction of hearing is due to a particular refinement (*saṃskāra*), then for the sense-faculties, there would be no plurality—

There would be no hearing of a collection of sounds, such as a clamor; for a single sound is not what is called a "clamor," since [a clamor] consists of the simultaneous hearing of sounds with distinct intrinsic natures.
If it is argued that because the establishment of difference depends on a distinction in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
the simultaneous hearing [of multiple sounds] is an illusion due to the rapidity of their occurrence;
In the continuous flow of notes such as *vaṃśa* and so forth, there would be a confused cognition due to the merging of the constituent *gamakas*;
and a refutation of this will be stated hereafter.
Therefore, because the capacity for each sense-faculty is restricted to a single mode of operation, the manifold nature [of sound] would not be heard as a cacophony;
if it is argued that only mere sounds (*dhvani*) are heard therein, they are not expressive (*vācaka*).
Indeed, in a cacophony, phonemes, words, and sentences are not heard,
because only mere sounds are perceived.

Furthermore, the sense organs possess specific capacities for the articulator (the speaker), but not for the sounds (dhvanis). To believe that there exists something distinct from those sounds is an excessive claim. //256//

For we do not perceive sound and the expressive word as having distinct forms; rather, upon hearing the sequence of phonemes at once, we determine that the very essence of the word is one and the same.
Therefore, how can we engage in linguistic usage preceded by a determination while failing to determine it?
Consequently, this [cognition] is merely a particular sound.
[The word] is designated by its phonemes and so forth. Furthermore:
"While other sounds remain present, how can that which expresses [the meaning] be heard?
Therefore, the resonance (dhvani) is not distinct from it, nor is it separate from it."
For when an object is directly perceived, the instruction of another is not more authoritative; thus,
while other speakers remain silent, this person speaks.
Hearing only the sound, one realizes that the conditions for its perception lack the capacity to produce anything other than that [sound].
For if they were capable, [they would produce it].
That which is produced by them would be perceived;
however, since the conditions themselves possess that very nature,
how could they initiate a different object within the clamor?
For indeed, when there is no difference in the cause, a difference in the effect is not logical;
for it has been stated that this would entail the consequence of difference being causeless.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the expressive word is not heard amidst a cacophony, because the divisions of words and sentences are perceived.
Or else, how could there be a cognition of distinct sounds based on a restriction of [individual] capacities? (257)

Although those sense organs possess specific capacities, they hear sounds restricted to various forms such as individual syllables, yet they do not [hear] words in this same way; what, then, is their aversion toward words? As it has been said: "It is not established that sounds are distinct from the expressive [words]."
Thus, how are they not established?
Because the meaning is understood from the speech;
for it is not [the case that] the sound—

The cognition of the meaning of a word arises from a portion that is smaller [than the whole]; yet that [portion] is not something other than the whole. Therefore, this cognition of the intended object, which consists of the complete form of a word or a sentence, does not arise from [its] incomplete [parts].
It is thus established that the nature of sound (śabda-rūpa) exists without succession,
while the sound-manifestations (dhvani) consist of successive parts.
That is not so; for a non-sequential [cause] that is distinct from what possesses sequence has already been refuted. Moreover, such a position leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Because there is no connection between a preceding and a succeeding part of the constituent elements of action (*karma-bhāga*), and because the meaning is not understood from a single part alone, one must admit that— just like a word (*śabda*)— there exists a complete form distinct from those parts which serves as the cause for the comprehension of meaning in gestures such as hand-signs. This would have to be accepted as being of the nature of action (*karman*).

It is logical that the distinct portions of phonemes or actions, which occur sequentially and arise from the application of their respective instruments, produce the cognition of an object according to convention, as they are the objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in a sequential manner. Furthermore:

Those by whom sounds (dhvanis) are accepted [as the expressive elements], for what reason would those [sounds] not be non-expressive when this [meaning] is manifested by those very sounds, even though it is already expressive? (258)
It is claimed that the denotative word, manifested by the successive parts of sound, expresses its meaning;
yet even that [word] they do not manifest all at once,
because of their sequential occurrence.
Nor does a single part alone manifest the word, because that would entail the consequence of the other parts being useless; [this applies even to] a single phoneme—

And because its entire form is not perceived at the time of [its] manifestation, this perception of it— which lacks the apprehension of all [its parts] simultaneously— is like the perception of sound, [occurring] despite the presence of the totality of the conditions for perception.
How could one accomplish a purpose?
For what distinction is there between the existence and non-existence [of things] when both are absolutely unperceivable, regarding those purposes that are to be accomplished through perception?
Nor is it a means of proof by mere proximity, because it depends upon manifestation; and this [manifestation] occurs sequentially for both the existent and the non-existent.

The effect [of meaning] is impossible to accomplish through sounds (dhvanis) because their utility is equal [to that of phonemes]. Since it is likewise so in that case as well, enough with further discussion.
Therefore, there is no authorlessness (apauruṣeyatā) either in the phonemes or in the sentence.

If it is argued that a sentence is the sequential order of phonemes, it is not so, because there is no difference between the phonemes themselves. A sentence is not a non-human (apauruṣeya) verbal entity that is a distinct object from the phonemes. What then?
For us, a sentence is characterized by the sequence of phonemes.
If it is argued that this [Veda] must be proven to be non-human in origin, we say no; because there is no difference in the sequence of the phonemes,
this [sequence] is not a distinct entity.
[This is] from the phonemes;
because division is perceived in that which is visible, [but not] in that which is invisible, therefore...
Because there is no means of apprehension due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*),
and because in the absence of a sequential order possessing distinctness, only the mere phoneme (*varṇa*) remains everywhere; thus, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before follows.
And there can be no fixed arrangement of these [moments], because it would contradict another sequence. //259//
If the sequence of phonemes were uncreated and those [phonemes] were not numerous and of the same kind,
such that some would have a fixed order while others could be permuted at will;
rather, if there were only one *a* in the three worlds, and likewise only one *ga*, then [the word] "agni" [could never arise].
It would be "syāt" (it would be) and not "gaganam" (sky), because the prior-posterior relationship between the phonemes *a* and *ga* is fixed;
this is true even for produced things that possess a determinate sequence of causes and transformations.
It is impossible to reverse the sequence [of causes and effects],
just as in the case of the seed, sprout, leaf, and so forth, or the seasons, the year, and so forth.
How much more so, then, for those things whose nature is an unshakable state,
which are unconditioned and somehow persisting, since it is impossible for them to exist otherwise without abandoning their prior state?
Or else, because it would follow that there is either abandonment or destruction;
this applies especially in the case of an eternal sequence.

Thus, this difference in sequence at each step would have to result either from a difference in the phonemes themselves due to the production of something unprecedented (*apūrva*), or from a plurality of phonemes;
and that is not accepted [by you].
Moreover:
There is an absence of spatial and temporal sequence because [the phonemes] are described as being all-pervading and eternal.
Furthermore, this sequential order of the phonemes would have to be either produced by space, or...
Just as in a row of ants,
or as determined by time, such as in the case of seeds, sprouts, and so forth;
that [sequence] is of two kinds.
It is not possible [for it] to exist within the phonemes (*varṇa*),
because of [its] pervasiveness and eternality. [Otherwise, there would be] mutual spatial...
For occurrence through exclusion consists in spatial priority and posteriority;
that is not possible in the case of phonemes, because everything is equal in respect to space.
And like wind and sunlight, or like the self and so forth,
existence occurs through the exclusion of time; this is the temporal sequence of priority and posteriority,
because when one [moment] does not exist, then the other exists.
That too is not possible in the case of eternal things, because everything would exist at all times;
nor is there any other alternative.
In that case, how could a sequence of phonemes constitute a sentence that is to be proven non-human in origin?
Furthermore, the fault regarding [the Veda's] impermanence and non-pervasiveness has already been stated previously. //260//

Now, if one should desire that this fault not arise by asserting that phonemes are non-eternal and non-pervasive, those two positions have already been refuted; thus, it is no solution. Furthermore, the view that a sentence is the sequence of manifestations is also untenable, as the theory of eternal manifestation has already been rejected.
The sequence of the forms of phonemes is not the sentence;
what then?
It is the manifestation of them. That [manifestation]—
Just as [speech] occurs in a sequential manner according to the sequence of conditions for the manifestation of its own phonemes,
so too is the claim that "sentence is an ordered succession" false;
for that [succession] has already been refuted in the case of eternal [phonemes].
Because it has been refuted [that a universal is the cause].

It has already been explained that manifestation (*vyakti*) is simply a particularity of being an effect (*kāryatā-viśeṣa*), consisting in those things that produce cognition through the direct application of causal capacity (*sākṣāt-śakty-upadhāna*).
Since that [result] is established through activity alone, the instruments possess the nature of being effects. //261//
Indeed, when a form is perceived from a certain [cause],
the world designates it as an effect based solely on that perception which is inseparable from its own perception;
this [perception] exists even in the case of colors.
And that very same [substratum] is the basis for those [sounds] elsewhere as well;

it is not something distinct. Therefore, since the grounds for accepting [the existence of such a substratum] are equal in both cases, why are the phonemes (varṇas) not considered the effects? They are not.
And this establishment of being an effect based on perception—
what then?
It is that which [exists] only when [the cause] exists.
[The notion] "it exists" is based on existence (sattā). From what is that existence established, such that it would not prove [the thing's] being an effect?
For if this [existence] were unestablished, the thought "it exists in this way" would not occur.
Therefore, the establishment of existence is that which proves it,
and that [establishment] is indeed perception itself.
This is indeed true, provided that its prior existence has not been established;
for that establishment of existence is precisely that which is preceded by non-establishment.

[Objection: But surely that form is unestablished which is useful for such a consciousness without any intervention; it is indeed established, yet because of the deficiency of other factors, it is not utilized. [Response: If this is so, how can there be no difference between what is utilized and what is not utilized?

Nor can difference be untouched by the nature of the word, because that very excellence [of the word] would have to be established as its utility, which would entail that it is the cause of that [difference].
For that alone is rightly considered useful in a given case whose existence brings about the establishment of the probandum;
even if it were to assist through an excellence [of another], the same undesirable consequence would apply to it.
Therefore, the distinction of states, which consists in the application of unimpeded capacity, certainly does excel that which is other than it;
and the dependence of that which lacks such excellence has already been refuted.

And since that [manifestation] is established solely through the operation of the instrument, it possesses the same properties as every other effect. If such a manifestation were to manifest [the universal], then everything would be manifested, or else nothing at all, because there is no distinction [between them]. To explain:
That which causes another's cognition by means of its own cognition is considered a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) when the object is already established;
for example, a lamp. Otherwise, what distinction would there be between it and a producer (*kāraka*)? //262//

In the world, that which causes the cognition of another by means of its own cognition is established as a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), like a lamp and so forth; however, if it were already established [prior to the object], it would follow that the momentary substrate of a similar kind (*samānajātīyopādānakṣaṇa*) is already established. That is not the case, because that very excellence (*atiśaya*) which is the cause of cognition depends upon that causal complex (*sāmagrīpratyaya*).

Furthermore, those [reasons] such as "being an agent" (kāraka) which have unestablished apprehension— like a potter and so forth with respect to a jar and so forth— and even recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and the like, which are intended as reasons for establishment, do not fulfill the definition of a reason (*hetu*). As for whatever subsequent cognition of the letter *a* is non-different from the prior cognition of the letter *a*, [it likewise fails].
"Objects are likewise," and so forth;
even that is not capable of proving the non-difference between two particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because its intrinsic nature is established,
there is no contradiction even if there is a difference in the scope of reference when speaking in general terms.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for two cognitions directed toward the same object to exist in a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, since their production or non-production depends on whether the cause is present or absent;
and because even when [the cause] is present, that which has not yet arisen cannot have it as its cause, those two [cognitions]...
The state of being the cause of all distinct [effects] [is established].

In that case, even though there is no difference in the single [cause], because that which is capable [of producing effects] is not observed [to do so simultaneously], it contradicts reason for two successive cognitions to have a single object. This is because of the cognition...

Even if there is a difference in the nature of their appearances, it is illogical to claim they have the same object on the basis of a similarity in name; for this would lead to the over-extension [of the argument] to jars and other things.
In that case, because it contradicts what is observed, it lacks probative force.
If this is argued, then here too, by what is the absence of contradiction established? As long as such denotability is not proven to be pervaded by a difference in meaning, it remains doubtful.
There is a distinction.

And since sound, which possesses a distinct nature for each individual production, enters into auditory perception, why is it not established as one [in the same way] as jars and other such things? In that regard:
Furthermore, it may be argued that the difference in appearance [of the object] arises from the difference in the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*).
Moreover:
because perception occurs through the operation of the complete collection of causal instruments (*karaṇa*).
And [the property of] being an effect is necessarily [restricted], because that [property] is impossible in the case of a manifestor. //263//
For there is never a non-perception of sound when the sense organs are functioning;
nor does the operation of a manifestor necessarily cause the object to be perceived.
Even in some cases where there is light, there is no perception of jars and the like; therefore,
this perception occurs as a rule due to its [the sense organ's] operation.
[The cognition] of sound would [arise] from that [manifestation],
because it is impossible for that [cognition] to be established through the activity of one who is not its agent.
If it is argued that [sound is perceived] because it is all-pervading and eternal;
If it is argued that there is now confidence regarding jars and the like because they are not accepted as being so [momentary], then what of it?
Is sound intended to have a property identical to that [of the object]? And it has been stated that there is no excellence whatsoever in it; and once that has been refuted...
Regarding [the objection] that [sound] is all-pervading and eternal:
there is no fault [in our position] because jars and other such things have other manifestors;
for it is established that light is their manifestor.
If potters and the like were merely manifestors [of the form],
they would be exactly like that; however,
they go beyond that.
Therefore, due to the excellence of the manifestor, they are indeed producers,
because there is no other possible mode of assistance for that which assists;
this is the same even in the case of words.

In that case as well, because of the excellence of the instruments due to their being in a location suitable for the senses and other such factors, and because the properties of the causal factors (kārakas) such as the potter are observed in the instruments,
it is precisely that [instrument], such as a lamp, [which performs the function].
Furthermore, because there is no other manifestor for any other object,
their causes would have to be the manifestors of those [objects].
Therefore, the individual entity (*vyakti*) is not the manifestation (*vyañjanā*) of the word;
for its manifestation must be either an excellence produced by the vocal organs, the removal of an obscuration,
or cognition itself, as there is no other possible alternative.

In that case, there can be no production of an excellence [in the nature of the entity], because it would entail the consequence of impermanence; for such production is characterized by the loss of a prior form and the emergence of a subsequent one. Now, if...
If their manifestation were the removal of the obscurations to that nature, then in the case of non-existence, what indeed would be the efficacy of the collection of instruments? //264//

For indeed, instruments that do nothing toward an obscuration cannot be called "capable. Furthermore, disappearance is a non-existence (*abhāva*), and it has already been explained that a non-existence is not an effect.
This also applies to sound.
It has also been stated that for that which is eternal, there can be no obscuration because of its incapacity.
Therefore, there is no application of instruments toward obscuration, nor is there any incapacity on their part. That—
Because sound is not perceived in the absence of activity,
it is therefore logical that these [causes] should produce sounds; otherwise, [it would not be so].
Because there is no distinction in the word [denoting them], it would follow that other things are also manifested;
if this were accepted, all causes would be rendered purposeless. (265)
If even those instruments that possess the same properties as all other causes were merely manifestors, then nothing at all would now be an effect;
and this is not tenable.
Because it would follow that all causes are purposeless,
since a real entity cannot have any particularity added to it.
Because the absence of an obscuration is not an effect,
and because cognition is established in the same way as a real entity, [it is] cognition.

If something were a causal factor (*kāraka*) by virtue of its own nature, then by the same logic, it would follow that other things of that same kind would also be such factors; consequently, everything would result in being an effect.
Therefore, this...

The collection of factors considered to be causal agents would be entirely useless, as it would exist neither in the manifestation nor in the action; and thus this world would be devoid of activity, lacking both that which is assisted and that which assists.
This would also be the case if words were eternal.
Recognition, which is considered a means of proof along with the application of existence and so forth,
is not a valid example [for proving permanence], because all entities are subject to momentary destruction.
For it has been stated, and will be stated again, that all entities are momentary because destruction is causeless;
furthermore, those things which possess origination arise from something else.
Because it is impossible for existence to be accidental,
this recognition— which involves the application of the term "existent" and so forth— does not apply to anything that possesses a stable and unitary nature.
It is argued that this is indeed contradictory, since it is observed in cases such as lamps, where there is a transformation of successive distinct natures; [we reply:
no, because there is a deceptive appearance of similarity due to their non-distinct birth.
Because [the notion of identity] exists with respect to lamps and the like due to delusion,
on what basis is it asserted that there is "non-different birth"? For that very non-difference [of the lamp] exists everywhere throughout its preceding and succeeding states.
If it is argued that, because it is an object of thought,
difference is likewise [an object of thought], then let there be doubt for that very reason; and yet, it is not so.
Success [is achieved] from that which is doubted.
If it is argued that there is oneness because of the non-perception of distinction, we say no; for existence and non-existence are established through the temporal sequence of cognitions.
Because their intrinsic nature is characterized by distinction.

If subsequent cognitions had arisen previously with their causes already present, they would have been produced just like the preceding cognition; however, the fact that they have not arisen indicates a deficiency in their causes.
Because that which is capable produces [the effect], while that which is incapable does not subsequently acquire capability; or,
if it were to acquire it, stability would be impossible.
Therefore, this so-called "correct application" is in fact merely the production [of the result], because the agent possesses the capacity [for it];
for if [the result] were already capable by itself, that application would be useless.

The term "application" (*prayoga*) is also said to be simply the production of that which is capable of accomplishing the desired goal; this may depend upon a material cause (*upādāna*) of a similar kind, or it may be independent, as in the case of the application of an axe or the application of an action and so forth.
As for the one who thinks that recognition occurring in the presence [of the object] is indeed perception, and that from that very perception the establishment of stability [of the object] follows—
this too we shall refute later.
A fallacious reason (*kuhetu*) is also something to be rejected. There is not even a single phenomenon (*dharma*) that follows after another of its own kind;
this is because all phenomena [are devoid of such continuity].
Because of this state of affairs,
and because the thesis of universal stability contradicts reasoning as it has been stated, other eternal causes are also subject to the faults of verbal expression.
If cognition were not based on a person (puruṣa), there would be a contradiction with what is accepted, with what is perceived by direct perception, and with what is established by inference. //267//
If the manifestation (*vyakti*) is the cognition (*buddhi*), then the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) is what is to be proven.
For, in establishing its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*), there is an equality [of arguments], since cognitions are admitted to be qualities of persons (*puruṣaguṇatva*).
This [position] is refuted.
Indeed, it is directly perceived that these cognitions arise from those things reckoned as persons or from the qualities of persons, such as mental attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, what is called "being an effect" (kāryatā) is nothing other than the specificities of existence (bhāva) and non-existence (abhāva).
And that existence is perceptible; non-existence, too, characterized by non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), is perceptible.
We shall state that this is established by implication (*sāmarthya-siddha*).

For that very reason, the fact that cognitions are the product of a person (*puruṣa-kāryatā*) is [known] because this [cognition] possesses a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with [the person] is to be inferred. Furthermore:
Furthermore, the distinction between the sequence and the phonemes has been considered by means of the *sphoṭa*.
How could that [distinction] be merely superimposed by conceptual construction, or how could it be independent of a person? (268)
The sequence that is distinct from the phonemes has already been refuted in the course of the investigation into the *sphoṭa*.
Nor is it of the nature of the phonemes,
because the nature of a real entity cannot transcend these two alternatives.

This would be an error of cognition (*buddhi*) in which there appears the superimposition (*samāropa*) of that form onto things that do not possess that form; this is what constitutes "sequence" (*ānupūrvī*).
And how could that [sequence] be non-human (*apauruṣeya*)? [For it is produced by] cognition...
Because of its fabrication and re-establishment;
moreover,
because there is nothing whatsoever that is absolute.

Since intrinsic nature does not exist, your sound must be non-eternal. Furthermore, whether it be causeless or caused by something else, it would have to be eternal and not dependent upon human activity; therefore, it is not of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
How is it understood that sound— or any other entity— is non-eternal? Because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent.
For the destruction of entities does not arise from anything;

therefore, it would have to be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those entities themselves, because the entity itself arises from its own causes as possessing that property (*taddharman*). And [it is] not [the case that] an entity—
It has a specific intrinsic nature,
because that [nature] is about to be refuted;
therefore, it is an entity (bhāva).
It would have the nature of being merely that.
Therefore, it is established that every entity whatsoever— whether sound or anything else— that partakes in existence is non-eternal.
It is not established;
for that very destruction is not proven to have another birth.
For instance, wood by fire and a jar by a staff— such are seen to be the causes of the destruction of things;
this is the conformity with presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka).
They say that this is not the definition of a cause and its effect;
for when the preceding [moment] ceases by its own nature, another arises, transformed through dependence on specific conditions.
Or let it be that fire is the cause of the destruction of the wood.
Is that destruction, produced by fire, the wood itself,
or is it something distinct?
If a different entity from fire were produced, the wood would still be visible. //269//
Because there is no destruction.
What is the meaning? When one thing arises from another thing, why is it that the wood is not seen as having become something non-existent, or why is it not perceived?
For in this way, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
If it is argued that "that very thing is its destruction," then if the object produced by fire were non-existence itself, it would not be perceived because it has ceased to exist.
"Let it be that this has the name 'non-existence' (abhāva). Even so,
how can one thing be the destruction of another?"
For it is not logical that a piece of wood would cease to be seen merely by giving a certain thing a name;
nor is one thing the destruction of another.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
and because there is no distinction [between it and others], that which is a real entity (*vastu-bhūta*) as a distinct object (*arthāntara*) from those others [would have to be admitted].
If it is argued that the nature produced by fire in wood is its destruction, but not [the destruction] of everything, then what is the relationship [between the wood and the destruction]?
If it is the relationship of substratum and dependent, [then...]
No, because that [relation] is about to be refuted.
If you argue that it is due to the relationship between producer and produced, then what of the case of fire? It arises from the wood alone.

If it is argued that there is no fault because [the effect] arises in dependence upon that [cause], then what kind of dependence can there be for one who acquires no excellence (*atiśaya*)? Or, if there were such an acquisition, the production of yet another [distinct] entity would occur.
Previously, however, the cause of non-falling was observed to be exactly that;
therefore, it is from fire alone [that this occurs].

If it is argued that [the cause] is the prior destruction, then what is the connection between this [destruction] and the prior [cause]? That same logical difficulty remains, and there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, since fire assists toward a subsequent excellence that is necessarily capable of being connected with destruction, it must produce something entirely new; otherwise,
the thing would be perceived in its previous state.
Furthermore, the "destruction of wood" is said to be the non-existence of the wood;
and non-existence is not an effect.
Moreover, that which produces it is precisely a non-producer, and thus it is not to be depended upon.

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, if that which lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were distinct from it, then a functional entity (*bhāva*) that excludes it would be established as having intrinsic nature itself; how then could it be called "non-existent"? Therefore, this is not [the case].
If one thing were the destruction of another, why is the wood not seen? //270//
What is this contradiction between the existence of another object and the perception of the wood?
If it is because of its being grasped by that [other object], then it is not the case that there is no obscuration by it;
for if the wood were not seen because it is grasped by that other object, [then that would be the case].
It would follow that [the term] "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to wood;
however, this is not tenable. For an obstruction would impede vision, but it does not impede the functional capacities of substances, such as impact and so forth.

And if there were an obstruction to everything, would not the substance itself be destroyed by this very [obstruction], because of the removal of all its capacities? Furthermore, the same undesirable consequence would follow as in the case of fire.
There would be an infinite regress; or, if its capacities such as the power of impact remain undiminished, what is destroyed by that other [cause]?
And if there were a destruction called "arising from fire," [what would happen?]
Because the object is apprehended, the wood is not seen;
therefore, destruction would itself be destructible, and from that, there would be a further arising. (271)
There is the perception of the wood.
For that which possesses origination must necessarily perish through destruction; once that [destruction] has perished, [the wood is no longer perceived].
Furthermore, wood and other such things would [re]emerge;

and upon the killing of the killer, Caitra would not be reborn. If it is argued that it is the same here as in those cases, [we reply] no, because the killer does not die [along with the victim]. (272)
Furthermore, even when the destruction of destruction occurs, there would be a restoration of the entity.
If it is argued that this is not so—just as when a killer is killed, the victim does not return to life—we say: no.
[The opponent says: "No, because that [fire] is the cause of its destruction.
[The author replies: We do not say that when the causes of destruction—such as fire or a staff—cease to exist, the entity must necessarily come into being. What then?
Since existence and non-existence are characterized by absolute non-apprehension,
when those [two] cease, what other course remains for the persistence of intrinsic nature?
For [it would mean] the destruction of Caitra.
It is not a conceptualization of destruction;
what then?
It is a conceptualization of the staff and so forth.
For his death is like a mere destruction;
and upon its cessation, there would surely be a rebirth for him.

Even if destruction were non-different [from the object], the wood itself would be the destruction; because it [the wood] exists, [destruction] would be causeless. There is no other possibility than this. Destruction is not a separate entity from the wood.

That very thing remains as it is; and since that already exists beforehand, what efficacy do fire and the like have here? Therefore, because they provide no assistance, they are not required by it in any way whatsoever.
Nor does it deserve to have a relationship with this [object] such that "this belongs to it," because that [relationship] is based upon a mutual benefit.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even if there is assistance through a succession of steps, this dilemma necessarily follows:
is that assistance a different entity (*arthāntara*), or is it that very same thing?
Even if it were a different entity (*arthāntara*),
the same inquiry as to how it could provide assistance and so forth would remain exactly as before; the same applies if it were not a different entity (*ananya*).
Therefore, since an existing form cannot transcend being either identical to or different from itself,
and since the production of assistance is characterized by the actualization of that form,
that which is devoid of performing those actions— either that [form] or something else— is not an agent at all; thus, it is neither a cause for anything nor a non-cause.
It does not depend [on anything else].
Therefore, it is established that this entity is by its very nature of that same essence (tat-svabhāva).
Furthermore, even if destruction were causeless, because it would be eternal, there would be no distinction between the entity and its destruction.
If it follows that there must be coexistence [of cause and effect], how can there be permanence for that which is non-existent? //274//
It might be argued: "Even for that [entity] whose destruction is causeless, it must necessarily be eternal;
thus, the entity and its destruction, characterized by its non-existence, would exist simultaneously. No, because of its [the entity's] being neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Because it is not connected with the nature of phenomena (*dharma*);
for this conceptual construction cannot exist when [the object] is non-existent,
since those two possess the nature of real entities (*vastu*).
And because destruction is nothing at all,
it could not have concomitance with anything for you; yet destruction does occur.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Even the consequence that non-existence must be perishable because it is non-existent is not tenable;
for it is not accepted that an entity is destroyed by means of its destruction. //275//
How could a non-existent destruction destroy an entity?
Therefore, the entity would be indestructible;
thus, this [objection] is simply not applicable.

Because the destruction of an entity is not admitted [to occur] through destruction. For how could one who says that "destruction" is simply "nothing at all" accept the destruction of an entity on that basis?
Now, if destruction does not exist, how can an entity be said to be destroyed?
For things that do not undergo destruction of non-existence are not reckoned as "destroyed" during their present state; indeed,
one who does not possess a certain quality by means of that [quality] cannot be so designated.
It is designated or perceived by that [cause] in such a way,
just as a horse is [designated] by its horn. Indeed, it is not the case that destruction simply does not exist.
But there is no entity that becomes [the destruction] of an entity;
rather, the very entity itself, characterized by momentary duration, is destruction.
This is its own nature, which—[is perceived] by the subsequent...
It has been stated that those who analyze time designate destruction as "having occurred" according to conventional perception; for nothing whatsoever ever happens to an entity,
since that very entity simply arises in such a manner from its own causes.
Therefore, it has not been destroyed by anyone;
rather, it is its very own nature by which it is said to be "destroyed."

How, then, is it said that destruction is now causeless? It is for the purpose of making that known—that a perishing entity is independent of anything else—that this state [of destruction] is called "causeless," having superimposed a distinction upon it by means of the mind. (276)
An entity that has arisen does not undergo destruction from another, because it arises by its very nature as such; thus,
for the purpose of negating any other property dependent on something else,
one mentally conceives of a property as if it were a distinct entity from the substratum by making known its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Having analyzed [the matter], when there is a desire to know that alone, it is the very nature [of things] that is described in such a way.
However, those of dull intellect— deceived by mere sounds because they have seen such [expressions] in some instances—
superimpose upon that [nature] a quality of destruction, whether with cause or without cause, and [conceive of it as] an entity.
Or else, by means of a reflection on existence based on an unstable reality, they agitate themselves.
If this conceptualization of non-existence [arises] even from the existence itself, then it is the same;
for indeed, even if destruction is not produced by something else, it occurs from the existence itself.

This dilemma regarding identity and difference is the same [in both cases]. Therefore, whether there is a separate entity or not, why is existence not perceived? Even in the case of non-separateness, that very thing remains as it is.
Since nothing at all has arisen for it, how can it be said to have "perished"? Is it not thus stated here: "Nothing happens to it; it simply does not exist"? (277)
Thus it has been said. For this destruction, or indeed anything else, does not happen to the entity; rather, he says: "that very entity simply does not exist."
For if one were to state the existence of something, existence would not be negated by it; and thus,
there would be no cessation of existence.
When the relevant topic has been introduced, that which is irrelevant would have been stated;
for indeed, there is no entity whatsoever that is not produced by the existence of something else.

In that case, if it were not itself existent, it would not be "existent. Furthermore, this "not being" is a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), not an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*).
Otherwise, even here, if something were to exist, there would be no distinction between the forms of negation and exclusion.
There would be a distinction between the two cases because the affirmation is primary;
and thus, since there is no negation, there would be no exclusion (paryudāsa) of anything anywhere.
For if something were to be excluded from something else, then it would be touched by that which is distinct from it,
through the exclusion of the latter. That...
Furthermore, when it is said that "there is no [existence] and there is cessation everywhere," there is the cognition of some positive entity (bhāva) itself; thus, by this,
only the existence of another thing would have been stated,
not the mutual distinction between those two.
And in the absence of non-discrimination, there can be no exclusion (paryudāsa).
Thus, due to the lack of negative concomitance (vyatireka), positive concomitance (anvaya) would also not exist.
Because that [entity] has the characteristic of abiding in a single intrinsic nature;
and its abiding could only occur if there were the exclusion of anything other than itself,
yet that [exclusion] does not exist— thus, there is no [conceptual] activity.
The world would become extinct.
Therefore, when it is said that "something undergoes destruction," it must be said that it does not exist by itself.
Indeed, a rule observed in one domain cannot be applied everywhere merely because of a similarity in sound;
for it is not the case that [the word] "donkey" [applies to everything].

The characteristics of a child should be applied even to a human being from the moment of naming. Likewise, the rule observed in the case of "Caitra’s son" does not apply to destruction, because of the contradiction.
Thus, the purpose for employing such a designation has already been explained. Therefore:
For this conceptual distinction would exist only if there were a positive entity (bhāva), since a prescription [of existence] must conform to a real thing.
A positive entity necessarily depends upon that which is coming into being,
and that [coming into being] is nothing other than its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Because that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot be involved in any activity;
for "activity" means...
The arising of such an intrinsic nature—
how could that belong to that which lacks intrinsic nature?
How, then, does conventional usage such as "the horn of a hare is non-existent" occur?
It is certainly not said that "the rabbit's horn is something existent"; rather, in this way, a negation of its existence is simply being made, as in "it does not exist.
Furthermore:
It is the speakers themselves who, by means of some context, superimpose this [nature] upon it as if it possessed such activity and thus demonstrate it.
But it is not so;
for in that case, reality consists in the discernment of all objects, not in the merging of anything [into one].

Indeed, destruction does not [inherently] exist in an entity because that entity continues to be present. Even this [destruction], if it is merely described in such a way by speakers and does not exist in itself in that manner, then nothing at all is lost; this is precisely what we accept.

Therefore, an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that exists in itself does not transcend the two conceptual alternatives, namely "identity" (*tattva*) and "otherness" (*anyatva*). Indeed, for an intrinsic nature, otherness is simply non-identity.
For even in the case of form and taste, their mutual distinctness is not something other [than themselves]; there is no essential connection [between them].
If it is argued that they are different,
what is this so-called "invariable concomitance" (pratibandha) by which [the cause] would not exist without [the effect],
yet [the effect] is not of a different nature?
If it is argued that this refers to "birth," then there would be an inexpressibility among all causes with respect to one another.
And thus, since everything is in some way useful to everything,
nothing would be distinct from anything else;
and in this way, even the so-called "ineffability" [of the relation] is simply the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
This would merely be stated by means of another word;
there would be no difference in meaning, as it would not follow the actual nature [of the object].
We speak of otherness;
and since that indeed exists among things possessing intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in relation to one another, it is precisely otherness.
And there is no relation called "dependence" other than the essential connection characterized by origination from that;
for that which is not dependent [cannot have such a relation].
Because there is no deviation or contradiction [between them],
they are distinct due to their difference in properties,
which is established by cognition.
If it is argued that there is an "invariable connection" (*pratibandha*),
this might be so:
that which is inseparable from the cognition [of the object].
"That cognition which [perceives] that [object], because that [object] necessarily appears within it, is itself of a different nature from that [object] and thus inexpressible as being that. No;
for it is itself devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For that very reason...

Its nature is that which appears; for if it possessed a nature, there would be the undesirable consequence of its appearing as such [a nature], and because that which does not appear is non-existent among perceptible objects. If it were imperceptible...

Furthermore, if cognition does not possess that form [of the object], whose realization would it depend upon? And for whatever depends on something else for its realization, its own manifestation as intrinsic nature does not perish—
just as in the case of blue and other objects, whose realization depends upon illumination.
Or what is its connection?
It is that when that which has the nature of non-self is being perceived, it presents itself spontaneously.
For in this way, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that "that which is being perceived has that [prior moment] as its material cause (*upādāna*)," [we reply:]...
What is this meaning of "appropriation" (upādāna)?
It is not the relationship of cause and effect, because that is not accepted [as the definition].
Or, even if such a [causal] relationship is admitted, cause and effect do not mutually establish one another's cognition;
for it is cognition itself that is invariably concomitant with them.
If you say it is "proximity," we reply:

surely that very [proximity] is said to be untenable when there is no connection (*pratibandha*). Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no connection whatsoever between what is not an effect and its cause.
Even the claim that "the cognition of X is inseparable from the realization of Y" would only hold true if that [cognition of X] were present;
for there is nothing whatsoever that does not appear in consciousness by way of its own nature, unassociated with what is not its own nature.

Knowledge [of it] exists; because that [knowledge] does not exist, the definition of the inexpressible nature of the object-form is not established. Therefore, that [object] must in reality partake of being either identical to or different from [the knowledge]. For one who holds that nothing at all happens to an entity when it perishes—by him [it must be admitted as follows]:
It has been stated that "existence does not come to be," and likewise, "non-existence does not come to be. //278//
Furthermore, when he says that this is the non-existence of an entity,
that too is simply said to mean that it is not an entity at all.
For in this way it is turned back;
because a positive affirmation is impossible within a negation,
there is therefore no cause whatsoever for its destruction.
For it is thus:
If some effect were to exist, then another [cause] might be required;
but what thing that accomplishes nothing could possibly be required by anyone? (279)
For a cause exists only when there is an effect;
and it has already been stated that for a perishing entity, there is no effect whatsoever.
Therefore, that which is called the cause of destruction does nothing at all to the entity; being thus ineffective, it is not to be depended upon.
How then [is this so] now?
An entity that has not produced any excellence (*atiśaya*) is said to be "destroyed" while remaining in that very same state.
But surely, even when an excellence is produced, it is that very same [entity] which has produced that excellence; how then can it be said to be "destroyed"?
Therefore, this [entity] in that state is not what is called "destroyed.
It is destroyed by that [cause] through which it itself ceases to exist.

It has been stated that this is not because of the production of a different entity; for indeed, by the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*), it is not the case that something which was previously non-existent becomes existent. This is because non-existence is devoid of any designation of excellence whatsoever.
Because [non-existence] is characterized by the distinction from the nature of all entities through their cessation, and because an entity is characterized by the occurrence of its arising;
therefore, there is no attribution of an entity to non-existence whatsoever.
By this [same reasoning],

even in the case of causelessness (*ahetukatva*), the objection regarding the fault of existence being perishable (*sattā-nāśitva*)— namely, that destruction would occur after having previously not existed— is refuted. (280)
Furthermore, even for one who thinks that although destruction is causeless, because it comes into being after not having existed, its existence and impermanence are unavoidable;
for even that which comes into being after not having existed becomes causeless.
As for the claim that it is contradictory,
that too is refuted by this very [argument],
because no entity whatsoever is admitted [by us].
Just as for some living beings aversion is desired [only] toward certain objects, so too destruction is the inherent nature (svabhāva) of entities, provided they are not unproduced. (281)
Furthermore, it might be argued:
"Let it be granted that this is indeed the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of these entities— that they have the property of abiding for only a single moment."
But that [nature] will belong only to those things that possess origination;
for not every [quality] is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of everything, just as the nature of resistance is not shared by all.
This is true; nevertheless:
Due to the restriction of the intrinsic nature of the cause, there is a restriction of the intrinsic nature in the effect.
In that which is impermanent, there is no diversity of form, because there is an absence of differentiating factors. (282)
Indeed, neither resistance nor any other intrinsic nature (svabhāva) possesses a specific restriction without cause;

rather, whatever the capacity of its own cause may be established as, such is the fruit that arises. Thus, from the restriction of the intrinsic nature of the cause follows the restriction of the intrinsic nature of the fruit.

Even if this [destruction] were accidental, the same fault already mentioned would apply. For we do not perceive any entity that possesses a nature restricted to the production of perishable things, any more than we perceive a nature restricted to its own specific cause or the nature of resistance.
By which [cause] that [destruction] would arise from that very birth and not from another,
since destruction is observed in all things born in every possible form.
But surely this too is uncertain: that things which arise in all their forms perish, because those [forms] are not seen to be exhausted;
for causal complexes are observed to possess diverse potencies.
In that regard, it might be argued that there could be some [consciousness] which produces an imperishable self. No;
because this discussion concerns the knowable.
Those things which, having been known by someone, at some time, or in some place, are no longer known [cannot be said to produce such a self].
We say that their destruction is necessarily concomitant with their existence;
it is precisely those produced things that are established as impermanent. For this possibility does not exist: that they [should] produce cognition...
Furthermore, intrinsic natures that have not perished would neither produce [their effects] nor depend upon another,
because the nature of producing those [effects] has already been established;
and when they do not depend [on anything else], nothing [further] occurs for anyone.
Perhaps some cognition might be excluded;
however, nothing of such a nature exists,
because everything is known by someone at some time.
If there were an incapacity even for the causal efficiency of mere cognition, the thing-in-itself would not exist at all;
for such is the definition of a real entity.
We shall explain this later. And because its destruction is invariable, that [destruction] is necessarily connected with existence (*sattā*).
For this very reason, their relation must also be rejected as being eternal.
Precisely for this reason, because destruction is connected with the mere entity (*vastumātra*) as has been stated, it is like sound (*śabda*).
The eternality of the relationship [between word and meaning] must also be rejected. Furthermore, that power of the word called "fitness" (*yogyatā*),
which is described by the followers of Jaimini as the basis for the comprehension of meaning, is a distinct entity.
It is not so; for indeed,
"capacity" is simply a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) of the form of entities.
This has been stated previously. Or, even if it were a different object [than the word], the power of the word is nonetheless refuted by the defects of relation already mentioned. (283)

For indeed, many kinds of faults have been stated in the argument that the relation [between word and meaning] is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). By that very [argument], that verbal capacity (*śabda-śakti*) has already been refuted; thus, it shall not be discussed again.
Furthermore, the mere fact that [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) does not, by itself, constitute a means for the knowledge of things as they truly are.
Fire and other such things are observed to exist otherwise [i.e., even without smoke], yet they are not corrupted by the fault of the person. (284)

Granted that Vedic words may indeed be authorless (*apauruṣeya*), nevertheless, it is certainly possible for them to be causes of non-correspondent cognition (*ayathārtha-jñāna*). For [this does not arise] merely from the imposition of human defects (*puruṣa-doṣa*).
Thus, there is a delusion of cognition regarding objects,
because even things such as lamps— which are devoid of those [objects]— generate false cognitions with respect to blue lotuses and the like.
Therefore, these words would be independent of linguistic convention (*saṃskāra*) and,
by their very nature (*prakṛtyā*), would be causes for the manifestation of meanings due to their specific intrinsic essence (*svabhāva-viśeṣāt*).
If it is argued that, like fire and so forth,
false manifestations necessarily [arise] because a cause for such necessity is absent, and thus [the claim of necessity] is untenable;

What is the cause for the restriction that manifestation is non-false? Therefore, why is it not postulated that there is a natural restriction of manifestation as non-corresponding to reality, just as there is a restriction of manifestation corresponding to reality?
Alternatively, just like fire and so forth, there would be a causality for the cognition of both [the object and its absence] regarding objects;
for fire and the like are not indeed non-human (apauruṣeya).
Just as things that are causes of true cognition in one instance are likewise so in all instances,

so too, even if words were not of human origin, both [properties] would apply to them. Let it be that fire and such things, being produced, undergo alteration in other cases according to the conditions.
Furthermore, this [property] does not exist in the case of eternal words.
But surely such a property exists elsewhere as well, since even those [words] function otherwise by the power of convention (*saṃketa*).
Furthermore, if these [words] were to abide in a nature that produces their effect, there would be no dependence on anything such as convention (*samaya*);
consequently, the cognition of objects would occur for everyone at all times. But this is not the case. Therefore, words do not possess an abiding nature. Moreover:
If that [cognition] is held to be uncreated, it could not even be the cause of knowledge;
for from eternal things, which lack causal efficacy as real entities, nothing whatsoever can arise. //285//

If sound were unproduced, there could be no cognition of objects from it; for it is impossible to conceive of a capacity for producing cognition in that which possesses an identical form both at the time when cognition arises and at other times.

Thus, because there is no difference in form that could be distinguished such that "this is a producer" and "that is not," it is not the case that what is a non-producer of this [effect] is exactly the same as what is its producer.
[The capacity] is endowed [with it]. Furthermore, dependence upon anything else has already been refuted.
Therefore, eternal entities possess no capacity whatsoever for producing cognition.
Since if there were no production at any time, it would follow that there is perpetual non-production,
and because we do not observe the continuous occurrence of effects, it has already been stated that these [causes] are in no way producers.
Furthermore, those cognitions which occur with respect to space and so forth—things considered to be eternal—are not produced from the intrinsic nature of those objects. For it is thus:
they arise from the latencies of conceptual construction and have superimposed objects as their domain.
Cognitions arise therein as mere [mental constructs], not having external objects as their domain. //286//
For a cognition whose object is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) necessarily conforms to the presentation of its corresponding capacity;
thus, when that [particular] exists, provided its cause is capable, that cognition certainly arises.
Therefore, if there were any cognition of the particular characteristic of eternal entities, [it would follow that they are not eternal].
Everything would exist at all times.

For individual manifestations (*vyakti*), which are specific effects, being employed in some way or another in some place, must have as their cause the acquisition of a particular excellence (*atiśaya*) capable of producing that [effect].
It is logical that [cognitions] depend upon specific objects; likewise, if an eternal entity, which is not a specific effect,
were perceived by someone, it would depend upon its cause for that perception.
It would be logical that it should be perceived by that very [consciousness] which produced it;
however, because its intrinsic nature is fixed,
that is not possible.
It would either be perceived by everyone equally, or it would not be perceived by anyone at all; for if it were seen by someone, no supersensible entity could be eternal.
And this is not the case.

Therefore, independent of the capacity of external objects and having superimposed things as their domain, these delusions— which are empty of external objects— arise for everyone regarding space and so forth, relying solely upon internal material causes, namely the awakening of the latencies of conceptual construction.

Therefore, words do not have the property of non-reversibility; or, even if they did possess that property, from what [source] would this [reliability] arise, such that they produce a cognition of objects that is not false?

[The opponent replies: "It is indeed so. For in such statements as 'Fire is the remedy for cold,' the capacity of fire to counteract cold—which is already well-known in the world—is merely being made manifest; thus everything is the same.
Since worldly usage proceeds according to conventions established by one's own whim, what is this [of yours]?"
There is a doubt as to whether the world understands in this way merely by conforming to its own convention, or rather due to the inherent nature of words;
for even [words] being turned back by the will of the world [would not change their meaning].
Furthermore, since words are observed to have different meanings in other contexts, even when conforming to worldly convention,
it is possible for them to have a different sense;
therefore, for someone [to claim] non-perversion—
Even if all [cognitions] were seen [to be valid], their status as such would not be established;
for even if they possess an unconditioned nature (*akṛta-svabhāvatva*), some might still be restricted to false objects. This is because of [their] intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If, because of a lack of thorough knowledge, there were doubt everywhere;

and if [you argue that] "falsity is seen only in things produced, therefore the unproduced word has true meaning" because the negative concomitance (vyatireka) pervades the contradictory [i.e., falsity]; //287//

Now, since every statement whose object is false is produced (*kṛtaka*), and because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the reason cannot exist elsewhere, it follows that what is unproduced (*akṛtaka*) must have a true object— even without a positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
For when one thing is not pervaded by another, one might suspect its absence there;
however, two contradictory things cannot coexist in a single locus.

Since there is no possibility of something belonging to a different class [of things], and because there is no other way [to establish the relationship] except through this, the desired object is established; furthermore,
since the logical mark (liṅga) serves as its means of proof, the observation of positive concomitance (anvaya) is useless, as the conclusion is established by negative concomitance (vyatireka) alone.
This is true if the relationship of pervaded and pervader between the two counter-examples were established;
however, that is not established, because:

When the impossibility [of the reason] in the cause has not been stated, the existence of that [cause] is also suspected, because even contradictory entities are observed to have a common pervader. //288//
If the absence of the reason in the counter-example of the probandum were established, then the exclusion of the reason would pervade the exclusion of the probandum; however,
that is not possible there.
We do not perceive any means of valid cognition [for such a claim].
Furthermore, it is not logical for an affirmation that is not contradictory [to the fact] to be a proof for a negation, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is it the case that what is observed in one place cannot possibly exist elsewhere,
for we observe even mutually contradictory things coexisting separately,
just as in the case of impermanence.
Regarding [the properties of] being produced immediately after an effort and its opposite:
it is not the case that such a thing is non-existent simply because it is not perceived, for:
It has been stated that non-existence is not established because [the probans] is not perceived anywhere;
since non-existence is unestablished, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful. //289//
For this person is not merely a human being capable of seeing everything, such that by the cessation of his vision he would no longer exist [in that capacity].
For one whose knowledge [depends upon] the existence of the object of knowledge...
One who speaks thus does not deviate from the truth and would be justified in saying that something does not exist simply because it is not perceived.
For those things which exist may remain unperceived due to the remoteness of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), location (*deśa*), or time (*kāla*). To illustrate:
Who is capable of verifying, or otherwise determining, whether a statement—whether unauthored or otherwise—is true regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses?
Furthermore, this has already been established: even in the case of objects perceived as such in some instances, [their status remains uncertain].
Furthermore, how could there be a change into something else? For example, in a certain place, neem fruits may become sweet, and myrobalan fruits [sour] due to a specific preparation;
yet, one who does not perceive this now should certainly not reject them.

Therefore, we see no contradiction in the fact that something might be both uncreated and have a false object; for it has already been stated that this non-perception does not establish the absence of things whose nature is invisible. By that [reasoning],...
Because there is no certainty that whatever has a false object is entirely of human origin, there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). For instance:
[is there] positive concomitance (*anvaya*), negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), or existence (*sattva*) in the subject of the probandum (*sādhya-dharmin*)?
If the means of proof are established by cognitions that have the result of certainty regarding that [object], [then the means of proof are valid]. //290//
And thus it has been said:
"Only that which expresses what is certain for both [parties] is a proof or a refutation;
however, that which expresses what is established for only one or what is doubtful requires further proof."

Thus [it is said]: "For who would deny the possibility of that whose contradiction has not been observed? Therefore, this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is non-probative because it is subject to doubt. Furthermore: "Where the negative concomitance of the counter-example to the probandum (*sādhya-vipakṣa*) is described..."
That alone would be its similar instance (sapakṣa); therefore, every logical reason (hetu) would be positive (anvayin). //291//
Whatever has a false object is entirely of human origin;

this pervasion of the opposite of the probandum by the opposite of the reason would be established if its absence were proven to be absent [wherever the probandum is absent], for that which exists in the absence of it cannot be pervaded by it.

Furthermore, the very establishment of the exclusion of two heterogeneous [classes] is itself the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), because the probandum (*sādhya*) is characterized by the exclusion of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

And since a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) is established through a double negation (*pratiṣedha-dvaya*), what [need is there for] a pervasion (*vyāpti*) that lacks both positive and negative concomitance?
This is established; therefore, there is no such thing as a "non-concomitant" (ananvaya) reason,
because the exclusion of one [alternative] is inseparable from the establishment of its dissimilar class.
It might be argued that the same would apply even to the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth; but it is not so,
because the exclusion of a negative counterpart (*vyatireka-vyavaccheda*) has the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpatva*).
The exclusion of the nature of an entity does not entail the presence of that entity;
however, the exclusion of non-existence necessarily brings about the presence of an entity.

Because existence and non-existence consist in their mutual exclusion, negation (vyatireka) has the nature of non-existence; and that negation, being itself excluded, brings about the presence of existence. This is not the case with selflessness and so forth, because they are specific attributes of intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
For the self is "selfless" because it is not independent with respect to action, enjoyment, and the locus [of experience],
since the characteristic of the self consists in that very independence.
That nature of selflessness is not merely the cessation of the self;
otherwise, since properties such as being produced would be impossible in the case of a mere non-entity (nirupākhya), selflessness could not be established on that basis.
If it is argued that there is no fault because one apprehends a thing as being without self through the exclusion of a self, [we reply:
by means of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), it is precisely that very thing which is touched upon.
The nature of things (vastu-rūpa) results in selflessness (nairātmya).
Even for one for whom the exclusion (vyatireka) is not of the nature of non-existence, there would be no establishment of existence upon the exclusion of the nature of existence.
There is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Likewise, even in the case of selflessness (*anairātmya*), there is no establishment of existence. For example, [in the argument] "this living body is not selfless because it possesses breath and so forth," [there is no concomitance] between the two counter-examples (*vipakṣa*).

In the investigation of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, selflessness is observed only where there is the absence of breath and so forth; and since it does not exist in the absence of those [breaths], even though it does not itself arise, it does not establish the existence of breath and so forth in the self.
Likewise, even in the case of the probandum, [the self] would be excluded solely by means of breath and so forth,
because breath and the rest do not exist in the absence of a self.
The [arguments] beginning with [the first] do not refute that [selflessness] nor establish a self,
because existence is not established therein.
Nor can the establishment of a self occur through the cessation of selflessness.
Even if one demonstrates the absence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is still the risk of over-extension (*prasaṅga*).
Therefore, when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established, there is no pervasion by the contrapositive (*viparyaya-vyāpti*).
And the establishment of that [positive concomitance] is itself the establishment of the positive pervasion (anvaya).

Alternatively, if it is not established, then even if the exclusion of its absence (vyatireka-nivṛtti) were established, that [positive pervasion] would remain unestablished; thus, the same undesirable consequence applies to the probandum as well.
Therefore, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) for the pervasion of negative concomitance (vyatireka);
rather, falsity is pervaded by being of human origin (pauruṣeyatva).

Even upon the cessation [of the speaker] in the case of non-human (apauruṣeya) [Vedic texts], there is no guarantee of their having true meaning, because other possibilities exist. However, this [concern regarding truth] would apply to words only if they were restricted to two categories; for if one category were excluded, there would be no other alternative.
Because of their non-existence, those [words] might indeed be meaningless; thus, the desired conclusion is not established.
If it is argued that they are not meaningless because there is comprehension of meaning:
This would be a human activity,
like the conceptualization of other objects;
for example, even though they do not have that [ultimate] purpose, there are works such as the life stories of Bharata, Urvaśī, and others which serve as a subject matter.
Others explain it otherwise, and according to that, some have such an understanding. Thus,
this conceptualization of meaning regarding meaningless things is produced by persons, but not by the words themselves.
That which is produced by its own nature does not depend upon human instruction, just like [the illumination of] other objects;
for fire and the like do not require such [instruction] for their natural manifestation. However, it is logical that a person teaches while describing the operation of his own convention (*saṃketa*).

Since there is no difference between the two—being established by human composition and being established by nature—in their dependence upon instruction, and since there is no other distinguishing feature, it is difficult to determine that one is natural while the other is of human origin.
If it is argued that there is a distinction consisting in its correspondence with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [we reply: ...

We shall refute this later [in section 15514], namely that there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses (*atyantaparokṣa*).
[This applies] to two things possessing the same property (*samānadharmī*).

Because there is only the distinction of agreement with valid means of cognition regarding their respective meanings, [one might argue that] while one is non-human (apauruṣeya), many more [of these] are now non-human. Yet, there are indeed some sentences produced by persons as well.
Since they are of such a nature, the same logical consequence applies to them as well:
like those [other words], these too would have a meaningfulness intended by human agency and would be dependent upon valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore...
And we perceive this to be contradictory: that these mantras are both [efficacious] and authorless (*apauruṣeya*). For instance:

if mantras were merely conventional agreements (*samaya*), then it would be logical for them to accomplish some specific purpose for someone, provided these mantras were the convention of someone—just as [the rules] established by me.

If this very sentence, which binds together the intended meaning, were composed— either out of deference to the intent of another, thinking "I shall connect [this] with this meaning," or for some other reason—
then, through the application of such counsel, the goal might at some point [be attained].
The accomplishment [of the meaning] is logical for reciters, as it is from the convention of poets;
nevertheless, if there were an inherent power of the entity, it would exist without distinction even elsewhere. //292//
Indeed, the accomplishment of the purpose does not arise from the mantras through human convention;
what then? It is the very nature of things that these [mantras], when applied in a certain way, yield results. Therefore, that...
Since the form of the phonemes is everywhere indistinguishable, the result would follow even from a mantra employed in any manner whatsoever;
for the mantra consists of the phonemes alone and nothing else— its sequence [is merely incidental].
If it is argued that [the mantra] is the sequence,
the fact that the sequence is a distinct entity has already been refuted;
it has been demonstrated that there is no sequence other than the phonemes themselves.
And if there were no distinction [between the mantra and its constituent phonemes],
then the phonemes themselves would be the mantra;
and since they are indistinguishable everywhere, they would yield results at all times.

However, an eclipse (upaplava) is observed even from the slightest deviation in the sequence [of ritual performance], due to the non-performance of some part, the lack of proximity of the deity, and the incomplete violation [of the rules]. But in the case of a total failure,
it is due to the non-performance of some specific convention and the resulting absence of proximity.
There is neither benefit nor harm.

Furthermore, whether the sequence is a distinct entity or not distinct from its constituents, there can be no basis for the efficacy of a mantra— whether that mantra consists of the phonemes themselves or their sequential order— as a cause for achieving a purpose.
Since that which is eternal is uncreated, it is eternally present;
therefore, the accomplishment of its purpose would be constant.
For since the production of the effect arises from the power of the entity, and that power is unimpaired, there can be no deficiency in the effect.
It would not be so; for it is not logical that there be a deficiency in the effect when the causes are complete, as that would entail the consequence that [those causes] are not causes at all.
The desired result is not achieved through the mere employment of mantras alone.
If it is argued that this is because it depends upon an injunction (*vidhāna*), [we reply:
there is a lack of capacity in such dependence. //293//
If mantras were to acquire some excellence of intrinsic nature either from their ritual application or from elsewhere, then that [cause] would have to be depended upon as being efficacious therein;
however, this is not the case for eternal things.
It has been stated that [the cause] exists.
Therefore, why would this [cause], being incapable [of producing the effect], be required?
Thus, those who do not require [anything else] would either always produce [the effect] or never at all, since there is no excellence [in their nature].
