If such were the inherent power of an entity, it would follow that everything could be established for you;
moreover, dependence on a difference in the agent is not logical for that which cannot be modified by refinement.
If mantras were to bestow success solely by virtue of their own inherent power (*bhāva-śakti*), they would not exclude anyone— neither the sacrificer nor another;
for an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be something that does not apply to others.
It occurs because it cannot be diminished by that [cause], nor can it be increased by anything else,
since there is no relationship of cause and effect with anything whatsoever; this is due to proximity or distance.
Because [the self] does not exist, for this very reason it cannot be modified; therefore, there is no agent either. Consequently, it would be the agent who should enjoy the fruit.
For even in the case of an entity that is to be modified, it is indeed a difference in the nature of the thing itself that constitutes the differentiator.
The restriction [of meaning] would arise from the difference between speakers regarding capacity, but not regarding convention. //295//
For conditioned phenomena (*bhāva*) are impermanent because they possess specific qualities that are to be produced (*ādheya-viśeṣa*).
Due to that cause, when there is a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-bheda*),
they would become otherwise in other instances because they have acquired a specific excellence (*atiśaya*).
Not in the case of non-difference;
for when there is no distinction in the cause,
there can be no distinction in the effect.

Because, in the case of a specific [result], it would follow that it is causeless— this has already been stated previously. Therefore, these mantras, being productive of results due to an excellence of their own nature, would not fail to produce their effects even when employed by Śūdras and others.
Because there is no difference in the nature of two persons designated as a Śūdra and a Brāhmaṇa;
for [nature] does not conform to the will of a person.
There is a change in the nature of objects that are invariably connected with a difference in their intrinsic being due to a difference in the conventional usage of names.
If it is argued that there is a difference in genus (*jāti*) between those two,
that [difference] indeed consists of a difference in configuration (*ākṛti*), quality (*guṇa*), and capacity (*śakti*).
In the case of difference, it is observed as in the instance of a cow and a horse;
furthermore, people understand this [difference] without being taught.
However, we do not perceive even the slightest specific quality belonging to either of these two in that same manner.
And not perceiving [it],
how could we comprehend difference? As for this which is called—

In the world, there is a distinction in usage and a distinction in cognition; even in the absence of a real distinction in genus (*jāti*), this may occur through the performance of specific functions and through association, as in the case of designations such as "physician" or "merchant.
Therefore, these mantras, when employed without distinction, produce a result that is likewise without distinction.
[If they] were to attain their own nature [independently],
then they would grant results without distinction. However,
when the result arises from these [actions] by virtue of convention (*samaya*), then this fault does not apply.
Because for the author of the treatise (samayakāra),
there is a necessity regarding the arising of results according to his intention;
for entities function according to their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) by way of that [intention].
They deserve to be subjected to logical consequences (*prasaṅga*);
they do not function according to human whim,
because their operation occurs in whatever way [is logically necessary].

Furthermore, as for the statement that "the agent enjoys the fruit," we observe that this "application" (prayoga) consists either in the production of something capable of achieving the desired object, or in the transformation of the continuum (santāna-pariṇāma).
Both of those [causes] would have to produce a specific distinction; otherwise,
for those things to which no distinction can be imparted, what could an instigator do such that one person enjoys a certain fruit from them while another does not?
If "application" (prayoga) means manifestation (abhivyakti), that has already been refuted.
For it has already been stated that there is no manifestation whatsoever of eternal things, such that a manifestor could be the agent. Furthermore,
if manifestation is cognition, and if that [cognition] is connected with results because of its source, [then the agent would be the one who experiences the result].
There would be a connection between the scripture and its fruit, for the speaker is indeed the cause of its manifestation. //297//
For the manifestation of a word's own form does not consist in a transformation of its nature from something else, nor is it the removal of an obscuration;
rather, it is the cognition of that object, because when it is not being heard, it is designated as "unmanifest.
In this regard, if the speaker were the cause of the cognition, then the same would apply to the listener as well.
He too would enjoy the fruit just like the speaker;
for there is no other state belonging to the speaker than that [state of being] the cause of the cognition of that [object].
If it is argued that the distinction is that the cognition of the external adjunct belongs to the hearer and not to the speaker,
then what benefit does the speaker provide to the hearer?
If it is argued that the hearing of sound occurs because of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) [which is the conjunction with the sense organ],
is this not indeed the very same [conjunction] as before?
It is questioned: "How then [is it so]?
Because there is no connection; because of the presentation of the object.
This person might become his disciple;
however, that is not possible for him in any way whatsoever, because of the impossibility of transformation.
The conditioning of the sense faculties and so forth have also been explained.

If it is argued that there is a distinction between the speaker and the listener based on their respective cognitions—namely, "He makes me hear" and "I hear"—this is not so; for if such a distinction existed based on mere illusion arising from what are neither benefactors nor beneficiaries, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, because a cognition is observed even elsewhere through delusion,
and because such a cognition would not be tenable if there were no assistance whatsoever in any way.

Because this consequence would apply equally to all things in relation to one another; furthermore, even an error occurs elsewhere only when there is some benefit [derived] from something and through a certain degree of proximity.

That [manifestation] would also not exist if there were no benefit whatsoever. Therefore, since there is no distinction between the speaker and the listener in being the cause of manifestation, the connection with the result would be equal for both.
Furthermore:

The purpose of the vocal organs would be for sounds that are not manifested; otherwise, mental recitation (*manojapa*) would be useless, for sound is indeed within the range of the sense of hearing. (298)
Sound is characterized by being apprehended by the auditory organ;
for if one were to deviate from this, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Objection:
But in that case, the same consequence would apply to universals (*sāmānya*) as well.

We do not say that it is the word itself [that is produced]. However, sound must necessarily possess that characteristic, because there is no other characteristic for it. In this regard, if the agent were the cause of the manifestation of mantras whose nature is sound, then [the mantra] would remain unmanifested—
The reciter who employs the organs that have the Vedas as their object is not joined with the fruit of the mantra, nor is one who recites mentally;
for at that time, no object is perceived by the ear.
We analyze this:
a mantra does not have a non-verbal nature;
even if that cognition is considered its manifestation, it is because it is indirectly produced from that [mantra].

For even when one meditates with the mind, there is no cognition resembling a mantra apart from the hearing of sound. Therefore, because it originates from sound, that too is indeed a manifestation of sound.
In this way, there would be an infinite regress.
It may be so; for even the conceptual constructions regarding words and their referents have an origination through a continuous succession.
They, too...
If it were argued that they would be so [i.e., have the same meaning] for that reason, it is unestablished, because of the persistence of conceptual construction. //299//
We do not say that every cognition arising from a word is its manifestation (*vyakti*). Rather, that which has it as its object is its manifestation;
for it is the conceptual construction of the mind (*mano-vikalpa*) that possesses that [word] as its object.
[This is] unestablished. For we shall demonstrate that conceptual constructions do not operate upon particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Indeed, those [constructions], according to their respective natures, arise from the awakening of internal latencies for conceptual construction (*vikalpa-vāsanā*), without depending on the presence of external objects.
Because [the cognition] exists even when external objects of destruction do not arrive.
For that which does not depend upon the presence of the existence of something is not its cause; and how can that which is not a cause be an object?
Therefore, the mental construction is not the manifestation of the word, since the speaker would have to be its possessor.
The cognition produced by that [word] and having that as its object is the manifestation of it.

"The agent is that which has that [word] as its basis. To this it has been replied: "The same consequence follows for the listener as well. Furthermore, when the word is employed for the sake of producing that cognition, the word operates upon the person.
Because it produces knowledge regarding that [object], the person does not reside in the word;
for there is no benefit to the self of that [word] by means of it. And yet...
The claim that "the person is the user of words" is an unconventional (alaukika) convention.
Insofar as the attainment of results occurs through the employment of mantras whose very nature is sound,
mental recitation is useless, because conceptual thought does not touch upon the form of the sound.

Because the authors of conventions speak of things possessing both specific and general natures with the intention of expressing them as a single entity, there is no contradiction in their usage; however, this does not apply to the actual nature of reality.
The formulator of the convention, however, having synthesized the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa)— which is the object of the sense faculty— and the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa)—
which is the appearance in conceptual construction— according to conventional usage, would announce the convention; and according to that convention, he would bring about the intended object.
There is no fault in cases such as mental recitation (*manojapa*);
however, if the fruit is obtained through the intrinsic nature of the object itself, it would not occur if there were contact with that which lacks such an intrinsic nature.

Regarding what was stated— that there is no sequence (ānupūrvī) other than the phonemes— it follows that if such a sequence did not exist, there would be no difference in perception between hearing "sara" and "rasa."
If it is argued that there is no difference in the resulting effect,

[we reply: indeed, in words such as *sara* and *rasa*, there is no difference whatsoever among the phonemes (*varṇa*), nor is there anything other than the phonemes from which a difference in effect could arise.
And we observe that their two manifestations are distinct, and their sequence is indeed unequal;
yet there is no difference in their cause.
A distinction in effects is logical;
therefore, that [cognition] exists as something possessing distinctions, from which this difference in apprehension arises. This is true.
That [consciousness] has the person as its support. //301//
For it is thus:

the sound that arises from a cognition produced by the cognition of the origination of a particular phoneme is apprehended by hearing as having that [phoneme] as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). (302)

One who has knowledge produced by that [perceptual] knowledge, but whose hearing is not proficient in the scripture, subsequently produces a memory within himself by depending upon that [prior] memory. //303//
Thus, this causal relationship among the phonemes—consisting of their sequence—is said to be purely human, belonging to those cognitions that apprehend its causes. (304)

For vocal intimation consists of the utterance of phonemes, words, and sentences, which are originated by the mind. In that process, by means of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) of the mental state that originates the sound *sa*, the mental state that originates the sound *a* is produced.
Likewise, the utterances of the *repha*, the vowel *ā*, and the *visarjanīya* have each preceding one as their condition; thus,
these phonemes (*varṇa*) are mutually caused by one another and arise from their own respective causes.
When [the letters] arise in a sequential order,
and even at the time of hearing, they— moving slowly and depending upon the auxiliary cognition that consists of the knowledge of the preceding letter— generate their own cognition, then...
They depend upon the recollection of the preceding phonemes and merge into that memory; thus, these phonemes possess a distinct nature in their causal efficiency, cognition, and manifestation.
Furthermore, the nature [of speech] which has the property of being produced is called "sequence," as it is differentiated by the variations in human articulation (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*).
Apart from that, the form of each individual phoneme (*varṇa*) is indeed something entirely different.
Distinct from the refinement of the agent, it acts in conjunction with it to produce a diversity of effects. //305//

Therefore, indeed, there is not just a single nature for the phonemes within words, because they differ according to the distinctions in the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) of the agent’s mind; and that [nature], when accompanied by others, produces a distinction in the effect.
That sequence of phonemes proceeds from the act of composition; for those things established by desire, there is no contradiction with a fixed order [if it were otherwise]. //306//

It has been stated that the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of phonemes is a specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) produced by conditions existing in a cause-and-effect relationship. Furthermore, since this [order] is created by the conceptualization and deliberation (*vitarka-vicāra*) of a person, the phonemes do not possess a fixed sequence; for their sequence is established in accordance with one's will (*icchā*), without contradiction.
It possesses a specific sequence and a regular order.

For it is not possible, by one's own will, to arrange the sequence of those things whose order is fixed— such as the Himalayas, Vindhyas, and Malaya mountains, or seeds, sprouts, and so forth— with respect to space and time.

Because it is possible to produce [the effect] from that very [source], and because when there is a sequence of conceptual constructions (vikalpa) reckoned as human attributes the [effect] exists, and when they are absent it does not exist,
the relationship of cause and effect is established for both humans and the sequence of phonemes.
The entire sequence of phonemes [is derived] from persons, like the principle of fire and fuel. //307//

Since burning occurs when fuel exists and is absent when it does not, even a fire that has not yet been seen to have fuel is not "without fuel," because it would be impossible for such a thing to be restricted by place and time;
and if there were such restriction, that very thing [the fuel] would constitute its fuel.
Because fuel is characterized by being the material cause of burning,
so too this sequence of phonemes would manifest by itself without support, if it did not depend upon the conceptual construction of a person.
Even with effort, it could not be [produced],
because it does not arise from that;
if it were possible in some cases, then everything would be so.

Because there is no distinction; for if that which exists when something else exists were not distinguished from it, then the relationship of cause and effect would apply everywhere, even in cases where one thing is not produced by the other.
It would be refuted,
because its definition consists of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); [therefore,] another definition [is required].
Or it should be stated:
it follows that all entities, such as jars and the like, would be both artificial and non-artificial.
Because such conceptualization is possible even in that case,
and because there is no distinction [between the two],
another person indeed performs those actions only after first observing the performance by someone else, without being aware of it.
And since there are some who hold that [the world] has a creator, let there be for all or for some an adherence to the view of non-action (*akriyā*).

Therefore, this entire sequence of phonemes (*varṇānupūrvī*) is the work of a person, because it does not transgress the nature of things (*vastudharma*) whose causal relationship is well-established. Precisely for this reason:
The uniqueness of those men who perform the sequence known as Mantra is established by their knowledge and power, because others lack these two. //308//
If this sequence of phonemes were capable of neutralizing poison and so forth, and no other were, then anyone else who knew it would likewise apply it in that same way;
but this is not the case. Therefore, [it is not the sequence].
This sequence, which produces effects by its very nature, is understood by only some; therefore,
there exists a person who perceives objects beyond the senses,
for this matter is not capable [of being known otherwise].
It is not possible to distinguish [the one from] the other by thinking "this is it," because no specific, unmixed characteristic mark (*liṅga-viśeṣa*) has been established;
for even when both are perceived directly, one cannot discern whether they are mantras or non-mantras unless they have been taught.
Even if they were taught, since their essential distinction (*svabhāva-viveka*) is not perceived in any way, [the distinction must be made] elsewhere through their function (*kārya*).
Because it is established through correspondence, and because that [correspondence] cannot be perceived prior to the performance [of the action];
nor does this sequence act as a causal factor by its own nature, since for some [result] there is swift accomplishment,
for another it is delayed, and for yet another it depends upon the observance of vows and so forth.
Because even from a single action, both benefit and harm are observed for some [beings],
even while they are carrying it out.
Furthermore, because mantras are sometimes inconsistent,
this kind of thing is not logically possible regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is without distinction everywhere, it is logical that a person (*puruṣa*),

acting according to his own will, might favor one being and not another due to the influence of the commonality of their essence (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) and so forth, or simply because of such lack of distinction.

If it is argued that success or failure occurs either through the accumulation of merit and demerit resulting from the violation of vows and so forth, or by the very nature of the self consisting of merit and demerit, we say: no.

For even among those vows that are contrary to the Dharma— such as those characterized by cruelty, theft, sexual misconduct, and base actions— they are observed in the *Ḍākinī-tantras*, the *Bhaginī-tantras*, and so forth.
And because of those specific accomplishments (*siddhi*),
as well as the fact that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena is not of such a kind, we shall explain this at the appropriate occasion. [Regarding] loving-kindness (*maitrī*)—
And for those devoted to the dharma of purity, it is precisely because of that [purity] that there is the attainment of some success,
while in its absence there is failure; yet again, when there is success,
it does not arise from a single uniform action.
That which is contrary to it is dharma, and its opposite is adharma.
How, then, does one experience the desired fruit of dharma through a vow or other practice that is essentially of the nature of adharma?

Indeed, that desired fruit is not the maturation (vipāka) of the vow and so forth themselves; rather, it is the maturation of prior karma—just as the acquisition of a village results from the performance of [the ritual] for killing a Brahmin. But of that [karma]...
The future fruit of a vow whose nature is unrighteousness (adharma) is undesirable;
however, that application of mantras and so forth is a ripener (pācaka) of that [same] action which has a desirable fruit, because it provides some kind of assistance to it.
Because the capacity for assistance is manifold,
that dharma— which consists of the maturation residing in a particular person— is performed by him; through the propitiation of that [person], it bears fruit accordingly.
If it is argued that because the dharma of the maturation of the assistance provided by that application has been performed,
the fruit of that action arises from that assistance even without a person— [we reply: no, because of the form of the person.
Because it would follow that the practice of intrinsic nature and the inclination [toward it] would be useless; and if even that [intrinsic nature] were to provide assistance,
then a specific person possessing extraordinary qualities is established.
For it is precisely through faith in that [person] that one performs acts such as the neutralization of poison;
therefore, mantras are composed by persons.

Even those who, though ignorant of the ritual manuals (*tantra*), compose certain mantras by their very nature as fruit-bestowers, independent of any practical application— the power they possess is due to the sovereign majesty [of the Lord], because they proceed according to the principles taught by Him. (309)
Even some common carriage-drivers who are experts in the arts perform certain tasks using mantras composed by themselves;
likewise, there are others who are agents but lack any extraordinary power.

Regarding the statement "of mantras": no, for they are empowered only by those who possess such power. Indeed, it is by that [empowerment] that they become capable, provided they observe the convention and proceed according to its instruction.

Because those who are independent of instruction at that time lack the capacity; for even in that case, it is only through the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth in that specific form that [the result occurs].
Therefore, it is indeed dependent upon that [concentration].
That should be inferred as being of such a kind;
moreover,
he too is of such a kind, possessed of great power.
Thus, because of possessing a power that is not shared by others, it is specifically a particular person who is established [as the author].
Mantras should be declared as being produced and authored by persons by one who desires their results;
for the employment of those that are unauthored is impossible, and no results arise from those that are not employed.
Because of the usage [of the term] "fruit," one who desires [the existence of] a fruit must state that mantras are produced and are of human origin;
for it is observed that fruits arise from those things whose fruits could not otherwise be possible without the superintendence of a person.
Like poetry and other works produced by convention, the proof of human incapacity has been refuted by this very [argument]. //310//
For it has been established that mantras are produced by a person and yield their fruit through his presiding over them;
thus, the arguments intended to refute the existence of some being possessed of such excellence have also been refuted.
As for the proofs that are described—such as intellect, sense organs, speech, masculinity, and so forth—[they are irrelevant].
That which resembles a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāsa) is not in accordance with reality; for there is no comprehension [of the object] through the method of remainder (śeṣavat). //311//

As for the argument that [the soul] is excluded from excellence because it possesses intellect, sense organs, and speech— just like [ordinary] manhood— that is simply non-probative with respect to the general category of exclusion.
Because the two means of proof are impossible;
for indeed, the refutation of those who do not perceive supersensible objects is not possible regarding such things.
Because even for these [logicians], this is due to ignorance;
for this very reason, the contradiction is unestablished.
Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no contradiction in the coexistence [of two things] with something that is not contradictory.
Nor can there be the establishment of another generality, because it is impossible to know the non-existence of a particular;
for in such cases, non-perception is rejected as a logical reason,
even when there is equality in terms of masculinity and so forth.
Furthermore, it has been stated that because some particularity is observed, and because a particularity is possible, identity is not established. Therefore, this is an inference *śeṣavat*.
Because there is doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), [the reason] is incapable even if its presence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is not observed; moreover,
the followers of Jaimini who speak thus contradict their own doctrine by their own words.
For instance:
"Words do not say, 'This is the meaning' or 'This is not the meaning';
this meaning is to be conceptualized by persons, and they are possessed of passion and other such afflictions. (312)
In that case, what causes the distinction that one person is a knower of reality while another is not?
Likewise, why is it that, despite the fact that all possess masculinity, some among you are knowers while others are not? (313)
Indeed, these Vedic words do not cry out in this manner, "O Brahmins,
you must accept this meaning of ours and no other"; rather, with their specific meanings and relations unmanifested, they simply rush toward the hearing.
In that regard, one person conceives of a certain object, while another conceives of another;
yet there is no [inherent connection] among words.
There is no specific intrinsic nature (svabhāva-pratiniyama) by which [words] would correspond to one object and not another;

rather, they are seen as entering into this or that object solely by virtue of convention (samaya). Since their connection with objects is not determined and is beyond the senses, only an ignorant person, being afflicted by defects, [perceives them as such].
It is not logical to say that one person explains reality while another does not. If it is argued that he alone—
and no other— knows it due to some excellence in his intellect, sense organs, and so forth,
then from what source does he derive this excellence of suprasensory knowledge?

Likewise, is another observer not seen to be possible with respect to objects remote in space, time, and nature? For there are no arguments for rejecting that [possibility] which do not apply to this [case].
Just as this [person] possesses this distinction even though the means to achieve that [knowledge] are possible for him, so too might it belong to another;
therefore, non-attachment alone is appropriate.
If he whose speech accords with valid cognition is the knower of the object, [then why not others?].
For indeed, there is no possibility of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding things that are absolutely beyond the senses. //314//
It might be argued: "We do not adhere to any particular exposition based on the authority of a person.
What then?"

Because of corroboration by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); even among many commentators, he who harmonizes [his interpretation] with means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the like is accepted.
That is not so;
for since no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operates with respect to supersensible things such as the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*),
it is precisely because of the impossibility of such [other means] that scripture (*āgama*) is invoked for the purpose of understanding them.
Otherwise, even if that [scriptural authority] exists, there would be no comprehension because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not operate; and consequently,
since the object is understood from [the word] alone, scripture would not be a means of proof at all,
[just as it would not be] from anything else alone.
If it is argued that there is no cognition even regarding supersensible (atīndriya) objects,
how can something be both supersensible and yet an object of perception and other such means of knowledge?
Furthermore, if those [means of knowledge] were to establish their objects only by depending upon scripture even with respect to their own domain,
then there would be no cognition of fire from smoke and so forth without scripture.

Indeed, when a scripture is already in operation, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought; rather, it is simply that the operation of that very scripture is not recognized. If [it is argued that this is because] it is being established by something capable in itself...
What excellence does the addition of that suffix (*āgama*) nourish for it? For if it is incapable,
it will not even accomplish the occurrence of the suffix itself.

Furthermore, how could the activity of scripture—which is connected to objects beyond the senses and is itself beyond the senses—be established by another means? Moreover, the definition of scripture would be as follows: for instance, [The original Sanskrit text continues: tad-viṣayaka-jñāna-janana-samartho yaḥ śabdaḥ sa āgama iti / na caitad yuktam / tathā hi / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] And that which is capable of producing a cognition whose object is that [dharma], such a word is scripture. But this is not tenable; for instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: yo 'pi manyate codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharma iti, tasyāpi codanāyāḥ svataḥprāmāṇyaṃ na sidhyati / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Even for one who thinks that dharma is an object characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā), the intrinsic validity of that injunction is not established. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: codaneti kriyāyāḥ pravartakaṃ vacanam āhuḥ / tac ca na pramāṇam, bhrāntādivākyavad apratyayitapuruṣavākyatvāt / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] They say that "injunction" is a statement that impels one toward action; and that is not a valid means of knowledge, because it is the speech of an untrustworthy person, like the speech of someone who is deluded and so forth. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: atha vā codanālakṣaṇatvaṃ dharmasya na sambhavati, vedasyāpauruṣeyatve pramāṇābhāvāt / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Alternatively, the state of being characterized by injunction is not possible for dharma, because there is no proof for the non-human origin of the Veda. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: pauruṣeyatve hi vedasya kartur abhiprāyānurodhena tadarthasyānyathātvam api sambhāvyeta / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] For if the Veda were of human origin, its meaning might even be otherwise according to the intention of the author. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: tasmād atīndriyārthaviṣaye sarvam āgamaprāmāṇyam āśaṅkāspadam eva / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Therefore, regarding objects beyond the senses, all authority of scripture is indeed subject to doubt. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: yadi punar āptapraṇītatvena vedasya prāmāṇyam ucyeta, tadāpy āptatvasya durjñānatvāt tadanupapattiḥ / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] If, on the other hand, the authority of the Veda is asserted on the basis of its being composed by a trustworthy person (āpta), then even that is untenable because trustworthiness is difficult to ascertain. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: na hi kaścid dṛṣṭasarvārthajñānasampannaḥ puruṣo vidyate, yena praṇīto vedo 'visaṃvādī syāt / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Indeed, no person exists who is endowed with the knowledge of all things perceived, by whom the Veda might have been composed so as to be non-contradictory. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: ato nityanirdoṣatvam eva vedasya prāmāṇyanibandhanam iti cet, tad api na / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] If it is argued that the very state of being eternally faultless is the basis for the Veda's authority, that too is not so. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: nityatve hi vedasya jñāpakatvam eva na sambhavati, akṛtakasya jñānajananasāmarthyābhāvāt / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] For if the Veda were eternal, its status as a communicator would not be possible, because that which is unproduced lacks the capacity to generate cognition. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: tasmād āgamasya prāmāṇyaṃ durghaṭam / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Therefore, the authority of scripture is difficult to establish. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: evaṃ ca sati paralokasādhanāni karmāṇi na sidhyanti / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] And this being the case, the ritual acts that prove the existence of the next world are not established. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: tatra yadi kaścid brūyāt—asty ātmā, asti paraloka iti, tasya vacanam apramāṇam eva, pūrvoktanyāyena / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] In that regard, if someone should say, "There is a self; there is a next world," his statement is indeed not a valid means of knowledge, according to the reasoning stated previously. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: tasmād atīndriyārtheṣu na kasyacid āgamasya niścayaḥ / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Therefore, regarding objects beyond the senses, there is no certainty concerning any scripture. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: yat punar ucyate—āmnāyasya kriyārthatvād ānarthakyam atadarthānām iti, tad apy ayuktam / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] As for what is further said—"Because the sacred tradition (āmnāya) has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless"—that too is incorrect. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: jñānam api hi phalavattayā śrutam, "tarati śokam ātmavit" ityādi / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] For even knowledge is heard of as having a fruit, in such passages as, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: tasmād āgamaprāmāṇyavicāre 'pi na tāvatā dharmasiddhiḥ / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Therefore, even in the investigation of the authority of scripture, the establishment of dharma does not follow from that alone. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: iti // [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Thus. [The original Sanskrit text continues: atra pratividhīyate / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] To this, the following reply is given. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: yad uktam atīndriyārthasambaddhā āgamapravṛttir atīndriyeti katham anyena siddheti, tatrocyate / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] Regarding what was said—that the activity of scripture, which is connected to objects beyond the senses and is itself beyond the senses, how can it be established by another means—to that it is replied: [The original Sanskrit text continues: na hy asmābhir āgamasya svataḥprāmāṇyam iṣyate, kiṃ tarhi parataḥ / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] For we do not accept the intrinsic validity of scripture; rather, it is extrinsic. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: tathā hi—āptapraṇītatvena vedasya prāmāṇyam / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] For instance—it is by virtue of being composed by a trustworthy person that the Veda possesses authority. For instance: [The original Sanskrit text continues: āptatvaṃ ca rāgādidoṣarahitatvam, sarvajñatvaṃ ca / [Sanskrit text omitted per instructions] And trustworthiness consists in being free from defects such as passion, as well as omniscience. For instance: [The original Sanskrit

That speech which is consistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and is produced by such [an author] is what constitutes scripture (*āgama*); thus, the claim of being "authorless" (*apauruṣeya*) is rendered meaningless. (315)

Even though the claim regarding scripture is equal [in both cases], since scripture is established as scripture in some instances by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the characteristic of scripture would consist in the words being in conformity with valid cognition; it is not the fact of being non-humanly produced. For even if that [non-human origin] were equal across all objects, it would not lead to comprehension because it is not contradicted by valid cognition.
Even if that [object] exists, it is undesirable because it is not corroborated by another means of valid cognition elsewhere.
Furthermore,
if knowledge independent of scripture were possible regarding an object that is absolutely beyond the senses, [then there would be no need for scripture].
It must be accepted that there exists someone who knows objects beyond the reach of the senses. //316//

If it is maintained that a person’s knowledge regarding an imperceptible object is not dependent on scripture and is not in accordance with reality, then it would follow that there exist persons who perceive objects beyond the senses; for the other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which are preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*), are impossible in the absence of such perception. Perception—
Scripture is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, since the operation of other means of valid cognition, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*), draws [the object] toward it, the excellence of a person (*puruṣātiśaya*) could not be precluded.
Therefore, there is no operation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding supersensible objects;
for this very reason, scripture (*āgama*) functions with respect to specific objects.
Because he lacks full comprehension, this Jaimini or whoever else, being himself possessed of passion and other defects, does not know the meaning of the Veda by himself, nor from another source;
nor does the Veda itself make it known—so how can there be any understanding of the Veda's meaning? (317)
For every person indeed, whose mind is not free from the delusion of defects,
does not himself know that specific determination of objects which transcends the senses; nor does another make it known to him.
For that [objection] would lead to an equally problematic consequence;
indeed, a blind person being led by another blind person does not find the path.
Nor does the Veda explain its own meaning by itself,
for that would entail the consequence of rendering instruction useless.
Thus, this word, whose meaning is not fully understood, is merely a useless tumor; like a thorn bound by the sinews of false views, it is difficult to extract and causes suffering.
Regarding the Vedic revelation, "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," what is the authority for the claim that its meaning is not "one should eat dog-meat"? (318)
With respect to any given matter, for a statement such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," which is devoid of both proximity and remoteness [of meaning],
the intended sense is that one should pour substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into a particular fire, and not that one should eat dog meat.
Thus, we do not perceive any superiority [in this view].
But surely, this same logical consequence applies everywhere:
how can people of the present day [understand] the meaning of the words of teachers who are beyond their perception, according to the [teachers'] own intention?
Do they follow [the teacher's] intention or its opposite?
No; for a tradition is possible through the teacher’s manifestation of his own intended meaning. Indeed, it is not...
This is possible for words that lack an instructor;
and one who speaks with the intention of communicating with the world maintains the conventions established by the world, and therefore—
The accomplishment of that purpose would not belong to words that are not of human origin,
because there is an absence of any effort on the part of anyone in that regard.

Moreover, the wise, adhering strictly to logic (*nyāya*), engage with what is to be abandoned, what is to be adopted, and their underlying basis, rather than by mere conventional report (*pravāda*); thus, the [alleged] consequence is not the same. We shall demonstrate this in its proper place. Now, [one might object]:

One might think that even regarding matters such as the structure of the world, which fall outside the scope of logical reasoning, an object can be understood from the words of a person whose reliability is possible. This is not so;
because there is no basis for trust.
For it is not the case that because something is unerring in one instance, it is so in all instances;
this is because deviation is observed.
Furthermore, because there is no established pervasion (vyāpti) between that [scriptural statement] and non-contradiction in practice,
this definition of scripture is accepted only out of necessity.
This is accepted; however, no certainty arises from this.
Therefore, it has also been stated that scripture (*āgama*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the knowledge of the meaning of words that are not of human origin does not arise from tradition.
It is not reasonable to fail to understand [the matter] because it is neither established by reasoning nor by worldly consensus; for even in that case,
if there is a well-known worldly expression,
it serves as the basis for understanding.
In this regard, who is the seer of supersensuous objects?
It is he by whom the meaning has been discerned among words that possess multiple meanings. (319)
For this worldly convention does not arise from a relationship between word and meaning that is not of human origin.
What then? It arises from convention—that is, from the convention of the authors of their respective treatises—just like the usage of the Pāṇinian system and others.
Because it depends upon instruction; for instruction is not possible regarding that which is not of human origin, since no one could know it.
Because it is beyond the reach of the senses;
for if it were perceptible by the senses, it would follow that one could apprehend it by oneself.
Like form and so forth; furthermore,
since it is not established that independent persons are non-deceptive in their instruction according to reality, there is no confidence in such teaching.

If it is argued that, like the Veda, its commentary is also authorless (apauruṣeya), having come down through an uninterrupted tradition, and therefore the establishment of the meaning [of the Veda] follows from it—
[we reply that] this too consists essentially of words.

The same objection applies: how is its meaning known? For a person can indeed, by seizing the matter by the horns, inform even an ignorant person of the meaning of words he himself has composed; thus, there is a means for understanding the meaning of human utterances.
[This] is the means [of understanding]. However, a word that is not of human origin does not act in this way;
nor is anyone capable of knowing its restriction of relation anywhere. Thus, there is simply no comprehension.
Regarding its meaning:
furthermore, the Veda or its commentary, when being taught by one person to another, continues as an unbroken tradition; in this regard also, there is a convention (*samaya*).

[This is] a refuge. For those who cause the loss of the scriptures—whether out of self-aggrandizement, or out of hatred for that [system], or with the intent to humiliate those who have entered it, or due to the vice of being a rogue, or from some other cause—they are seen to compose [their works] otherwise than [the original]. Furthermore, in this regard:
Surely you have forgotten your own facial expression due to your attachment to your own doctrine;
for since a person overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions might even speak what is false, his word is not a valid means of knowledge.
Therefore, why is this not also examined here— whether it is possible or not?
He himself, while teaching the Veda and the meaning of the Veda from [the perspective of] cognitive distortion (*upaplava*), [teaches it].
Or he might teach it otherwise;
for it is heard that certain individuals have recovered lost branches [of the Veda].
Even now, there are some [scriptures] with few students;
likewise, even for those with many students, it is possible that at some time they might somehow be destroyed.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for there to be the expectation of an abundance [of followers] based on the confidence in a person who is highly esteemed,
and because of those propagators themselves—
Because it is possible for others who have forgotten what they have studied, or for others due to the fear of losing their reputation and so forth, to provide instruction otherwise; therefore,
based on that [instruction].
And because those devoted to it understand it without critical inquiry, and because understanding is frequently observed among many students due to [the influence of] a person deemed reliable;
for that reason as well, somehow...
Because deception is possible;
furthermore, because there are only a limited number of commentators—
Furthermore, regarding this matter, we hear from you as well that there is indeed a succession of persons (*puruṣa-paramparā*).
In that regard, there might be someone who is hateful, ignorant, or deceitful; thus, there is no confidence [in such a tradition].
Therefore, [the Veda] is not established through an authorless commentary, nor through worldly convention based on social agreements.
The establishment of the meaning of the Veda:
even though words have multiple meanings,
because we observe them used in linguistic practice, there may be for some [words] an unestablished meaning or one that is not commonly known.

Furthermore, because the suspicion regarding [the speaker's intention] is not removed everywhere by observing the etymological derivation [of words], for even when all [words] are employed according to their actual meaning,
they produce cognition in accordance with convention without deficiency; thus, there is no distinction between what is desired and what is undesired.

Among persons in general who are indistinguishable regarding all matters and whose connection with objects transcends the senses, who could discern that single object which is beyond sensory perception,
from which a worldly understanding might arise?
Moreover,
he himself does not follow what is universally established in all cases; for:
Furthermore, words such as "heaven" (svarga) and "Urvaśī" are observed to denote meanings that are not conventionally established (*arūḍha*),
being analyzed precisely by this [method]:
[they refer to] the abode of a particular person who surpasses humans (*atimānuṣa*).
"Heaven is a locus of pleasure, possessing various implements; the celestial nymph (apsaras) dwelling there is named Urvaśī"—this is popular worldly talk.
Disregarding that, [the author] offers a different interpretation of the meaning.
How could this person, while acting [in one way], establish the validity of his own linguistic usage regarding other words?
If it is argued that he accepts them there because there is no contradiction, we say no;
for here too, the object is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
Because contradiction is unestablished;
for even elsewhere, the absence of contradiction is difficult to ascertain. Moreover, due to his dullness, he might not perceive that the attainment of heaven from the Agnihotra is contradictory.
Furthermore, contradiction and non-contradiction consist in the operation of subverting and establishing means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
and these are not intended to apply to that which is beyond the senses (atyakṣa).
How, then, can there be cognition by virtue of that?
Nor is there non-contradiction solely because of the occurrence of the verbal expression, for that would lead to the same consequence in other cases as well.
Scripture is authorless;
from its proclamation, the establishment of the object [of knowledge] occurs.
However, when there is further consideration of contradiction therein, there is no confidence.

It might exist in scripture; yet even if that [scripture] exists, because the object does not correspond to it, it functions as an invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), since there is room for suspicion regarding other [objects] as well.
As it has been said: "The Agnihotra..."
In the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the alternative of teaching the consumption of dog-meat does not occur,
because such a thing has been considered [and rejected] in other sections of the scripture.
No; because its meaning is not fully understood,
and because such an interpretation of the meaning would be unavoidable even in other passages.
For if this mass of words were non-human (apauruṣeya) and its meaning were known in some instance, then from it there would be comprehension of the meaning;
however, they [the Vedas] are mostly...
"Even though all [people] are indeed blind, they are led about at will. Therefore, regarding other words of that same kind, let there be a conceptualization of exactly that same sort. (320)

Furthermore, there is the well-known common usage among people, which is "the statement," yet that is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for such a sentence as: "One who desires heaven should offer the Agnihotra."
And from that, furthermore, there is the comprehension of the meaning: "Is this the desire for what is hated? (321)
What is called "established renown" is nothing other than common worldly report;
and since all those people are enveloped by ignorance such as passion and the like, their words regarding the true nature of things cannot be considered reliable.
Therefore, their common report is not an authoritative means of knowledge;
for in the absence of even a single instance of correct practice, mere abundance does not constitute meaningful proof.
Like the false conduct of a Persian mother,
there is again a comprehension of an object beyond the senses based on the words of those very persons;
how then can that same thing be simultaneously both detestable and desirable?
Now, if one disregards established consensus and engages in conceptual construction, there is no basis for it;
since established consensus is not a valid means of knowledge, what could be the basis for grasping it? (322)

If it is argued that there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) based on the well-known principle that "the occurrence elsewhere [of a cognition] through the reversal of what has been attained is joined with the perception of qualities and defects," we say no;
for attainment is characterized by the operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For any apprehension whatsoever belongs to one who does not accept common consensus as a means of valid cognition; it is a cognition by way of that [consensus],
because its attainment is precluded by logic.
Since the occurrence of conceptualization regarding self and other is equal in both cases, what is the point of conforming to common consensus?
Moreover, this—
Doubt regarding the ascertainment of the meaning of a word arises precisely from its established usage, because it is observed therein that words function with multiple meanings. (323)
The determination of a single meaning for words does not arise from common usage alone, because doubt originates from that very source;
for in the world, words are seen to have multiple meanings, and worldly discourse is based on conventional understanding. Therefore—
Since words have multiple meanings, it is not logical to restrict them to a single meaning.

Otherwise, because there is no impossibility [of other meanings] due to the inherent multiplicity of the word's capacities, those who do not perceive a restrictive factor must necessarily entertain doubt. (324)
This is an intermediate verse.

Therefore, regarding words whose distinctions of meaning are unknown, one who explains them after having determined a single meaning— which is beyond sensory contact and is a superimposition lacking a basis— [is acting erroneously].
We do not perceive any distinction between this [teacher] and other heterodox founders (tīrthakara), since we see that Jaimini, under the guise of that [system], has merely stated his own view.
For instance:
The verbal expression of one who is devoid of the activity of stating that meaning, by way of superimposing it upon it, does not surpass his own [actual] speech; rather,
by performing such an act, he would merely be illuminating his own false pretension.
For instance:
"This person says, 'This is a post; this is the path,'" while another says, "I myself say so. Let the difference between these two be examined. //325//

Whether one attributes an activity devoid of intention to an inanimate post by means of superimposition while teaching, or whether one accepts the speech as originating from an independent agent, there is no difference between the two cases except for the dullness of comprehension on the part of the insentient object.

Moreover, if there were a restriction to a single meaning, Jaimini would have known this; for from what source does such a restriction arise, whereby a word that is capable of [denoting] all things is restricted to the illumination of only one meaning?
For no meaning of a word is restricted by its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because it is capable of [denoting] everything;

and if it were incapable, then since that incapacity does not cease, it would be impossible for persons to bring about the application or removal of something that cannot be enjoined in any particular instance.
Or by whom could those things beyond the senses be known, except through the speaker's intention expressed in words? (326)
For when a word is composed by a person, it might at some time and in some place convey that [intended meaning] through a particular intention; thus,
for words preceded by intention, a restriction of meaning might indeed be perceived.

But in the case of that which is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), even if a restriction of meaning exists, how could it be known? Because there is no distinction in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Or, if such a distinction were present, it would be directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) by itself.
Because it would follow that there is cognition [of the object],
and because even if it were not perceived, it could not be known by anyone;
furthermore, there is no distinguishing characteristic [to differentiate them].
For all words are devoid of proximity or remoteness with respect to all objects; therefore,
the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) is the cause for restricting them [to a specific object], and linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is that which reveals it.
In that which is not of human origin, that [intention] does not exist; how then could it have that single meaning? //327//
For a word is restricted to an object by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not by its own nature (*svabhāva*),
because it is equal everywhere due to its lack of restriction in any particular case; even where there is a restriction, [it is still determined by intention].

Because there is no fixed rule for denoting those [senses], it would follow that all words could denote the sense organs; therefore, [the word "instrument"] has the characteristic of communicating the intention in order to manifest the speaker's desire to speak.
A convention is established [in the case of human speech].

However, in that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), there is neither intention to speak nor convention, because there is no one’s intention; thus, there is no restriction, nor is there knowledge thereof.
If there were a restriction by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it could not be applied elsewhere by that [nature] again.
If the word were inherently attached to objects independently of convention (*saṃketa*),
it has been stated in this regard that there would be no restriction because of the lack of a necessary connection (*apratibandha*).
Moreover,
if the relationship between the signifier and the signified were inherent, it could not be assigned at will according to one's desire by means of the speaker's intention.
Furthermore, linguistic convention would be purposeless;
for a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is accessible to the senses does not depend upon terminology and the like for its own cognition,
just as in the case of the distinction between blue and other colors.
However, cognitions that depend upon those [conventions] do not possess the nature of real entities.
What then? They are conventional, like royal insignia and the like;
and whatever is conventional—
It is illogical for that [word] to be restricted by intrinsic nature, because its operation proceeds according to one's will;
precisely because of that convention,
there is no specific intrinsic nature.
And how could there be a restriction regarding the individual manifestation? //328//
A convention (*saṃketa*) is a function according to one's own will; it can be established only here and not elsewhere, so there is no contradiction.
And that [convention], being created by persons according to their own will, applies to that very [object].
There is no restriction that it manifests its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and not another;
for where there is independence of will, what kind of restriction could there be? Therefore, the conventional designation (*saṃketa*) would not manifest only its intended fitness (*yogyatā*). //329//
This is an intermediate verse.
For it is said that since such a truth as "fire is cold" exists, another person has stated that other [statements] are also [unreliable] because they belong to a portion of the Veda. (330)

But another, rejecting the definition of scripture as being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), desiring to establish the authority of the Veda in another way, says: "The Vedic sentences are non-false,
because they belong to the same part of the Veda as those [sentences] regarding which there is no disagreement, such as 'fire is the enemy of cold'."
"The statement beginning with 'medicine' [is an example of] this [type of inference].

This [inference] is like [the case of] taste, because of the identity of form, and like [the case of] cooking in a single vessel. Such [an inference] as this is rejected by the knower of logic (nyāyavid) because it is fallacious, being [an instance of] *śeṣavat* [reasoning]. //331//

17322 Thus, by himself, the Teacher [Dignāga], while exposing the fallacy of the Naiyāyika’s *śeṣavat* inference, [provides] as a parallel case [the following]: just as when fruits of identical form are established to have identical taste because they were placed within the same vessel, so too is the cooking of rice grains that are unseen [inferred] from those that are seen.
And that which is stated as a proof is actually not a proof;
the reasoning regarding its lack of probative power has already been explained previously.
And this definition of scripture has been stated by us:

it applies to every object that can be investigated, such that— provided there is no necessary connection (nāntarīyakatva) between words and their referents— the establishment or negation [of a property] occurs through the respective means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for each case.

It is better for one who is in doubt to act toward that [object], because there is the possibility of non-contradiction at some point; it is not so for a person whose activity is elsewhere, where there is an obstruction by a perceived means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, regarding fire—which belongs to the domain of common experience—its capacity to counteract cold...
Having demonstrated that his own designation is for the sake of truth, he states that everything is for the sake of truth;
yet even regarding a subject that is capable of being determined, the treatise contains much that is improper due to contradiction with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[The opponent claims: "An eternal person (puruṣa) possesses agency; [he produces] entities that are eternal and beyond the senses, as well as those that are perceptible by the senses; he is the uneven cause of entities, and their existence is likewise uneven. (332)

And [one who] asserts cessation through the two means of valid cognition, or something else within their respective domains, or that which is contradictory [to what is established] by means of scripture or inference; //333//
Without resolving the contradiction and without demonstrating the meaning of the scripture, he who claims to know the truth might as well win a harlot through sheer audacity. //334//

"The person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is neither fallen away nor newly arisen, and who is without prior or posterior form, is the agent of actions and the enjoyer of the fruits of those actions by virtue of being the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) and the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and so forth"— thus says the Veda. But that is largely shown to be untenable, as is its [claim of] eternity.
For certain entities, it is illogical for that which is non-momentary to transcend the nature of things (*vastudharma*).

Indeed, universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are not themselves perceptible, yet they are said to produce, maintain, and cease; and these irregular states of things cannot belong to that which is incapable of action prior [to their arising] and to which no specific quality can be imparted.
The state of being a producer in relation to another, the persistence of that which is not of the nature of an effect by virtue of its substratum,
and destruction through a cause— these and other such matters are established as contrary to what is known through perception and inference by means of an inference based on scripture (*āgama*).

The capacity of the *agnihotra* and other such rites to purify sin and so forth is thereby sublated. For one who speaks thus, there is a contradiction with valid cognition throughout the entire body of the Veda; furthermore, [the Veda] fails to provide a resolution regarding its relationship [to reality], its suitability as a means, and its expression of human goals.

Without demonstrating the doctrines of the treatises, one who wishes to establish his own faultlessness merely by asserting truths concerning subjects that are extremely well-known— even in the profound depths that are difficult to fathom due to the excellence of wisdom—
triumphs with audacity even over a procuress. It is said that there was once a certain woman...

17429 A harlot, having been seen by her own husband at the place of their disagreement and rebuked by him, replied to him: "Mother, behold the perversity of this man toward me! 17430 [She said: "In me..."
Without placing trust in his lawful wife, he does not [place trust] in those two others called "his own," which are like water bubbles.
Although she was solicited by that Jaratkāṇa, a rustic wood-gatherer, she did not unite with him;
for it is said that [the king] was devoted to her because of her beauty and virtues, and [she was sought after] by the chief minister.
"I desire the boy"—

this kind of statement, even though it contradicts perceptible means of valid cognition through its claim to counteract the cold of fire, [is accepted] regarding that which is absolutely beyond the senses.
If [it is argued that] inference based on non-contradiction regarding the object would thus establish it as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then what here [is] not a valid means of knowledge?
For indeed, among a person who speaks much, there is not even a single word that possesses a true meaning. (335)
Just as this statement of absolute truth is extremely difficult [to establish], so too is the statement of absolute untruth. In that regard,
how could a single statement, which is indistinguishable from the former insofar as it possesses some degree of correspondence, [be considered true]?

If that mass of words were of such a nature [as you claim], then no person whatsoever would be untrustworthy. Furthermore, this sound does not constitute either the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or the effect (*kārya*) of things within the speaker.
And apart from that [inference], there exists no non-deviation [of a reason]. //336//
To begin with, this speech is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the things expressed;
nor is it their effect (*kārya*), because it exists even in the absence of those things, arising merely from the speaker's intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). Nor is it anything else.
Nothing is invariably concomitant with anything else;
and since it is possible for that [effect] to occur otherwise even when there is deviation, it is illogical to have a cognition of that [cause] based on its presence.
If it is argued that the activity of denoters is caused by the perception of the denoted, this may be so;
for speech is indeed the effect of the denoter’s activity consisting in the perception of the denoted.
This being the case:
How could that [cognition], which possesses mutually contradictory objects, exist in a single place? //337//
If this restriction must be asserted— that a word does not function without a real entity as its object—
then there would be no occurrence of speech through the application of contradictory natures to a single entity amidst conflicting doctrines.
For it is not possible for a single word to be both eternal and non-eternal without being synonymous; therefore,
the scriptures are in no way necessarily connected with real entities.
Since these [cognitions] are established for the cognizer, how can there be a determination of the object from them? //338//

An ignorant person seeks authoritative scripture (*āgama*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of understanding the objects revealed by it; this is because those who have realized the true nature of reality do not depend upon instruction, and because an ignorant person lacks the capacity to discern a person of qualities that transcend the senses (*atīndriya*). This is the case with all verbal expressions.

Even for those who observe that [words] function even in the absence of the existence of the intended object, there must necessarily be doubt regarding the speech of persons whose words have not been observed to deviate; one must wonder whether it is true or not. Therefore, it is not logical to derive anything from any such statement.
[It is] impossible to ascertain [it].
Therefore, even through its cessation, the non-existence of an entity is not established.
As it has been said: because scripture has all things as its object, it is non-contradictory when the thing exists.
"The non-apprehension characterized by the cessation of that [cognition's] activity establishes its non-existence.
This [non-apprehension] would occur even if that [cognition] had all things as its object, provided there were an obstruction by another thing;
however, such [an obstruction] does not exist. Therefore, it has been stated that for one who desires to understand [the object], [the cognition] is unestablished.
Therefore, non-apprehension, which has non-ascertainment as its result, is not established. //339//
Therefore, even when the three means of valid cognition are absent, there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of remote objects.
[The claim that] the Veda is authoritative, the assertion of a creator for some things,
the desire for merit in ritual bathing, and the arrogance of the doctrine of caste— [all these are baseless].
The onset of distress and the desire to abandon evil—these are the five signs of dullness when wisdom has been destroyed. //340//
Thus ends the first chapter of the Pramāṇavārttika.
